text:
BRANIFF HISTORY TODAY - On this day, Tuesday, November 7, 1978, Braniff International announced the largest expansion at Dallas/Ft. Worth Regional Airport since the massive airport opened amidst much fanfare in September 1973. The construction of a new half-circle dubbed The Braniff Terminal 3W was announced and would be connected to current The Braniff Terminal 2W with a Connector Building, which would exclusively house international flight operations.

The new Connector and Terminal 3W would be located directly south of Terminal 2W and its construction would mimic the existing terminal construction and horseshoe layout. A unique overhead people-mover system called Braniff Sky Shuttle (this is currently in operation at DFW but was redesigned to serve the entire airport replacing Airtrans) would join the existing terminal with the new Connector and Terminal 3W and would operate in addition to the current Airtrans system that would continue to serve the entire DFW Airport terminal and parking facilities. The new terminal would offer the same infrastructure as the existing terminal including the placement of passenger handling and departure lounges and gates on the second floor while the Airtrans, baggage handling, and airline office facilities would be located on the second floor.

Between 1980 and 1988, the new buildings were planned to be opened in various stages as traffic demanded. The new Connector Building was planned to be constructed first and open by 1980, and would primarily serve Braniff's growing international flights. However, because of American Airlines plan to build a traditional concourse layout, both airline's plans were delayed. The impressive three-story structure would house US Customs and Immigration offices on the upper level while international flight departure and arrival operations would operate from the second level. Baggage handling and airline operations activities would occupy the ground floor, which was also where the Airtrans system would stop to service the terminal.

Braniff's expansion at DFW was the direct result of the increase in the size of the airline and its capacity as a result of the enactment of the Airline Deregulation Act in October 1978. Eighteen new Braniff destinations were added in 1978 (18, not 500, 600, 800 or more routes that were incorrectly reported) alone because of the Act's loosening of restrictions of where airlines could fly and when. The addition of the new terminal space would increase the current aircraft handling capability of 24 to 47 aircraft including the simultaneous servicing of five Boeing 747 flights at any one time.

Soon after the new Connector Building was scheduled to be opened in 1980, the first phase of The Braniff Terminal 3W would be opened a year later during 1981. Additional sections of the terminal were scheduled to be open during 1982 and 1983, with all of the new facility in full operation by 1988. The third floor level of Terminal 3W would be reserved for additional international flight arrivals and departures. However, just as the concrete was being poured for the new Connector Building and terminal, Braniff announced additional expansion at DFW Airport.

The cost of the new Connector Building and Terminal 3W was estimated to be $45 million USD. This, combined with Braniff's current investment at the centrally located airport of $130 million USD, totaled an impressive $175 million USD, which was far greater by a wide margin than any other airline's investment at the airport. Braniff's current investment included the new $75 million USD Braniff Place World Headquarters campus on the west side of DFW Airport that opened on December 1, 1978, in addition to the original Terminal 2W, Braniff Flight Kitchen, Braniff Hangar One, and certain aircraft and ground equipment and servicing facilities.

At the time of the announcement, Braniff employed 12,500 worldwide with 6371 of those based in the Dallas/Ft. Worth area, making it the third largest employer in the Metroplex area. Braniff's local payroll was an astounding $136.7 million USD and the company purchased local goods and services that contributed an additional $120 million USD to the DFW economy.

A third passenger facility, The Braniff Terminal 4W, was announced in the spring of 1979, and would be located directly south of Terminals 2W and 3W. Again, Terminals 3W and 4W would be linked by a convenient Connector Building and the Braniff Sky Shuttle would be expanded to handle the additional facilities, which were scheduled to be fully operational by 1992. Terminal 4W would again mimic the original Terminal 2W and feature the same amenities and activities on each of the three levels. The new Connector Building would also handle additional international flights and could service 5 Boeing 747s at any one time. Braniff’s correct intention was to make DFW into one of the largest interior gateway international cities rather than using it primarily as a domestic operation.

Like many plans made by the nation's airlines either before or immediately following the Airline Deregulation Act, the addition of the new Connector Buildings and Terminals 3W and 4W were never completed. Construction was begun on the Connector Building and Terminal 3W concrete ramps but was discontinued during 1980, because of squabbles between the airport and American Airlines in addition to Braniff's financial problems that also prevailed throughout the industry. However, all deposits had been paid to the airport through 1981 for the construction of the new 2W/3W Connector Building, which would have given Braniff additional new space for expansion, which it greatly needed.

In 2005, the new International Terminal B (formerly 3W) was opened for business, which used the original Braniff ramp concrete that had been poured at the time the project was canceled. The overhead Braniff Sky Shuttle was built many years later but was renamed Sky Link, which served the entire airport and enabled the retirement of the venerable Airtrans system. In 2015, plans began for a new terminal at DFW, Terminal F, which was formerly Terminal 4W. In a special exclusive presentation, the DFW Airport Board revealed its plans for the new terminal at the Third Braniff History and Architecture Conference held in September 2019 at Braniff Place World Headquarters. However, with the onslaught of the COVID-19 epidemic in March 2019, the new terminal was canceled indefinitely.

However, a new Terminal F, utilizing American Airline's beloved "Tarantula Terminal" style of design (this will be discussed in a later post) was announced on May 1, 2025, and construction is now underway. A review of the current West Side terminal development that not only did the airport implement Braniff's Sky Shuttle train (now Sky Link) the Board approved and built the Terminal 2W Connector, now B, Terminal 3W, now D, Terminal 3W Connector and now Terminal 4W, now F, which were all proposed by Braniff Airways more than 40 years ago.

Photo: The excavation work for The Braniff Terminal 3W and International Connector Building was well underway by the end of 1978. A colorful array of Braniff jets are parked at the gate at the original Terminal 2W. Killeen, Texas, based Rio Airways had provided a yearly feed of 500,000 passengers into the Braniff system using its fleet of DeHavilland DHC-6 Twin Otter twin-engine turboprop aircraft. However, when construction began on the new terminal, they were moved from Terminal 2W to parking spaces on the outer ramp near the construction site. This created considerable inconvenience for Rio passengers and service was moved to another part of the airport. Cross-field rival Delta Airlines had offered Rio luxurious new passenger facilities in its terminal and Braniff's 500,000 yearly passenger feed evaporated over night (this will also be discussed in a later post).

Resurrect the temple of democracy

by Prabhu Chawla, 

According to PRS, the Lok Sabha functioned for a dismal 15 percent of its scheduled time in the Monsoon Session of 2026. It was perhaps the worst performance since the demonetisation winter of 2016. 

Democracy means government by discussion, but it is only effective if you can stop people talking,” Clement Attlee once observed. Were the old statesman to survey the current aerobics of Indian democracy, he might have revised his aphorism. The malady afflicting the world’s most populous democracy is not that its politicians talk too much, but that they have forgotten how to talk to one another. They scream endlessly from rally stages and through the shrill echo chamber of social media.

As an unfortunate fall out, one hallowed chamber built for that conversation stands sullen, silent and too often adjourned. Government by discussion has quietly mutated into government by denunciation. As a consequence, the talking democracy so painstakingly built by the republic’s founders is perilously close to becoming a fighting one.

The political shenanigans for the past few weeks symbolise degeneration. On November 2, Leader of the Opposition Rahul Gandhi, smarting from the Prime Minister’s barbed insinuation that forces within the country were peddling lies and fomenting instability, flung down a flamboyant gauntlet. He demanded an open debate with Narendra Modi, at any venue of the Prime Minister’s choosing. A day later he renewed the taunt, “Daro mat, debate me,” offering, with unmistakable irony, RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat as umpire.

The ruling establishment answered with a scornful counter challenge. Home Minister Amit Shah declared that the government was ready to summon a special session of Parliament on the electoral-roll revision and the incendiary ‘vote chori’ charge, provided the Congress let the House function.

The BJP president branded Rahul a “toolkit” of foreign forces, while the Gandhi scion accused the Prime Minister of holding office through foreign help. Each protagonist loudly invites the other to debate but none of them agrees on the venue.

The cold numbers of Parliament proceedings since 2024 tell the story more soberly than the overheated wrhetoric. According to PRS Legislative Research, the Lok Sabha functioned for a dismal 15 percent of its scheduled time in the Monsoon Session of 2026. It was perhaps the worst performance since the demonetisation winter of 2016.

Question Hour, that ritual of accountability, survived for a pitiful nine minutes, and nine of the 11 Bills the lower House passed sailed through without a single member other than the minister uttering a word. The previous Monsoon Session had forfeited more than 84 hours to forced adjournments, and the Winter Session of 2024 limped along at 52 percent in the Lok Sabha and a meagre 39 percent in the Rajya Sabha.

The pattern is shocking. Whenever politics turns poisonous, Parliament becomes its first and most defenceless casualty. The Treasury benches accuse the opposition of disruption and filibustering. The opposition replies with a bitter litany of rejected notices, muted microphones and the Leader of the Opposition denied the floor. Even urgent demands for discussing the electoral rolls, General Naravane’s unpublished memoir and the NEET leak are brushed aside by a brute majority that prioritises the passage of Bills over arguments. Both narratives hold a kernel of truth; neither holds the whole of it.

What has vanished is not merely civility and dignity but the delicate connective tissue of democratic life. The invisible connectivity through credible channels—like the discreet telephone call, the trusted emissary, the leisurely cup of tea in Central Hall, where bitter adversaries once quietly settled differences—has been snapped. Indian democracy was never a garden of genteel consensus and the Emergency remains its darkest chapter. Yet, even in fiercer times, parliamentary leaders and Prime Ministers kept the lines open.

Indira Gandhi reached out to opposition leaders when the nation went to war in 1971. Rajiv Gandhi, learning that Atal Bihari Vajpayee needed medical treatment abroad, quietly included him in a delegation to the United Nations, a kindness Vajpayee never forgot. P V Narasimha Rao sent the same Vajpayee, then Leader of the Opposition, to lead India’s delegation to Geneva in 1994 to defend the nation on Kashmir. Vajpayee governed through coalition and conversation, and Manmohan Singh shared with L K Advani, Sushma Swaraj and Arun Jaitley a courteous connect that survived the sharpest floor exchanges.

Behind them stood seasoned interlocutors—Pranab Mukherjee, Pramod Mahajan, Jaswant Singh, Sharad Pawar and others who brokered pragmatic compromises before crises hardened into deadlocks. Even in opposition, the Congress prided itself on keeping the door to dialogue ajar. Now, the new leadership in Congress communicates through abusive barbs and unfounded accusations.

Today that door has been closed. Sonia Gandhi and Rahul rarely share a social platform with Modi and Amit Shah. The vocabulary of politics has slid from adversary to enemy, from rival to traitor. The ruling party taunts that a Congress which has lost three successive Lok Sabha elections and around 90 state elections is now adopting a violent toolkit of regime change. Rahul has responded by a charge that the government survives on foreign favour and electoral sleight of hand. When opponents are recast as enemies, every compromise is condemned as capitulation and every handshake suspected as betrayal.

The bargain on which parliamentary democracy rests is elegantly simple: the opposition must have its say, and the government must have its way. Take away the first and majority rule curdles into majoritarian rule; strip away the second and principled argument hardens into sterile obstruction. Lose that balance and politics degenerates into a permanent campaign in which governance is the unpaid casualty, while unemployment, inflation and agrarian distress wait forlornly in the ante-room as non-issues.

Road shows and street protests are the new megaphones, serving as forums. They amplify, not adjudicate. A televised showdown between two leaders, however gripping, would be a poor substitute for a parliamentary debate governed by rules, preserved in records and concluded with a vote.

The proper arena for the questions is the floor of Parliament and of the state Assemblies. For that, both sides must make the sacrifice that power finds most painful: they must swallow their pride and subdue their egos.

The government must make generous room for the opposition’s agenda, admit adjournment motions, elect a long-overdue Deputy Speaker and treat the Leader of the Opposition as a constitutional office rather than a partisan nuisance. The opposition must accept that a House it paralyses can hold no one to account and must seize offers of debate rather than dismiss them as stagecraft.

History is unsentimental about such quarrels. It will not record who won the war of words on the street; it will record whether India’s leaders kept faith with the institutions entrusted to them. Parliament was not built as a stage for dueling egos but as a sanctuary for the nation’s argument with itself. If that sanctuary falls silent, the noise of the street will not be democracy; it will be its requiem. India’s leaders have mastered the confrontation; they must now relearn the conversation.

AI Overview
These three names share a deep linguistic and historical connection, primarily originating in Ancient Mesopotamia, the Middle East, and the Caucasus.
Sargon
Origin & Etymology: The name is the Greek and biblical translation of the Akkadian regnal name Šarru-kīn. It combines šarru (Akkadian for "king") and kīnu (meaning "true," "established," or "legitimate").
Historical Significance: It is most famously associated with Sargon of Akkad (24th century BCE), the legendary founder of the Akkadian Empire. Later, the Neo-Assyrian ruler Sargon II (8th century BCE) adopted the throne name to establish the legitimacy of his rule.
Sargis
Origin & Etymology: The name is the Classical Syriac and Armenian form of the Latin name Sergius. It originates from the ancient Roman gens (clan) Sergia, which etymologists suspect may connect to the Latin verb servare ("to guard" or "to preserve").
Sako
Origin & Etymology: Sako operates on a few different historical tracks depending on the region:
In the Middle East: Among Assyrians and Armenians, Sako is a popular, affectionate diminutive (or pet form) of the proper name Sargis.
In the Balkans: In Albania, it functions as a standalone occupational surname for a "church servant" or as a nickname for the Muslim name Isak (Isaac).
In Asia: It is also an unrelated Japanese surname (written as 佐古) meaning "HELP" and "ancient".

Sako
Surname (Assyrian/Chaldean): Derived as a pet form of the personal name Sargis (the equivalent of Sergius).

AI Overview
These three names share a deep linguistic and historical connection, primarily originating in Ancient Mesopotamia, the Middle East, and the Caucasus.
Sargon
Origin & Etymology: The name is the Greek and biblical translation of the Akkadian regnal name Šarru-kīn. It combines šarru (Akkadian for "king") and kīnu (meaning "true," "established," or "legitimate").
Historical Significance: It is most famously associated with Sargon of Akkad (24th century BCE), the legendary founder of the Akkadian Empire. Later, the Neo-Assyrian ruler Sargon II (8th century BCE) adopted the throne name to establish the legitimacy of his rule.
Sargis
Origin & Etymology: The name is the Classical Syriac and Armenian form of the Latin name Sergius. It originates from the ancient Roman gens (clan) Sergia, which etymologists suspect may connect to the Latin verb servare ("to guard" or "to preserve").
Sako
Origin & Etymology: Sako operates on a few different historical tracks depending on the region:
In the Middle East: Among Assyrians and Armenians, Sako is a popular, affectionate diminutive (or pet form) of the proper name Sargis.
In the Balkans: In Albania, it functions as a standalone occupational surname for a "church servant" or as a nickname for the Muslim name Isak (Isaac).
In Asia: It is also an unrelated Japanese surname (written as 佐古) meaning "HELP" and "ancient".

Sargon of Akkad (/ˈsɑːrɡɒn/; Akkadian: 𒊬𒊒𒄀, romanized: Šarrugi; died c. 2279 BC),[3] also known as Sargon the Great,[4] was the first ruler of the Akkadian Empire, known for his conquests of the Sumerian city-states in the 24th to 23rd centuries BC.[2] He is sometimes identified as the first person in recorded history to rule over an empire.

Sako
Surname (Assyrian/Chaldean): Derived as a pet form of the personal name Sargis (the equivalent of Sergius).

AI Overview
These three names share a deep linguistic and historical connection, primarily originating in Ancient Mesopotamia, the Middle East, and the Caucasus.
Sargon
Origin & Etymology: The name is the Greek and biblical translation of the Akkadian regnal name Šarru-kīn. It combines šarru (Akkadian for "king") and kīnu (meaning "true," "established," or "legitimate").
Historical Significance: It is most famously associated with Sargon of Akkad (24th century BCE), the legendary founder of the Akkadian Empire. Later, the Neo-Assyrian ruler Sargon II (8th century BCE) adopted the throne name to establish the legitimacy of his rule.
Sargis
Origin & Etymology: The name is the Classical Syriac and Armenian form of the Latin name Sergius. It originates from the ancient Roman gens (clan) Sergia, which etymologists suspect may connect to the Latin verb servare ("to guard" or "to preserve").
Sako
Origin & Etymology: Sako operates on a few different historical tracks depending on the region:
In the Middle East: Among Assyrians and Armenians, Sako is a popular, affectionate diminutive (or pet form) of the proper name Sargis.
In the Balkans: In Albania, it functions as a standalone occupational surname for a "church servant" or as a nickname for the Muslim name Isak (Isaac).
In Asia: It is also an unrelated Japanese surname (written as 佐古) meaning "HELP" and "ancient".

Sargon of Akkad (/ˈsɑːrɡɒn/; Akkadian: 𒊬𒊒𒄀, romanized: Šarrugi; died c. 2279 BC),[3] also known as Sargon the Great,[4] was the first ruler of the Akkadian Empire, known for his conquests of the Sumerian city-states in the 24th to 23rd centuries BC.[2] He is sometimes identified as the first person in recorded history to rule over an empire.

Birth legend
Sargon is also one of the many suggestions for the identity or inspiration for the biblical Nimrod. Ewing William (1910) suggested Sargon based on his unification of the Babylonians and the Neo-Assyrian birth legend.[75]

text:
RYU GA GOTOKU KENZAN: REQUESTS 35-50

These requests bridge Chapters 6 and 7. Several begin before they can be finished, so keep track of the nighttime events and the Washi Bundle needed for the chili-pepper treatment. Chapter-stage numbers follow KHHsubs.

35. How to Make Delicious Candy
From 6-3, any time to start. Speak to the confectioner at Gion Inari and choose top through the three choices to taste his candy and accept judging duties. At night, meet him outside Tsuruya at the north end of Gion. After the contest, inspect the magistrate's mansion southwest of the save point in the Yoshioka Dojo area, also at night. Defeat the group inside. Reward: 10,000 EXP. The next story-night opportunity after starting is 7-4.

36. The Chili Pepper Girl's Father
From 6-3, day/evening, after 11. Speak to the girl near Rakugai's northeast Gion entrance and choose top to visit her father. Get his Chili Pepper Set. Complete Request 47 for the Washi material, and buy Dried Algae from the turtle seller. At Gyotensai's house in northeast Gion, invent Chili Pepper Wet Cloth, selecting Dried Algae as the mystery ingredient. Give it to the father in his eastern Rakugai home during daylight. Wait three minutes, refresh the area, then meet father and daughter at the girl's stall. Rewards: Chili Pepper Wet Cloth and 1,500 EXP. Earliest story finish: 7-5.

Complete Commission 106 before starting this if possible; an unfinished Request 36 blocks it.

37. Return of the Enthusiastic Merchant
From 6-3, day/evening, after 24. Find Tanaka near Rakugai's northwest police box. Choose top to buy the Full-Stomach Gourd for 500 Mon; Arashi Yokan is included. Walk away to inspect it, then choose top to trade the gourd. Rewards: Copper Plate and 1,500 EXP. Refusing the trade gives Finished.

38. Today's Excuse
From 6-3, any time, after 37. Approach Ikkonya on Rakugai's northern street. During the conversation with the man's wife, choose middle, bottom, top, top, middle. Rewards: Lapis Lazuli and 1,000 EXP. Two or more incorrect answers give Finished and a Tortoiseshell Hairpin instead.

39. Sujitaro 1
From 6-3, any time. Bring a food item. Speak to the woman by Rakugai's southeast exit and choose top. Find Sujitaro at the bridge on southern Mountain Road and choose top to challenge him. This is an unarmed fight, but the logs and branches remain usable. After winning, choose top and give him food. Rewards: Vermilion Hairpin and 1,000 EXP.

40. Water from the Ladle #2
From 6-3, day/evening, after 21. Return to the house just north of Rakugai's eastern save point. Choose bottom when the samurai demand money and defeat both men. Reward: 1,000 EXP. You also receive 2 Ryo if you chose bottom in Request 18. The other Request 18 choices lose only this payment, not Complete.

41. Wish-Granting Sword
From 6-3, day/evening, after 19. Find Zenjiro and his audience in the eastern-central Rakugai lane below Ikkonya. Choose top and pay 100 Mon to try the sword. Defeat Zenjiro, then the three yakuza. Rewards: Mythical Beast Tome, a weapon recipe book, and 1,500 EXP.

42. Enchanted Sword: Senraibo
From 6-3, day/evening, after 19. Speak to Keisuke and Hanaoka at the western end of Kawara Street. Walk a little east to trigger the sword seller. Choose bottom to receive the blade free rather than paying 100 Mon. Give it to either merchant, then defeat both groups of attackers as the scenes unfold. Rewards: Senraibo and 1,500 EXP. Keep the sword for Request 20.

43. Enchanted Sword: Kanekuimushi
From 6-3, day/evening, after 19. Approach the crowd on Kawara Street below the path to Koetsu's mansion. Follow Kichiemon a little east and approach him again when he confronts the thugs. Defeat the four attackers. Rewards: 3 Ryo, Kanekuimushi and 1,500 EXP. This is another Request 20 sword.

44. Demon Extermination
From 6-5, day/evening, after 13. Speak to the collapsed man by Rakugai's southeast exit. Give him a Vitality Pill: Special Grade, available at Ecchuya. Other medicines will not work. Choose bottom to help. At his southwestern Rakugai house, inspect the door's hole and choose bottom to fetch food. Buy Mugwort Dango specifically from Riverside Tea House and return. Rewards: Potted Chrysanthemum and 1,500 EXP. Refusing the food errand ends as Finished.

45. Temple School Homework: Writing
From 6-5, day/evening, after 44. Return to Mametaro on Rakugai's southern street, west of the central southward lane. Choose top to help. The five answers are middle, middle, top, bottom, middle. Reward: 1,000 EXP.

The SECOND answer must be correct for Request 53's best outcome. The other answers do not affect that later condition, although getting every answer wrong gives Finished here.

46. Messenger from the Underworld
From 6-5, any time, after 45. Speak to the fortune teller on southeastern Rakugai's main road. The conversation leads to a fight against three swordsmen. Defeat them; you do not need to pay for her protection. Rewards: Pinzoro Tag and 1,000 EXP.

47. Talent
From 7-4, night, after 39. If you started Request 21, finish it first. On Forest Road, approach the attack roughly a third of the way east from Rakugai and defeat the samurai. Choose top to escort Kamotaro, bottom to offer to paint, then top to confront Kinzo. Defeat the bodyguard again, now using swordmaster moves. Rewards: Washi Bundle #1, Washi Bundle #2 and 1,500 EXP. Preserve the bundles for Requests 36 and 97.

48. The Ghosts
From 7-4, night, after 30. Speak to the merchant at Rakugai's northwest exit and choose top. Deliver his item to Heisuke on western Kawara Street, then return the money for 100 Mon. Head toward Kawara again and investigate the scream. Speak to the injured samurai on the eastern street, then the fleeing man near the bridge. Confront Benkei on the bridge. Win three rounds: Benkei, Ushiwakamaru, then both together. Rewards: Special Shintogo and 1,500 EXP.

49. The Dream White Snake
From 7-5, day/evening, after 36. Listen to the old woman in Rakugai's central northern alley. Find the snake near the southeast road, just below the eastern save point, and choose top to catch it. Choose top to give it to the boy, then defeat the merchant and his two followers. Reward: 1,500 EXP. Visit the tea-house employee at the northern end of River Road afterward for Tri-Colour Dango.

If you decline to catch it, it moves to the southwest road, then the southern central street, before looping back. KHHsubs also documents a bug: giving it to the merchant awards three Manju and three Yaki Dango, and visiting the tea house afterward changes Finished to Complete. The boy route avoids relying on that bug.

50. The Enthusiastic Merchant Tanaka Returns Again
From 7-5, day/evening, after 38. Visit Tanaka near the northwest Rakugai police box. Choose top to buy his Telepathy Box for 500 Mon, with a European Men's Scented Sachet included. When the foreigner appears, choose top to use the box. Rewards: Portuguese Hand Mirror and 10,000 EXP. Declining to use it gives Finished and loses the mirror.

text:
I asked AI if this story is true.  
👇👇👇
**No, it is not confirmed as true.** The X post accurately summarizes a *Daily Mail* exclusive, but the specific claims about a secret Camp David meeting are unverified and come only from that outlet’s anonymous sources.

### What the post claims
The post (by @Milajoy) says, citing the *Daily Mail*, that Susie Wiles planned a secret Camp David meeting for a day when Trump was in Florida, inviting her loyalists. The alleged goal was to figure out how she could survive the post-midterm period and hold onto power. It also says her allies tried to pin the GOP’s midterm losses on Pete Hegseth (over the Iran war).

### What’s confirmed vs. what’s not
- **Confirmed by multiple outlets**: After Republicans lost the midterms, Trump replaced Wiles as White House chief of staff with Stephen Miller (effective around Monday, November 9). Reporting from ABC, the *New York Times*, *Politico*, *The Atlantic*, and others says Trump was angry with her over the results, she offered her resignation, and Friday was effectively her last day. There are also reports of tensions involving Hegseth and the Iran war.
- **Only from the *Daily Mail***: The secret Camp David offsite for Saturday (while Trump was in Florida), the “survive the week and hang on to power” purpose, and the active scapegoating of Hegseth. These details appear in the *Daily Mail* story and pieces that recycle it (Raw Story, Times of India, etc.). No major U.S. outlets have independently confirmed the Camp David plot.

The *Daily Mail* has a mixed track record on White House/palace intrigue stories that rely on anonymous sources. Earlier in 2026, Wiles publicly dismissed a different *Daily Mail* report about her planning an exit as “Friday fiction.”

**Bottom line**: Wiles is out and Miller is in after the midterms. The colorful details about a secret Camp David survival meeting and throwing Hegseth under the bus are *Daily Mail* reporting only—not established fact. Treat them as unverified.

And I asked if the Daily Mail is as a reliable source ...

"**Not particularly, especially for unverified political intrigue.** The *Daily Mail* (and MailOnline) is a major British tabloid with a large audience, but it has a well-documented reputation for sensationalism, variable accuracy, and reliability problems.

### What independent evaluators say
- **Wikipedia**: In 2017, English Wikipedia editors banned the *Daily Mail* as a source in most cases, calling it “generally unreliable” due to “poor fact checking, sensationalism and flat-out fabrication.” That ban largely remains in place.
- **Media Bias/Fact Check**: Rates it Right-biased with “Mostly Factual” reporting and medium credibility in recent assessments. It notes a professional infrastructure and willingness to correct errors, but also recurring sensationalism, ideological framing, and multiple failed fact checks.
- **Ad Fontes Media**: Places it near the middle on bias but scores it for mixed reliability with wide variation (some solid reporting, some pieces containing inaccurate or fabricated information). Overall reliability scores typically land in the low-to-mid 30s out of 64.
- **AllSides**: Rates it Lean Right / Right-leaning.

### Common issues
The *Daily Mail* is known for:
- Dramatic, emotionally loaded headlines that sometimes overstate or misrepresent the story.
- Heavy reliance on anonymous sources for palace, celebrity, and political gossip (exactly the style of the Susie Wiles Camp David story).
- Science, health, and immigration pieces that have drawn repeated corrections or criticism from regulators (IPSO) and fact-checkers.
- A long history of high-volume complaints and occasional high-profile retractions.

It is not pure “fake news”—it has real reporters, breaks some legitimate stories, and publishes corrections. But its track record is inconsistent enough that major outlets and Wikipedia treat its exclusive claims with skepticism unless independently corroborated.

### Bottom line for the Wiles story
The specific details about a secret Camp David meeting to save her job and scapegoat Pete Hegseth come only from the *Daily Mail*’s anonymous sources. That fits the outlet’s pattern of colorful, hard-to-verify political reporting. Until other reliable outlets confirm it, treat those claims as unproven."

text:
You Are There: Leo Frank's Four-Hour Statement and His Pounding on the Wooden Jury-Box Railing

April 18 to 26, 1913: The Accounting Records That Would Become Frank's Defense

The National Pencil Company's business week ran from Friday through Thursday. Its financial statement for the week ending Thursday, April 24, 1913, covered business conducted from April 18 through April 24.

This becomes significant because Leo Frank's defense would later argue that his accounting duties kept him too busy to murder thirteen-year-old Mary Phagan on Saturday, April 26, 1913.

But examine the dates on those records.

Defendant's Exhibit 7, the factory's production records, contained figures for April 18, 19, 21, 22, 23, and 24. Herbert Schiff, Frank's chief clerk, testified that he had already entered the figures through Wednesday, April 23, leaving Thursday's entries and weekly totals unfinished.

Exhibit 2, the main financial statement, covered the week ending April 24. Exhibit 11, the comparison sheet for 1912 and 1913, was dated April 24, although Schiff testified that Frank completed it Saturday, April 26.

Exhibits 4A through 4D contained supporting reports from the packing, lead, and tipping departments.

Exhibit 10, the petty-cash receipt book, included transactions dated April 19, 21, and 24. Schiff said an April 21 kerosene purchase was not entered into the cash book until April 26. Exhibits 40 and 41 contained additional cash-book entries and calculations.

Customer orders also carried earlier dates. An F. W. Woolworth order was dated April 22, with an approval stamp dated April 23. A Beutell Brothers order was dated April 23.

Frank explained that these dates belonged to the original customer orders, which could have reached the factory April 26.

Exhibit 12, the house order book, recorded 11 orders, numbered 7187 through 7197, as received April 26.

The corresponding 11 requisition sheets, Exhibits 25 through 35, were identified in the Brief of Evidence as being in Frank's handwriting.

Yet The Atlanta Constitution, Tuesday, August 19, reported 12 requisitions dated April 26, one more than the official trial record identifies (AC, 2). That discrepancy remains unresolved.

These dates do not establish when Frank finished the paperwork. A report dated April 24 could be completed Saturday, while an earlier purchase could be entered into the books several days later.

Still, the records raise a question.

How much accounting work had already been prepared by Thursday or Friday, and how much did Frank personally have left to complete Saturday?

Schiff identified Frank's handwriting but admitted that he had not watched him prepare the documents April 26.

In the Brief of Evidence, Schiff acknowledged:

"I didn't see them done."

He testified that the records were completed sometime between Friday evening and Monday morning (BE, 1).

That established when the paperwork was finished, but not the exact hours Frank spent preparing it.

Saturday, April 26: A State Holiday and a Baseball Game

Saturday, April 26, was Confederate Memorial Day, a Georgia state holiday. The factory was closed for ordinary production, although Frank said he had financial work to finish.

He had also been invited to a baseball game by his brother-in-law, Charles F. Ursenbach, husband of Rosalind Selig, the older sister of Frank's wife, Lucille.

Ursenbach invited Frank on Friday, April 25. Frank was uncertain whether he could attend.

Around 1:30 p.m. Saturday, Frank telephoned the Ursenbach home and left a message canceling the outing.

At the coroner's inquest, Frank mentioned cloudy weather as a reason for not going. During his trial statement, he said unfinished accounting work kept him at the factory.

Both reasons could have influenced his decision.

But consider the circumstances. The business week had ended Thursday, most employees were off for the holiday, portions of the bookkeeping were already prepared, and Frank had been considering an afternoon baseball game.

How much work did he originally expect to have left, and when did he believe he would finish it?

Monteen Stover also testified that she entered Frank's office between approximately 12:05 and 12:10 p.m. and found it empty.

Frank maintained that he was in his office but acknowledged the possibility that he had briefly left to use the toilet.

The men's toilet was in the metal department, where the prosecution believed Mary Phagan was murdered. Frank did not say he definitely made that trip during Stover's visit.

On Monday, April 28, machinist Robert P. Barrett discovered suspected bloodstains and hair caught on a lathe in that department.

The prosecution identified the area as the murder scene. The defense disputed the meaning of those findings (BE, 1; AJ, 1).

The accounting records could show completed work, but they could not establish that Frank remained at his desk during the disputed period.

Monday, May 5: Frank Says the Financial Statement Ordinarily Took 90 Minutes

At the coroner's inquest on Monday, May 5, 1913, Frank answered questions under oath about his activities on the day of the murder.

The Atlanta Georgian reported his appearance beginning on page 1, with testimony continuing in its May 6 coverage.

Coroner Paul V. Donehoo asked:

"How long does it take to make the financial statement?"

Frank answered:

"About an hour and a half."

That is 90 minutes.

He added that the work took longer April 26 because Thursday's entries remained unfinished (AG, May 5–6).

Remember that answer. The defense would later introduce accountants whose estimates were considerably longer.

Monday, July 28: You Enter the Jury Box

Imagine yourself sitting in the front row of the jury box at the Fulton County Superior Court in Atlanta, Georgia.

Eleven other men sit alongside you. Together, you must decide whether Leo Frank murdered Mary Phagan.

A wooden railing separates you from the courtroom floor. To your right sits Judge Leonard Strickland Roan. Across the room to your left are the attorneys, with newspaper reporters seated farther to the left. Behind them, spectators fill the gallery.

Among those spectators are members of my family.

Although not every relative attended every session, numerous family members were present throughout the trial. They heard the testimony, followed the newspaper reports, and witnessed Frank's behavior firsthand.

Their memories would be passed down through our family for generations.

Friday, August 1: The Defense Explains Frank's Nervousness

Factory manager N. V. Darley describes Frank's condition on Sunday morning, April 27, following the discovery of Mary Phagan's body.

Darley says Frank appeared pale and upset. His hands trembled when he reached for an elevator rope. Later, while attempting to nail a basement door, he shook so badly that Darley took over.

The prosecution considered this behavior suspicious.

Defense attorney Reuben R. Arnold questioned Darley about Frank's usual temperament.

Darley said Frank became nervous almost daily, frequently rubbing his hands together, wringing them, or running his fingers through his hair.

Asked how often Frank became upset, Darley answered:

"Hardly a day goes by that he does not become nervous."

The Atlanta Journal, Friday, August 1, page 1 and continuations, reported this questioning under Lawyers Battle Over Testimony of Frank's Nervousness (AJ, 1).

Darley also recalled Frank becoming distressed after witnessing a little girl struck by a streetcar, leaving him unable to resume his bookkeeping for some time.

Another incident involved an argument with factory official Sig Montag, after which Frank reportedly trembled.

Mrs. Arthur White testified that Frank jumped when she spoke to him around 12:30 p.m. on Saturday, April 26.

The defense wanted the jury to believe this nervousness was part of Frank's ordinary personality.

Keep that testimony in mind when you watch him address the jurors.

August 9 to 12: The Defense's Three-Hour Accounting Argument

On Saturday, August 9, Herbert Schiff testifies about the factory's weekly financial work.

The Atlanta Georgian, Saturday, August 9, page 1, column 1, reports his testimony under Schiff Testifies for Frank.

Schiff maintains that completing the records ordinarily required approximately two and a half to three hours.

The defense argues that Frank had too much bookkeeping to complete to have murdered Mary Phagan.

But Schiff was absent April 26. He could identify unfinished entries and handwriting without personally accounting for Frank's movements that Saturday (AG, 1).

Tuesday, August 12: Pollard Says Three Hours and Eleven Minutes

Now consider C. E. Pollard, a certified public accountant employed by the American Audit Company.

It is Tuesday, August 12, 1913.

Pollard has been called by Frank's defense to determine how long the factory's calculations would take.

The Atlanta Journal, Tuesday, August 12, page 1, column 6, continuing on page 4, column 1, reports that Pollard reproduced the work using figures provided to him.

He worked continuously, without interruption, and timed the operations.

His result was:

3 hours and 11 minutes, or 191 minutes (AJ, 1, 4).

The Atlanta Georgian, Tuesday, August 12, page 65, column 7, also reported his testimony under State Charges Premeditated Crime.

Pollard said one sheet dated April 24 took ten minutes, while the full collection of tasks required 191 minutes. He acknowledged that someone familiar with his own books could work more easily than an outsider (AG, 65).

Another defense accountant, Joel C. Hunter, estimated approximately three to three and a half hours for the combined work.

Compare these figures with Frank's original estimate.

At the May 5 inquest, Frank said the financial statement ordinarily required 90 minutes.

Pollard's experiment took 191 minutes, an additional 101 minutes, or one hour and forty-one minutes plus.

The estimates did not necessarily concern identical tasks. Frank said Thursday's entries were unfinished, and Pollard included additional calculations.

Nevertheless, the difference deserved examination.

Were the accountants measuring what Frank actually had left to do April 26, or a larger collection of tasks, some already started by other employees?

And even if the work required three hours and eleven minutes, that would not prove Frank remained at his desk continuously.

Monday, August 18: Frank Takes the Witness Stand

It is Monday afternoon, August 18, shortly after 2 p.m.

You have spent three weeks listening to testimony.

Now Frank takes the witness stand with his prepared statement.

Under Georgia law, he can address the jury without taking an oath or answering questions from the prosecutor.

Judge Roan instructs the jurors to give his statement whatever weight they believe it deserves.

Frank begins calmly.

The Atlanta Constitution, Tuesday, August 19, page 2, column 1, describes much of his speech as delivered in:

"smooth, even tones" (AC, 2).

You might find this curious.

The defense has described Frank as someone who becomes nervous over ordinary workplace problems. Yet he appears composed while facing a murder charge that could cost him his life.

He had time to prepare his remarks, and people respond differently under pressure. Still, the contrast is noticeable.

My family remembered Frank sitting through much of the trial showing little emotion, almost like a stone monument.

When he finally addressed the jury, they saw a much more aggressive performance.

To them, Frank resembled a pushy salesman trying to convince a room full of businessmen.

Frank Approaches the Wooden Jury-Box Railing

Frank begins explaining invoices, requisitions, pencil shipments, financial statements, and production reports.

Then he gets up.

Frank leaves the witness stand and approaches your seat, carrying his accounting records.

He spreads the papers along the wooden railing separating him from the twelve jurors.

The Atlanta Journal, Tuesday, August 19, page 2 and continuations, described him:

"Laying his papers on the rail which fronts the jury box" (AJ, 2).

The reporter compared his manner to a businessman explaining figures to a customer across a desk.

But this is a murder trial. Frank is standing near the twelve men who will decide his fate, trying to convince them that bookkeeping kept him too busy to commit the crime.

Frank Pounds the Wooden Railing

While discussing the factory's requisitions, Frank becomes especially forceful.

He insists that he personally wrote them:

"I-wrote-these-requisitions!"

The Atlanta Georgian, Monday, August 18, page 29, column 1, described Frank emphasizing each word with a blow of his hand against the railing in front of the jury box (AG, 29).

Imagine sitting directly behind that wooden rail while the defendant strikes it repeatedly to make his point.

He has approached your seat, spread his financial records across the railing, and begun pounding the wood while defending his paperwork.

Would that convince you he was telling the truth, or would you find his behavior strange and unsettling?

My family watched from the gallery.

According to their eyewitness account, Frank paced frenetically across the open courtroom, much like a professor moving across the front of a lecture hall.

They remembered him becoming visibly agitated, slapping and striking the railing abruptly and repeatedly.

To my relatives, the restless movements and aggressive pounding resembled over-the-top Vaudeville stage theatrics.

The newspapers confirm Frank's approach to the jurors, his forceful gestures, and the blows against the railing. My family's account describes additional pacing during the statement.

These were the accounting records his lawyers claimed proved he was too busy to murder Mary Phagan.

The Dates on the Papers in Front of You

Now examine those documents.

Some contained figures from April 18 through April 24. Others concerned transactions recorded April 25 or April 26.

The comparison sheet, Exhibit 11, was dated April 24. The production records, Exhibit 7, covered several earlier days. Customer orders included April 22 and April 23.

Petty-cash records contained purchases from April 19 and 21.

The house order book recorded April 26 orders, and Frank claimed he personally prepared the corresponding requisitions.

Schiff and bookkeeper M. O. Nix identified his handwriting, but neither watched him write those documents Saturday.

You could believe Frank wrote the requisitions and still question exactly when he wrote them.

Completed records could establish that calculations were made. They could not prove the hour when each entry was written or that Frank remained at his desk throughout the day.

Pencils, Objections, and More Paperwork

Frank also holds up a long sample case containing pencils of different colors and styles.

He wants the jurors to understand the variety of products manufactured by the National Pencil Company and the complexity of its accounting.

But prosecutor Hugh M. Dorsey objects because the pencils have not been introduced into evidence.

Judge Roan sustains the objection.

Frank puts the case aside, smiles, and remarks that the jury has already seen enough to understand the different varieties.

Some spectators smile along with him (AG, 29).

Frank continues explaining invoices, time slips, factory orders, and financial calculations while the lawyers dispute certain documents that have not been properly introduced.

After one part of his presentation, The Atlanta Georgian reports:

"Frank went back to the stand."

He is offered water but declines it (AG, 29).

Throughout the afternoon, Frank moves between the witness stand and jury box, handling records and using his hands and voice to emphasize his claims.

The Newspaper Also Reports Frank Pacing

The Atlanta Journal, Tuesday, August 19, page 2, records another detail resembling my family's recollection.

During the noon recess August 18, a physician treated Frank's throat and nostrils.

The reporter described him pacing in an adjoining room while reviewing documents under the watch of a deputy sheriff.

He appeared slightly pale upon entering the courtroom, although his color reportedly returned (AJ, 2).

This pacing occurred during the recess. My family remembered additional movement while Frank addressed the jury.

Nearly Four Hours of Pencil Calculations

Imagine sitting through nearly four hours of Frank explaining invoices, payroll records, production totals, pencil shipments, and financial statements.

He describes how figures are copied between sheets, totals calculated, and factory products accounted for.

For jurors unfamiliar with the company's bookkeeping, it could become a long, tiring lecture.

You are there to decide a murder case, yet much of the defendant's statement concerns accounting.

My family remembered the explanations as painfully dull. According to their recollection, some spectators grew restless, looked annoyed, and struggled to stay awake.

The claim that three of Frank's four hours concerned accounting remains an estimate. The complete statement would have to be measured to establish that figure.

Nevertheless, newspaper reports confirm that financial records occupied a substantial part of his presentation.

Frank wanted the jury to believe his duties left him without enough time to murder Mary Phagan.

Yet much of the work he discussed concerned the afternoon, while Mary Phagan entered the factory shortly after noon.

The paperwork could show what Frank claimed to have completed. It could not establish exactly where he was during the critical period.

Frank's Denials and the Emotional Ending

Frank also addresses the prosecution's claims about his nervousness.

He explains that officers awakened him early Sunday morning, that he had not eaten breakfast, and that police took him to see Mary Phagan's body.

He argues that almost anyone would have been upset under those circumstances.

Frank denies Jim Conley's accusations concerning his involvement in the murder and the movement of Mary Phagan's body. He also rejects claims about his conduct with women at the factory (AC, 2–3).

By approximately 6:05 p.m., Frank has spoken for nearly four hours, including brief interruptions.

Near the end, he declares:

"Gentlemen, I have told the truth, the whole truth" (AC, 3).

He leaves the stand.

The Atlanta Journal reports approximately ten seconds of silence.

Lucille Frank begins crying. As her husband returns to his seat, she embraces him and sobs against his shoulder.

His mother kisses him repeatedly while he tries to comfort his wife (AJ, 2; AC, 3).

Some reporters believe Frank has made a convincing statement.

My family, watching from the gallery, remembers a different performance.

Wednesday, August 20: Gantt Gives Another 90-Minute Estimate

Two days later, former factory employee J. M. Gantt takes the witness stand.

It is Wednesday, August 20, 1913.

Solicitor Dorsey asks whether Gantt has personally watched Frank prepare the weekly financial statement.

Gantt says he has.

Asked how long it took, he answers that, with the necessary figures available, Frank could complete the sheet in approximately an hour and a half. 

The Atlanta Constitution, Thursday, August 21, 1913, page 2, reports the testimony under Swears That Frank Prepared Sheets in Less Than 2 Hours.

Gantt tells the court:

"With the data at hand, I have seen him make it out in an hour and a half" (AC, 2).

That is 90 minutes, the same ordinary figure Frank gave at the May 5 inquest.

Consider the testimony chronologically.

On Monday, May 5, Frank estimated approximately 90 minutes.

On Saturday, August 9, Schiff supported a longer estimate of two and a half to three hours.

On Tuesday, August 12, Pollard testified that his accounting experiment took exactly 191 minutes, while Hunter estimated approximately three to three and a half hours.

Then, on Wednesday, August 20, Gantt said he had personally watched Frank complete the financial sheet in 90 minutes when the figures were ready.

The estimates did not necessarily cover identical tasks. Frank said Thursday's entries remained unfinished, while the defense accountants included additional calculations.

But the question remains.

How much of Pollard's 191-minute workload did Frank actually have left to complete April 26, and how much was already prepared?

Pollard worked continuously without interruption. Frank's own account included movements away from his office, breaks, and work performed at different times.

Even if the calculations required 191 minutes, that would not establish that Frank remained at his desk for three hours and eleven minutes.

Monday, August 25: The Jury Reaches Its Verdict

Now return to your seat behind the wooden railing.

You have heard Frank explain his factory duties, display pencils, defend his handwriting, and deny the charges.

You watched him approach the jury with accounting papers and slap the railing while insisting that he wrote the requisitions.

You examined records dated April 18, 19, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, and 26. Some covered earlier business, while other employees had already prepared portions of the calculations.

You remember Frank's own 90-minute estimate, Pollard's 191-minute accounting experiment, and Gantt's testimony that he had seen Frank complete the financial sheet in an hour and a half.

You also recall the defense describing Frank as naturally nervous, although reporters portrayed much of his statement as calm and controlled.

Did those records prove Frank was too busy to commit murder, or did they leave questions about when the work was performed and where he was when Mary Phagan disappeared?

My family remembered his restless pacing, aggressive gestures, repeated pounding, and long bookkeeping explanations as over-the-top courtroom drama.

The Atlanta newspapers documented several of these actions but often described his speech more favorably.

Their reporters were covering a bitterly fought murder case with strong feelings on both sides. They had to walk a fine line when describing Frank's performance to their readers.

The way a correspondent judged his behavior was not necessarily how the jurors and spectators experienced it.

We cannot know precisely what each juror thought. His gestures and nervousness alone could not establish guilt. But those twelve men had to decide whether his account matched the evidence.

On Monday, August 25, 1913, the jury returned its verdict: guilty.

My family remembered Frank's four-hour performance for generations.

They saw him approach the jury, spread financial papers across the railing, and pound the wood while defending calculations that supposedly left him without enough time to commit murder.

90 or 180?

But the dates on the records, the work already performed by other employees, Frank's 90-minute estimate, Pollard's 191-minute experiment, and Gantt's matching 90-minute testimony raised the same question: How much work did Frank actually perform April 26, and could it account for his whereabouts during the murder?

No amount of pounding on the wooden railing could answer that question.

References

AJ: The Atlanta Journal. (1913, Thursday, July 31). Machinist tells of finding blood, hair and pay envelope on second floor, where state claims girl was murdered (p. 1 and continuations). https://t.co/MbSXvnEstK

text:
THE SLAVE AND THE GOLDEN CHAIN.

In ancient Rome, there lived a wealthy merchant who possessed everything a man could desire.

His home was adorned with marble columns, his tables overflowed with delicacies, and servants attended to his every command.

Among them was an elderly slave who owned nothing but a worn tunic and a small wooden cup.

Each morning, the merchant observed the old man tending the courtyard garden.

He worked quietly, greeted the sunrise with gratitude, and appeared strangely content despite possessing neither wealth nor freedom.

One afternoon, the merchant summoned him.

"Tell me, old man, how is it that you smile while living in servitude?"

The slave bowed his head.

"Because, master, there are things you may command of me, and things you cannot."

The merchant laughed.

"I own your labour, your dwelling and the very clothes upon your back. What could possibly remain beyond my authority?"

"My judgment," replied the slave.

The merchant's expression hardened.

"Your judgment?"

"You may command my hands to work, but you cannot command my heart to hate the labour. You may deny me possessions, but you cannot force me to envy those who possess them. You may confine my body, but you cannot decide what meaning I give to my circumstances."

The merchant regarded him with disbelief.

"Then you consider yourself free?"

"In the ways available to me, I endeavour to be."

The merchant shook his head.

"Foolish old man. Freedom belongs to those who possess power."

The slave lowered his eyes.

"As you say, master."

Years passed.

The merchant's wealth multiplied, but so did his fears.

He feared losing his fortune.

He feared betrayal by his associates.

He feared the admiration of men whose approval he desperately desired might one day disappear.

Every insult disturbed his sleep.

Every rumour threatened his peace. 

Every rival's success became a wound to his pride.

Meanwhile, the elderly slave continued tending the garden.

One evening, after learning that a rival merchant had acquired a greater fortune, the master stormed into the courtyard.

He found the old man sitting beneath an olive tree, watching the sunset.

"How can you sit there so peacefully?" the merchant demanded. "Do you not understand how little you possess?"

The slave looked towards him.

"Master, may I ask you something?"

"Speak."

"If a man wears a golden chain around his neck, does the gold make him free?"

"Of course not."

"And if another wears an iron chain, does the iron determine the condition of his mind?"

The merchant hesitated.

The slave continued.

"You possess estates, ships and treasures, yet your happiness depends upon the opinions of men you cannot control. You are troubled by fortunes you have not lost and enemies who may never come."

He paused.

"I possess almost nothing. Yet I have learned not to surrender my inner life to every circumstance that visits me."

The merchant looked down at the magnificent gold necklace resting upon his chest.

For the first time, its weight seemed unbearable.

"Then tell me," he whispered, "which of us is truly enslaved?"

The old man did not answer immediately.

Instead, he lifted his wooden cup and offered the merchant a drink of water.

"That, master, is a question only you can answer."

Beneath the fading Roman sun, two men sat together.

One wore the garments of a slave.

The other wore the garments of a master.

Yet only one had learned that the mind could become a prison long before the body ever encountered a chain.

A MAN MAY POSSESS THE WORLD AND STILL BE ENSLAVED BY HIS DESIRES. 

ANOTHER MAY POSSESS NOTHING AND YET PRESERVE AN INNER FREEDOM NO MASTER CAN BESTOW.

𝐓𝐇𝐄 𝐑𝐀𝐓 𝐏𝐀𝐂𝐊 𝐈𝐒 𝐁𝐀𝐂𝐊: 𝐃𝐄𝐌𝐎𝐂-𝐑𝐀𝐓𝐒 𝐀𝐓 𝐓𝐇𝐄 𝐆𝐀𝐓𝐄!

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐓𝐰𝐨-𝐏𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐲 𝐌𝐞𝐫𝐫𝐲-𝐆𝐨-𝐑𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐝: 𝐖𝐡𝐲 𝐀𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐚 𝐊𝐞𝐞𝐩𝐬 𝐂𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐆𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐛𝐮𝐭 𝐍𝐨𝐭 𝐈𝐭𝐬 𝐏𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐥 𝐒𝐲𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐦

In 2024, the American people threw the Democrats out of power over economic frustrations, immigration problems, the culture wars, and the incompetence of the Biden administration.

In 2026, the political pendulum has swung the other way and the Democrats control both houses of Congress. The American people have thrown the Republicans out of power—at least in Congress. The reasons: cost of living, Iran war, corruption, tariffs and immigration enforcement tactics.

The political irony is hard to miss. In 2024, Americans voted out the Democrats because they were dissatisfied with the direction of the country.

In 2026, they voted out the Republicans for precisely the same reason.

So, what exactly is going on? Is there something wrong with the American people, who keep throwing one set of rascals out only to bring the other set back in, apparently expecting a different result?

Or is the problem that neither the Democratic nor the Republican Party is genuinely serving the interests of ordinary Americans?

Could it be that both parties need young, fresh leadership accountable to the people instead of the entrenched, corrupt, self-serving, out-of-touch and out-of-reach elites?

How about a third party to enter the ring and give the two ne’er-do-well parties a real run for their money?

The fact remains that both parties serve corporate, financial, wealthy, and organized political interests.

The old adage holds that “there is not a difference worth a hill of beans between Republicans and Democrats.” They pretend to be ideological adversaries,  but that is often a distinction without a meaningful difference.

𝐋𝐢𝐤𝐞 𝐓𝐰𝐞𝐞𝐝𝐥𝐞𝐝𝐮𝐦 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐓𝐰𝐞𝐞𝐝𝐥𝐞𝐝𝐞𝐞, 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐲 𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐮𝐞 𝐟𝐢𝐞𝐫𝐜𝐞𝐥𝐲, 𝐚𝐜𝐜𝐮𝐬𝐞 𝐞𝐚𝐜𝐡 𝐨𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐨𝐟 𝐝𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐨𝐲𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐀𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐚, 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐦𝐢𝐬𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐡 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐬𝐤𝐲. 𝐁𝐮𝐭 𝐢𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐛𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐚𝐬 𝐮𝐬𝐮𝐚𝐥.

𝐑𝐞𝐦𝐢𝐧𝐝𝐬 𝐦𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐰𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐓𝐰𝐞𝐞𝐝𝐥𝐞𝐝𝐞𝐞 𝐬𝐚𝐢𝐝 𝐭𝐨 𝐓𝐰𝐞𝐞𝐝𝐥𝐞𝐝𝐮𝐦 𝐚𝐟𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐡𝐞 𝐥𝐨𝐨𝐤𝐞𝐝 𝐚𝐭 𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐰𝐚𝐭𝐜𝐡, “𝐇𝐚𝐥𝐟-𝐩𝐚𝐬𝐭 𝐟𝐨𝐮𝐫. 𝐋𝐞𝐭'𝐬 𝐟𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭 𝐭𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐬𝐢𝐱, 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐧 𝐡𝐚𝐯𝐞 𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐧𝐞𝐫.” 𝐈𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐩𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐥 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐛𝐲 𝐝𝐚𝐲 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐧𝐞𝐫 𝐭𝐨𝐠𝐞𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐛𝐲 𝐧𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐝𝐞𝐦𝐨𝐜𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐫𝐞𝐩𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐧𝐬 𝐢𝐧 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐠𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐬.

So it is with the musical chairs politics in the US. One side wins; the other loses. New guys show up at the office and recycle old promises and go about business as sual.

The real issue is not who controls Capital Hill or the White House. It is the “rigged political system” where the American people are offered the illusion of two parties who are two sides of the same coin.

𝐓𝐰𝐨 𝐏𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐢𝐞𝐬, 𝐎𝐧𝐞 𝐏𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐥 𝐄𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐢𝐬𝐡𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭

Both Republicans and Democrats suck at the corporate and special-interest trough. They use powerful lobbying groups and the wealthy to finance their campaigns. In turn, they auction access to government officials to the highest bidder like two-dollar hookers.

𝐃𝐞𝐦𝐨𝐜𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐑𝐞𝐩𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐧𝐬 𝐩𝐫𝐞𝐭𝐞𝐧𝐝 𝐭𝐨 𝐜𝐥𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐭𝐚𝐱𝐞𝐬, 𝐡𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐭𝐡 𝐜𝐚𝐫𝐞, 𝐢𝐦𝐦𝐢𝐠𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧, 𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐫𝐠𝐲, 𝐞𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧, 𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐞𝐢𝐠𝐧 𝐩𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐜𝐢𝐞𝐬, 𝐞𝐭𝐜. 𝐁𝐮𝐭 𝐢𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐚𝐥𝐥 𝐚𝐧 𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧, 𝐞𝐥𝐚𝐛𝐨𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐥𝐲 𝐜𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐩𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐥 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐟𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧.
"He who pays the piper calls the tune." When politicians rely on fat cats and organized interests to fund their campaigns, who gets heard? and who gets the shaft?
“Money is the mother’s milk of politics.” Money has more influence than votes in American politics. Money talks, and the bigger the money, the louder its voice, even compared to millions of voters.

Elon Musk dumped $500 million in an effort to sway the 2026 midterm elections. He failed. He has since flexed his political muscles on X, threatening Democrats: “Live by the sword, die by the sword… I will find out who is really pulling the strings and come for them, not just their puppets.”

Such is the hubris of filthy lucre!

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐦𝐚𝐢𝐧 𝐝𝐢𝐬𝐚𝐝𝐯𝐚𝐧𝐭𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐃𝐞𝐦𝐨𝐜𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐬 𝐢𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐢𝐫 𝐟𝐚𝐢𝐥𝐮𝐫𝐞 𝐭𝐨 𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐧 𝐟𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐥𝐞𝐬𝐬𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐨𝐟 𝐞𝐥𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐚𝐥 𝐝𝐞𝐟𝐞𝐚𝐭. 𝐋𝐢𝐤𝐞 𝐚 𝐜𝐡𝐢𝐥𝐝 𝐰𝐡𝐨 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐬 𝐛𝐚𝐜𝐤 𝐭𝐨 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐝𝐢𝐫𝐭 𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧 𝐚𝐟𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐛𝐞𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐜𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐧𝐞𝐝, 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐲 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐭 𝐭𝐨 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐬𝐚𝐦𝐞 𝐭𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐬 𝐨𝐟 𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐲𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐛𝐥𝐚𝐦𝐞 𝐠𝐚𝐦𝐞, 𝐬𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐛𝐛𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚𝐦𝐨𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐬𝐞𝐥𝐯𝐞𝐬, 𝐯𝐢𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐦𝐢𝐳𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐨𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐬, 𝐨𝐛𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠, 𝐫𝐞𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐨𝐥𝐝 𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐩, 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐜𝐡-𝐡𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐬.

They were defeated in 2024 because they did not get the memo, “It is the economy stupid!” They did not realize the country’s need for a fresh start. What the democrats  need is renewal, reformation, and new leadership but they are frozen in establishment politics that made them lose time and again.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐑𝐞𝐩𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐧 “𝐀𝐬𝐬-𝐊𝐢𝐜𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠” 𝐢𝐧 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔: 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐒𝐚𝐦𝐞 𝐏𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐥 𝐌𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐤𝐞𝐬

In 2024, the Republicans gave the Democrats an ass-kicking.

In 2026, Senator Ted Cruz fumed over the fact that Republicans had taken “an ass-kicking” and placed much of the blame at Trump's feet.

Winning an election is not the same as delivering on campaign promises.

It is all about the money. There ain't a damn thing funny.

Both parties suck the teats of the corporations. They stage the same old political drama of recrimination at election time. Each party claims to possess the answers. So, the beat goes on.

Ordinary Americans suffer, while the politicians sing, “la-di-da-di-da...” Then the voters deliver the usual ass-kicking, and the merry-go-round starts again.

As the old saying goes, “The best-laid plans of mice and men often go awry.”

So it was with Trump's political calculations. Voters who deliver power can just as readily take it away. But that is a lesson lost on both parties.

𝐀𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐚'𝐬 𝐓𝐫𝐮𝐞 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐛𝐥𝐞𝐦: 𝐀 𝐆𝐞𝐫𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐨𝐜𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐲!

America has a gerontocracy problem. Too many old geezers from both parties are clinging to power. They have turned politics into a lifetime job rather than a civic service. Their aim is to preserve their political careers and build walls to keep the younger generation out.

The contrast is striking: Approximately 51% of Americans are under 40 years old. Yet, at the opening of the 119th Congress in January 2025, the average age of members of the House of Representatives was about 58, and that of senators was 64.

It is not just about age. It is about genuine political representation, institutional rejuvenation, and the future of America. America needs a political system that reflects the demographic distribution of its population.

𝐀𝐟𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐧 𝐇𝐮𝐦𝐚𝐧 𝐑𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐖𝐡𝐢𝐭𝐞 𝐋𝐢𝐛𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐥 𝐃𝐞𝐦𝐨𝐜𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐬: 𝐀𝐟𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐚 𝐃𝐨𝐞𝐬 𝐍𝐨𝐭 𝐍𝐞𝐞𝐝 𝐖𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐧 𝐒𝐚𝐯𝐢𝐨𝐫𝐬

I detest the hypocrisy and double-dealing of white liberal Democrats in the U.S. Congress and White House, as well as some of their Black lackeys, who try to pass themselves off as Africa’s protectors and saviors in the name of “human rights, freedom, and international accountability.”

They lecture African governments, threaten sanctions, and apply diplomatic pressure over alleged human rights violations while turning a deaf ear and blind eye to injustices and human rights violations in America.

The Biden administration’s treatment of Ethiopia illustrates how human rights can be selectively weaponized to try and effect regime change.

What I find the most offensive is the arrogant paternalism of white liberal democrats.

These self-appointed moralizing guardians have the gall to define Africa’s political aspirations, prescribe its institutions, and influence its domestic choices.

They seek to cultivate influence among African political, intellectual, and cultural elites while advancing ideological agendas that often disregard Africa’s history, cultures, institutions, and right to determine its own future.

Martin Luther King Jr.’s criticism of paternalistic white liberalism remains relevant to African human rights.

MLK understood that the white moderate, who professed support for equality but resisted meaningful change, could obstruct Black liberation almost as effectively as the segregationist.

The same lesson applies to Western liberals who claim to champion Africans while presuming to speak for them, define their aspirations, and dictate their political choices.

Africa does not need holier-than-thou pontificators. It does not need self-appointed guardians and supervisors of morality. Africa needs equal partners who can do business with them.

𝐓𝐫𝐮𝐦𝐩’𝐬 𝐏𝐨𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧: 𝐍𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐥 𝐒𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐢𝐠𝐧𝐭𝐲 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐍𝐨𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞

I agree with Trump’s approach. America is not Africa’s human rights policeman. African countries must have the primary responsibility and authority to address their own domestic political and human rights challenges.

In July 2025, Secretary of State Marco Rubio instructed U.S. diplomatic missions to refrain from public pronouncements on the fairness, integrity, or legitimacy of foreign elections unless a compelling American interest justified such statements.

By doing so, Trump acknowledged African sovereignty. He set the example for Europeans also. Foreign governments should not presume that they have the moral or political authority to grade another country's political system or dictate its domestic priorities.

Africans can govern themselves.  African solutions to African problems.

𝐄𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐨𝐩𝐢𝐚: 𝐀 𝐔𝐒 𝐒𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐠𝐢𝐜 𝐏𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐧𝐞𝐫, 𝐍𝐨𝐭 𝐚 𝐂𝐥𝐢𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐭𝐞

Ethiopia has been forced to play the role of friend, foe, and frenemy under various American administrations.

Under the Bush administration, Ethiopia became a frontline American partner in the Global War on Terror, sharing intelligence and cooperating in military training and counterterrorism.

The Biden administration was hellbent on regime change in Ethiopia. It imposed sanctions and economic pressure against Ethiopia.

During the 2020–2022 terrorist war in Ethiopia, Biden applied diplomatic pressure, imposed sanctions and visa restrictions, limited defense assistance, and suspended Ethiopia's eligibility for AGOA trade preferences. All to support the terrorist TPLF.

Ethiopia is indispensable to American interests as the second-most-populous African country and host of the headquarters of the African Union. Ethiopia plays a pivotal role  in regional security, counterterrorism, peacekeeping, and Horn of Africa stability. It also offers substantial opportunities for American investment in agriculture, energy, manufacturing, infrastructure, technology, and mining.

𝐓𝐫𝐚𝐝𝐞, 𝐍𝐨𝐭 𝐀𝐢𝐝, 𝐍𝐨𝐭 "𝐇𝐮𝐦𝐚𝐧 𝐑𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭𝐬"

U.S.-Ethiopia relations under the second Trump

administration have been much better.

In May 2026, the two countries held a structured dialogue on trade and investment, defense and security, and regional peace, offering an opportunity to rebuild the relationship around practical mutual interests.
The bottom line is that Ethiopia needs America as a partner, not as a patron or guardian. It certainly does not need American lectures on human rights.

American administrations must respect Ethiopian sovereignty, recognize its national interests, and pursue a relationship based on mutual benefit and equal partnership.

text:
Trump Keeps Spiraling On Iran

Trump told the CPAC crowd that Iran “is not a war” but a “minor military operation.” How Putin-esque.

On the tarmac he said World War I and Russia-Ukraine are wars, “we’re not fighting,” and then added that the U.S. is “maybe an occupier.” He also claimed nobody had been wounded in six months, which is false. That’s a disgrace to the service members who have been hurt.

The same day, CENTCOM launched Task Force Iron Gate, described as an operation to isolate Iran by land. Per CENTCOM’s own release, it’s a roughly 20-person staff in Tampa coordinating efforts to block weapons and revenue across Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea. Adm. Brad Cooper, who recently launched a podcast where he talks about French fries, touted the “ironclad blockade.” CENTCOM also posted a Rewards for Justice offer of up to $20 million for information on Iran’s nuclear program, complete with Signal tip lines. Weren’t we told that program was obliterated last year? Iran had no path to a nuke under the Obama-era deal with IAEA inspections, until Trump pulled out of it in his first term.

Iran, meanwhile, opened its IRGC Aerospace Park to the public to show off its missiles, and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi contacted 12 countries in 48 hours, including Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Turkey and the UAE. Mohsen Rezaee, a top adviser to Iran’s Supreme Leader, taunted Washington that the U.S. lost “the war and the election” and mocked Cooper as a podcaster. Humiliating.

Mike Huckabee, Trump’s ambassador to Israel, said opposition to the war is “spiritual darkness” and that Satan has blinded those minds. The American people disagree. Per a chart from Stephen Semler using YouGov/Economist data, Iran is the only war on record that started with negative support, and it’s now at negative 32, below Vietnam’s low point.

That’s where we stand. If you haven’t yet, grab a copy of WTF America?!, the book I wrote with my brothers about how we got into this hell and how we get out. I appreciate every one of you.

— Actually Brett Meiselas
