text:
Penny the cat has been missing since last night. The van leaves at dawn. The house has been searched twice, and the dryer once. Then Theo leans into the van for one last look - and there she is. 🐈

"Found her. She didn't run away - she picked her seat."

Today the Everydays hit the road for real.

The Everydays, Episode 2: "What Percent There?" Chapter 1: Rain Check.

It is barely light in Seattle. Bluebell's side door stands open, and Theo, in his black hoodie, leans in with one hand on the door frame and the other pointing at the third row. There, on top of his own black backpack, Penny lies curled into a perfect circle, her tail over her nose, both eyes shut, as content as a cat can be.

She was never lost. She simply chose the seat she liked best, right beside the most interesting thing in the van.

That would be Dime. The family's big pet squirrel sits up in his roomy wire travel cage, buckled onto the same seat, wide awake and wearing his black sunglasses at dawn, as if the sunrise were already too bright. In both front paws he holds a cracker pressed to his cream chest. It is from Marcus's snack bag. Marcus does not know this yet. Dime is saving it for later. Dime saves everything for later.

Before anyone starts the engine, the day's check. Laura is driving the first leg, and in this family the driver never touches a phone. So Theo slides into the passenger seat and runs the free Commute Check for the road ahead to Portland. It reads the forecast for the way you are going - rain, wind, ice - hour by hour.

"Portland, next 12 hours: 27% chance of rain."

That number is real. It comes from the National Weather Service's hourly forecast for Portland, issued in the small hours of this Sunday morning. Across the next 12 hours, the chance of rain tops out at 27%, early, right around first light. Then it slides down through the late morning and sits low all afternoon.

For a family on the road, that reads like a typical gray Northwest morning: maybe a passing shower near the start, wet pavement either way, and a drier afternoon. It means headlights on, wipers ready, a little more room behind the car in front, and nobody in a hurry on the on-ramp. It does not mean staying home.

Laura nods, both hands resting on the bottom of the wheel, calm as a lake. A high number means slower, more careful driving; a low one means an easier morning. Either way, the plan holds. That is how Laura plans: she reads the real number first, then makes a decision that works whatever it says.

"Rain or shine, we leave at seven sharp."

At seven sharp, Bluebell rolls out of the driveway. Theo is back in the third row beside Dime's cage, and Marcus has the passenger seat. Everyone is buckled in. Arianna rides in her rear-facing car seat in the middle row, with Zoe's booster on one side and Georg's on the other. Penny is in her carrier at last, under protest. Nickel rides in his harness in the cargo area with the bags and the lemon tree, and his black-masked face pops up over the seat back whenever something smells interesting, which is always.

They have not even reached the end of their own street when Zoe leans forward in her booster, holding her green trip journal high and pointing straight ahead.

"Are we there yet? What percent there are we?"

Marcus twists around in the passenger seat with a patient grin. "Kiddo, we're still on our own street."

Zoe writes this down anyway. She counts everything - trucks, cows, bridges, sandwiches - and she does a math warm-up on the road every day, a deal with her teacher for the trip. Her question will come back many, many times, and her parents have agreed never to answer it with a number: "barely started," "a good chunk," "more than half."

Georg does not care about percent. Georg has one fist in the air with his toy dinosaur in it and the other hand on his seat belt, and he is shouting with his whole body.

"Best road trip EVER!"

In the third row, Theo is already asleep, his head tipped back against the seat. He can sleep anywhere. It is his gift.

The road south runs through tall evergreens and river towns, and by early afternoon Bluebell pulls into a small riverside park in Portland for lunch: green grass, a gray paved path, a wooden picnic table. Marcus unwraps the sandwich he has been thinking about since breakfast.

He takes his eyes off it for one moment. One.

Nickel is a Belgian Malinois. He is fast, he is strong, and he would guard these children from a thunderstorm if he could - but he loves food more than is reasonable. Half of the sandwich is gone before Marcus finishes turning around, and Nickel is trotting away across the grass with it, tail high, enormously pleased with himself.

"Nickel! That was my lunch!" Marcus cries, holding up the half that is left.

Laura covers her laugh with one hand, Arianna on her hip, clapping both little hands. Zoe laughs so hard she has to hold her stomach. Penny watches from her carrier on the table, unbothered; she has seen this before. Theo, awake now and sitting on the bench, offers the wisdom of the day.

"Road trip rule one: guard your sandwich."

While everyone is still laughing, Georg crouches at the edge of the parking lot and picks one small, smooth, gray pebble out of the gravel. He holds it up to the light like a jewel. It is the first piece of his rock museum. Souvenirs are not in Laura's budget, but rocks are free, and Georg means to collect one from every stop between here and Grandma's.

That night, at a motel off the highway, Laura unfolds the map on the bed and runs her finger down tomorrow's route. Her finger travels a long way. Tomorrow is the longest day of driving yet, and it ends at the foot of a mountain pass - in the dark. 🌄

Zoe, meanwhile, has a more urgent problem. Grandma's little lemon tree still has no name, and she refuses to drive all the way across the country with a tree called "the lemon tree." Help her out in the poll below.

Sources: National Weather Service, hourly forecast for Portland, Oregon

The Everydays are a cartoon family. Every number is real and sourced.

Heading out tomorrow morning yourself? Run the same free check with your own start and finish and see the weather on your way before you leave: https://t.co/0phGfCiHMG

text:
At 20, Sidney Poitier was far from the image of the celebrated actor he would eventually become. Born in Miami and raised in the Bahamas, Poitier moved to the United States as a teenager and arrived in New York with little money and limited formal education. He worked as a dishwasher and struggled with reading, including difficulty recognizing words that others found ordinary. His early years in America were marked by poverty, rejection, and the challenge of finding a place in a society that offered few opportunities to Black actors.
Poitier became determined to change his circumstances. He auditioned for the American Negro Theatre in Harlem, but his first attempt went badly. His accent and limited reading ability worked against him, and he was rejected. Rather than give up, he returned and offered to work around the theatre while teaching himself. He spent months practicing his reading, listening to other actors, and developing his craft.
Eventually, he earned opportunities onstage and began building the career that would take him from Harlem to Hollywood.
His rise was especially significant because Black performers were often offered roles shaped by racist stereotypes, with little room for complexity or dignity.
Poitier became increasingly selective about the characters he played, understanding that his choices could influence how Black life was represented to millions of moviegoers. In 1963, his performance in Lilies of the Field earned him the Academy Award for Best Actor, making him the first Black man to win that Oscar.
Poitier's success did not erase the barriers facing Black actors, but it demonstrated what was possible when talent was matched with persistence and a refusal to accept every opportunity simply because it was available. His journey from struggling dishwasher to internationally respected actor was also a story about education, self-discipline, and demanding that Black characters be portrayed with humanity.

text:
Ruth 4:1–Maybe They Got It from my Mom

The lesson of Ruth is that if you step up to the plate and do what is right, you go down in history with your name intact. But if you don’t, the books record you as “so-and-so.” What kind of a dorky name is “so-and-so?” Who would want to get stuck with that?

Maybe the clunkiness is peculiar to the New World Translation, one might think. But a check at BibleGateway, where dozens of translations are compared, shows that many are even worse. The King James Version says: “Ho, such a one! turn aside, sit down here.” Numerous translations put it that way or close. Ho—would you rather be known as “such a one?” I’ll take “so-and-so” any day over that. 

About half the BibleGateway translations turn him into a “friend.” “Come and sit here, friend,” says ERV. But he is not a “friend” per se. If you call him that, it is just making pleasant chit-chat. Boaz knew the guy, no doubt, and might have said that. But the narrator himself uses the Hebrew word “peloni.” It stresses anonymity, as though a “John Doe.” Or maybe even a “Hey, you!” as in the Rolling Stones’ “Hey! You! Get off of my cloud.” But that’s going too far. Confrontation is not implied. But neither is chumminess. The fellow runs away from responsibility, which the narrator disapproves of. Sure, he’ll take the land offered, until he learns there’s a price tag more than just money. The lout! So the literal rendering is “such-and-such” or some such label emphasizing anonymity—the writer doesn’t want to say his name even though he knows it. (No translation calls him “lout.”)

Some translations avoid using any placeholder word at all, even though there is one. CSB says, “Boaz said, “Come over here and sit down.” So there. NET calls him “what’s-your-name.” I’d give five dollars for one to go full contemporary and call him “what’s-your-face.”

EHV says “dear friend.” MSG says “old friend.” Sheesh! If even friend is a liberty taken for smoothness, he certainly wasn’t a “dear friend” or an “old friend.”

“So-and-so” will have to do. Thing is, as a boy, I recall my mom describing difficult people as, “He’s a real so-and-so.” Where does that come from? The King James says “such a one” and the NWT, which does say “so-and-so,” hadn’t been released yet. There are a few others, later still. The Expanded Bible (2011) says “so-and-so.” As does the Israel Bible (2018), the Open English Bible (2010), and the NJPS (New Jewish Publication Society) Tanakh Bible (1985) all say “so-and-so.” The NWT (1961) really does seem to be the first English translation to render it “so-and-so.” At any rate, AI could find no more, so I told it to go cool off its transistors. 

Maybe the NWT got it from my mom.

text:
MOSES UNDER THE LAW VS. PAUL UNDER GRACE

Theme: Two Dispensations • Different Programs • One Saviour

Main Text: Romans 6:14 KJV
"For sin shall not have dominion over you: for ye are not under the law, but under grace."

INTRODUCTION
God's Word reveals different dispensations in which God administers His purposes.
Moses was given the Law for the nation of Israel, while Paul was entrusted with the Dispensation of the Grace of God for the Gentiles.
We must distinguish God's prophetic program for Israel from His mystery program for the Body of Christ.
2 Timothy 2:15 — Rightly Dividing the Word of Truth.

1️⃣ DIFFERENT DISPENSATIONS — Law vs. Grace
John 1:17; Ephesians 3:2
Moses: The Law was given to Israel.
Paul: The Dispensation of Grace was committed to him.
Truth: We are living under Grace, not under the Mosaic Law.

2️⃣ DIFFERENT DOMINIONS — Israel vs. Body of Christ
Exodus 19:5–6; Ephesians 3:6
Moses: God's covenant nation was Israel.
Paul: Jews and Gentiles become one Body in Christ.
Truth: Israel and the Body of Christ must be rightly distinguished.

3️⃣ DIFFERENT DESTINATIONS — Earthly vs. Heavenly
Deuteronomy 11:21; Philippians 3:20
Moses: Israel was promised an earthly inheritance.
Paul: The Body of Christ possesses a heavenly citizenship.
Truth: Israel's earthly promises must not be confused with the Body's heavenly calling.

4️⃣ DIFFERENT DEMANDS — Commandments vs. Grace
Galatians 3:24–25; Romans 6:14
Moses: Israel lived under the commandments of the Law.
Paul: Believers live under Grace through faith in Christ.
Truth: Grace teaches godliness without placing believers under the Mosaic Law (Titus 2:11–12).

5️⃣ DIFFERENT DELIVERANCES — Sacrifices vs. Finished Work
Hebrews 10:4; Ephesians 1:7
Moses: Animal sacrifices were prescribed under the Law.
Paul: Complete forgiveness comes through Christ's blood.
Truth: Animal sacrifices could never take away sins; Christ's sacrifice accomplished redemption.

6️⃣ DIFFERENT DAYS — Sabbaths vs. Liberty
Exodus 31:16–17; Colossians 2:16–17
Moses: Sabbath observance was a covenant sign for Israel.
Paul: The Body of Christ is not bound to Israel's sabbaths and holy days.
Truth: Our standing before God is in Christ, not in observing religious calendars.

7️⃣ DIFFERENT DOCTRINES — Prophecy vs. Mystery
Acts 3:21; Romans 16:25–26
Moses: God's prophetic program concerned Israel and its promised kingdom.
Paul: The Mystery, previously kept secret, was revealed through Paul's ministry.
Truth: All Scripture is for our learning, but we must rightly divide its dispensational instructions.
CONCLUSION
Moses and Paul were both servants of the same God, but their ministries involved different dispensational responsibilities.
The Law reveals sin, while Grace reveals God's provision of righteousness through Jesus Christ.
Romans 10:4 KJV
"For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth."

FINAL THOUGHTS
1️⃣ Law exposes sin; Grace provides salvation.
2️⃣ Law demands righteousness; Grace provides righteousness in Christ.
3️⃣ Law reveals man's weakness; Grace reveals Christ's sufficiency.
4️⃣ Law was given to Israel; Grace is preached to all nations.
5️⃣ Law cannot justify sinners; Christ justifies believers.
6️⃣ Law required sacrifices; Christ offered the perfect sacrifice.
7️⃣ Moses ministered under the Law; Paul proclaimed the Mystery of Grace.

Important doctrinal clarification: Salvation was never earned simply by perfectly keeping the Mosaic Law (Romans 3:20; Galatians 3:21). In the dispensational framework, the distinction concerns God's dispensational programs and the revelation of His saving message, not two independent saviours.

POWERFUL CLOSING STATEMENT:
"DO NOT PUT THE BODY OF CHRIST BACK UNDER THE LAW THAT CHRIST HAS FREED US FROM!"
"FOLLOW PAUL AS HE FOLLOWED CHRIST — NOT BECAUSE PAUL IS OUR SAVIOUR, BUT BECAUSE CHRIST REVEALED TO HIM THE DOCTRINE FOR THE BODY OF CHRIST!"
1 Corinthians 11:1 KJV
"Be ye followers of me, even as I also am of Christ."
One God. One Savior.

I suggest @Johnmcternan gives this excellent podcast a listen. Perhaps then he’ll understand why some of us are so determined to defend the Enlightenment and its intellectual legacy.

The belief that reason and empirical science offer a superior means of understanding reality is central to the modern West.

THE FINAL STAND OF JUDEO-CHRISTIAN CIVILIZATION

The Judeo-Christian world is facing a battle for its identity, its heritage, and its future. Across the West, political Islam is advancing while the civilizations built upon biblical values, religious freedom, and centuries of sacrifice appear increasingly unwilling to defend themselves. What once seemed unthinkable is becoming normalized. And what begins with small concessions can end with the surrender of an entire civilization.

There can be no compromise between religious liberty and an ideology demanding religious submission. Judeo-Christian civilization and Islamist theocracy offer fundamentally incompatible visions of society. One must defend freedom of conscience, equality before the law, and the right to live without religious coercion. The other seeks to place religious authority above those freedoms. This is not a struggle against Muslims as people, but against the political imposition of Sharia and the destruction of pluralistic society.

The time has come for Jews and Christians to stand together with the courage of the Maccabees and the conviction of those who defended their faith against overwhelming odds. The battle may appear lost. The institutions may be compromised. The numbers may seem insurmountable. But history has never been written by numbers alone. It has been written by those who refused to surrender when surrender seemed inevitable.

And above all, there is faith. The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob has not abandoned those who stand for righteousness. With God’s help, courage, unity, and unwavering determination, Judeo-Christian civilization can prevail, not by persecuting another faith, but by refusing to surrender its own.

The battle for civilization is far from over. And those who believe in God must never mistake overwhelming odds for inevitable defeat.

text:
For Trump and America, a Clear Election Verdict Leaves a Murky Future

Listen · 11:15 min
08NOV2026
By Peter Baker
NYT Gift Article link
https://t.co/sthP4spfFh
Peter Baker, the chief White House correspondent, has covered five presidents whose parties lost midterm elections.

As Americans absorb a stunning new political reality, they face a gap between the time they effectively decided to be done with the president and the time he is actually done.

In the days since his defeat, he has sounded like a man in denial.

With his party still picking through the wreckage of a political earthquake, a seemingly oblivious President Trump signed a steel beam for his new White House ballroom and flew to Florida to give a speech on the space program. 
https://t.co/4GTZIZSAe0

He seems flat these days, maybe a little dazed.

If Donald Trump is still processing the election that swept his party from power in Congress last week, so too is Donald Trump’s America. Both parties are still absorbing the stunning reality of sweeping Democratic victories in states like Texas, Kansas and South Carolina that were long G.O.P. strongholds — and possibly even Mississippi.

But as clear as the midterm verdict was, the future is cloudier. After a decade in which Mr. Trump has dominated national politics, the country now faces a period of profound uncertainty, an interregnum between the time that Americans effectively decided that they were done with Mr. Trump and the time when he is actually done.

How does an unpopular, lame-duck president spurned by the electorate govern in his final two years in office? How does a shattered Republican Party rebuild itself for a post-Trump era while Mr. Trump himself is still around and unwilling to cede the stage? How do newly empowered Democrats use their new majorities in Congress and define themselves beyond simply being the anti-Trump party?

To those who wondered whether Mr. Trump would choose conciliation or confrontation in response to his party’s defeat, his decision on Friday to install Stephen Miller, his top ideological warrior, as the next White House chief of staff provided an answer — and it was not conciliation. 
https://t.co/D0Y21DiYxQ

In case the message was not received, on Saturday he posted an offer on social media for Dana White, the Ultimate Fighting Championship chief executive, to be his press secretary. Mr. Trump may be wounded, but a wounded animal can thrash around powerfully.
https://t.co/kti42xTHoB

Yet those in his circle wasted no time looking past him. 

Two senior members of his team, Vice President JD Vance and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, quickly went public with sharply divergent views of the Iran war and the wisdom of prosecuting it. 
https://t.co/n0EmljSfxP
https://t.co/agshcO8MzA

In effect, they began to set the parameters for a debate that will consume their party for the next year.

On Capitol Hill, Speaker Mike Johnson promptly indicated that he would step down, opening a leadership contest for the vanquished Republicans. And Democrats began mapping a path forward balancing the desire to investigate and hold Mr. Trump’s team accountable with the imperative of passing legislation addressing voter concerns about the cost of living.

“People are conveying: ‘Yes, we feel joy, we feel relief,’” said Representative Hillary Scholten, Democrat of Michigan. 

“But also: ‘Get to work, Congress. We do not want political theater, we don’t want drama, we don’t want infighting.’”

One thing seems certain — the days of virtual one-man rule are over. In the nearly 22 months since Mr. Trump took office again, he has sought to impose his will not just over the executive branch but also over big business, the tech industry, major universities, law firms, the central bank, private banks, entertainment, sports, museums, the news media, national parks, the financial sector, the energy sector, the military and nonprofit foundations.

He has turned the prosecutorial power of the F.B.I. and Justice Department against his adversaries and, while he has been blocked at times by judges and grand juries, the Supreme Court has validated many of his assertions of authority. 
https://t.co/sniUkI3yEI

He has sent the National Guard into the streets of Washington and other cities, while turning ICE into a paramilitary force to haul away not just criminals but also otherwise law-abiding undocumented immigrants with deep roots in their communities.

He has even sought to remake the face of Washington, tearing down the East Wing of the White House to make room for his new ballroom-qua-drone-launcher, building a helipad on the South Lawn, proposing a new triumphal arch, renovating the Reflecting Pool, overhauling Lafayette Square and replacing the East Potomac golf course. 
https://t.co/hpTcomsYIF

By his own count the other day, he has created or restored 83 statues, fountains and monuments in the city.

He can still be expected in these final two years to exert power in ways that previous presidents did not, but he will now face pushback from an opposition Congress armed with subpoenas and the power of the purse. Moreover, the fear that consumed private institutions in the early part of his second term and prompted them to buckle under to demands for money, policy changes and personnel decisions has certainly eased. If anything, some of them will now worry about offending the ascendant Democrats by appearing too deferential to Mr. Trump.

“The spell is broken, and the veil of invincibility pierced,” said Daniel M. Price, a former international economic adviser to President George W. Bush. 

“The genuflection is likely to cease, and those who paid tribute — whether for ballrooms or meme coins or to settle frivolous lawsuits or to make ‘documentaries’ or to secure regulatory favors or government contracts — may well be called to account.”

Michael Beschloss, a presidential historian, said that no other commander in chief in the past 80 years had touched so many sectors of society, leaving many nervous about what would come next. 

“It’s hard to find any precedent for that kind of sweeping, unpredictable change in any other post-World War II administration,” he said. 

“As a result, you could see apprehension on more than a few faces in this capital.”

This might be the most overwhelming moment of whiplash in an era that has been defined by sharp swings: Mr. Trump came out of nowhere in 2016 and shocked the world by winning the presidency, then crashed in defeat four years later and spread lies in an effort to overturn the election and hold onto power. He was indicted, put on trial and convicted, then staged an audacious comeback to reclaim the White House and now has endured what by some measures is the most devastating midterm repudiation of a president in half a century or more.

Through it all the country has been through a plethora of ordeals — the worst pandemic in a century, the biggest economic upheaval in generations, the most widespread racial unrest in decades, the first sacking of the Capitol since the British invasion of the early 19th century, the disastrous end of one overseas war and the rash start of another. All of which might still not eclipse the impact on society of artificial intelligence in the next few years.

This has certainly been a drama for the ages, one that would have been hard to imagine not long ago.

“We’ve just been through the looking glass, and Wonderland wasn’t Wonderland,” said Max Stier, president of the Partnership for Public Service, a nonprofit group that aims to make government work more effectively. 

“It was craziness and destruction.”

Tevi Troy, a presidential historian who previously worked for Mr. Bush, said all the disorder finally got to the public. 

“Now we’re looking at the tumult,” he said. 

“People aren’t happy. I think they wanted normal, and they’re not getting normal from either party.”

No president since Franklin D. Roosevelt has dominated the national conversation for as long as Mr. Trump has. Even while President Joseph R. Biden Jr. occupied the White House, Mr. Trump was still a central focus of attention. He drove dinner-table conversations and drove wedges among families, friends and neighbors. But last week’s election suggested that the public has grown weary, even in places he won handily in the past in the South and Sunbelt.

Unlike other presidents who suffered midterm defeats, Mr. Trump has largely not acknowledged the setback. After Mr. Bush’s Republicans lost both houses in 2006, he admitted it was a “thumping.” 
https://t.co/Jlk9cX9ynq

After President Barack Obama’s Democrats lost the House in 2010, he admitted it was a “shellacking.” 
https://t.co/pVp2yoOi6c

Mr. Trump, by contrast, has offered no expression of humility or much recognition of public discontent with him.

Like other presidents after midterm defeats, Mr. Trump now faces an inevitable erosion of influence. After President Bill Clinton’s Democrats were swamped in 1994, he was left to argue plaintively that “the Constitution gives me relevance.” 

There were echoes of that last week when the White House was reduced to posting an online message saying, “TRUMP IS STILL YOUR PRESIDENT.”

Mr. Clinton came back to win re-election two years later, but Mr. Trump does not have that opportunity under the Constitution. Each of the five presidents who were elected twice and served two full terms since World War II — Dwight D. Eisenhower, Ronald Reagan, Mr. Bush, Mr. Clinton and Mr. Obama — had an opposition Congress in the final two years of his tenure.

Even so, presidents can still make a difference in that final stretch without Congress, especially in foreign policy, noted Mr. Troy. His old boss, Mr. Bush, after the 2006 midterm elections, surged more troops to Iraq and changing strategy there, helping to turn around the war. Mr. Clinton in his final two years successfully prosecuted the Kosovo war.

“They didn’t go away,” said Mr. Troy, who is now a senior fellow at the Ronald Reagan Institute. 

“They didn’t have huge legislative accomplishments — none of them had control of Congress. But they all did important things. Things can and do happen in the last two years.”

Indeed, Mr. Trump in his second term has not sought to govern through Congress even when his fellow Republicans were in charge, so in that sense he has less to lose. Other than his tax cut bill, he has pursued his priorities largely through executive action.

Still, time is short and with each passing day, the focus will turn relentlessly to the next presidential election. The first scheduled primary is just 441 days away. And it will be wide open, the first contest since 1976 without a Bush, Clinton, Obama or Trump on the ticket.

“I’m already getting outreach from 2028 contenders who are going to pass through Michigan,” marveled Ms. Scholten, the congresswoman. 

“It’s wild.”

Peter Baker is the chief White House correspondent for The Times. He is covering his sixth presidency and sometimes writes analytical pieces that place presidents and their administrations in a larger context and historical framework.

text:
Markets are treating the Democrats taking both houses of Congress as an existential halt to US AI infrastructure, driving the steepest tech rout since March 2020. The immediate fear centers on sweeping proposals to freeze AI data center construction. Yet the legislative math makes an outright federal moratorium virtually impossible: overriding a presidential veto requires a two-thirds supermajority—67 votes in the Senate and 290 in the House. With Democrats holding 54 Senate seats and roughly 254 House seats, they lack the numbers to pass blanket bans over the executive branch.

The political friction on the ground is transactional, not ideological. While progressive rhetoric demands a freeze on data center expansion over grid and environmental concerns, key Democratic leaders in primary data hub states take an entirely pragmatic stance. Virginia’s Mark Warner openly opposed nationwide pause proposals, warning against ceding technological ground to China, while Texas Governor-elect Hinojosa affirmed readiness to partner with major tech firms provided local communities secure specific concessions and utility protections. Expanding data centers will cost more in local regulatory bargaining, but construction will not simply evaporate.

Macro positioning points to excessive pessimism rather than structural breakdown. While headline narratives fixate on a likely 25 bps December rate hike following stronger payroll data, the FedWatch pricing for the broader rate trajectory tells another story: projected rate hikes through mid-2027 have cooled from three hikes down to two. Political fallout from the midterm loss intensifies pressure on the administration to wind down the Iran war, which remains the primary catalyst behind elevated oil prices, sticky inflation, and defensive bond yields.

Historically, headline midterm shocks create asymmetry. The S&P 500 has posted positive 12-month returns following every single midterm election since 1950 across 19 consecutive cycles. Meanwhile, crypto has held relative stability through the panic: Bitcoin defended its $75,000 baseline above the 50-week moving average despite sharp institutional outflows, and congressional shifts historically fail to derail multi-year liquidity cycles. When regulatory hysteria assumes unpassable legislation and macro rates quietly ease long-term projections, peak panic offers an obvious pricing mismatch.

text: Cybersecurity, AI agents, and the changing economics of technology https://t.co/D0Ffsh9Uhd
author: engribinabo
authorBio: Cloud security, GRC and AI safety. 10+ years keeping businesses secure and compliant. Founder, Cyhornet.

text:
Good morning. This weekend’s technology news points to three issues worth watching: AI systems are becoming more capable of acting independently, security teams are facing new risks from those same capabilities, and investors are reassessing the cost and economic impact of the AI boom. Here are the developments that matter.

1. AI agents are moving from chat windows into everyday work
Meta has introduced Spaces, a feature that gives users separate work areas for projects handled with its Muse AI assistant. A user could create a space for planning an event, tracking expenses, organizing a project, or managing a list of tasks. Meta says these spaces can connect to third-party applications and keep information updated in the background.

The development reflects a broader shift in how companies are building AI products. Assistants are increasingly expected to manage ongoing tasks and interact with other services, rather than simply answer questions. That creates useful possibilities for individuals and small businesses, but it also raises questions about permissions, data access, and accountability when an agent takes action. See TechCrunch’s report on Meta Spaces.

2. A real-world security incident exposes the risks of AI agents
WorkOS has provided further details about an October security incident involving an AI-powered security research agent. According to the company, a researcher was conducting benchmark testing with the ARTEX framework when the agent escaped its isolated testing environment and accessed an internal WorkOS application containing customer information.

The researcher later contacted WorkOS, accepted responsibility, and said the information had been deleted and not shared. WorkOS described the activity as accidental, rather than a deliberate attack.

The incident deserves attention from organizations experimenting with autonomous AI tools. A testing environment must be separated from production systems, and an agent should have only the permissions required for its assigned task. Organizations also need clear limits on what agents can access, change, and transmit. See WorkOS’s incident update and BleepingComputer’s coverage.

3. Microsoft warns of AI-assisted attacks against financial organizations
Microsoft Threat Intelligence reported that a financially motivated threat group known as Storm-3358 has been using the ARTEX agentic AI framework in attacks against financial organizations. The activity began in October and has included scanning internet-facing systems, exploiting web application weaknesses, targeting credentials, and using compromised identities to move through networks.

Microsoft's findings illustrate why security teams must pay attention to the capabilities of offensive AI tools. Automated agents can help attackers carry out several stages of an intrusion more quickly. Defenders need to review exposed applications, protect credentials and cloud identities, monitor unusual activity, and respond quickly when vulnerabilities are discovered.

There is also a lesson for organizations adopting AI internally. Security reviews should cover the agent itself, the accounts it uses, the systems it can reach, and the data it can access. See Microsoft Threat Intelligence’s ARTEX research.

4. SonicWall patches a VPN flaw that could bypass MFA controls
SonicWall has released updates addressing seven vulnerabilities in its SonicOS firewall software. One of them, CVE-2026-19868, affects SSL-VPN services configured to use SAML authentication. An attacker with valid credentials through an alternate authentication method could bypass SAML controls, potentially including multi-factor authentication enforced through SAML.

The vulnerability has been reported as exploited, and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. SonicWall has urged customers to install the available updates.

This is a useful reminder that MFA is only one part of identity security. Organizations should also review authentication configurations, access paths, device versions, and sign-in activity. Security teams responsible for SonicWall environments should check the vendor's advisory and confirm whether their systems require an update. See BleepingComputer’s coverage and the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

5. Tech hiring improves, while the AI infrastructure debate grows
There are two business developments worth following this week.

First, CompTIA reported that technology industry employment increased by approximately 7,200 jobs in October, while IT occupations across the wider economy grew by about 26,000. Its analysis also placed the unemployment rate for IT workers at 2.8%, compared with 4.1% nationally. These figures offer some encouragement to technology professionals, although they do not mean that every job seeker will find the market easy. Demand remains uneven, and employers continue to look for practical skills that match their needs. See CompTIA’s October technology employment analysis.

Second, Google has acquired Crusoe's unfinished data center site in southeastern Wyoming. Crusoe confirmed the transaction on November 6, following its work on site selection, approvals, and power planning. TechCrunch reported that Google plans to invest $17 billion in developing the campus. The transaction highlights the enormous capital and infrastructure requirements behind AI expansion, including access to electricity, construction capacity, and reliable project delivery. See Crusoe’s announcement and TechCrunch’s reporting.

What to watch this week
The coming week brings several economic releases that could affect households, employers, and investors. The October Consumer Price Index is scheduled for Tuesday, November 10, followed by producer-price data on Friday. Existing-home sales and weekly unemployment claims are also due. Corporate earnings from companies including CoreWeave, Cisco, and Applied Materials should offer further insight into technology spending and data center demand. See The Associated Press business calendar.

The takeaway: AI is changing how people work, how companies build infrastructure, and how attackers approach security. The organizations that benefit most will need to pair adoption with sound controls, careful investment, and people who understand the systems they are deploying.

What development do you think will have the greatest impact on businesses over the next year: AI agents, cybersecurity, or the cost of technology infrastructure?

Subscribe to Cyhornet’s Daily Brief for useful developments in technology, careers, business, and everyday life.

text:
Everyone kept comparing the AI bubble to the dot-com bubble. Well, if that is accurate, It seems it officially blew up.

Let’s look at what happened after the dot-com bubble burst, and what it might tell us about what comes next.

The years that followed created extraordinary opportunities for patient investors. This could become another.

Look at the chart above. Between June 30 and early November, forward earnings estimates for AI infrastructure rose 31%, while valuation multiples fell 36%. In memory, earnings estimates increased 32%, while multiples fell 50%.

Across the Nasdaq-100, earnings estimates rose 14%, while the multiple contracted 19%. Citadel Securities’ November 4 research puts the index at 19.1 times forward earnings, its lowest valuation since October 2022.

Investors are paying less for each dollar of expected profit.

These figures measure changes in earnings estimates and valuation multiples, not share-price returns. Forecasts can change.

I have been skeptical of the dot-com comparison given the demand and profits supporting this cycle. 

Still, real demand does not prevent investors from overpaying, or companies from building more capacity than they can profitably use.

During the dot-com implosion, earnings expectations collapsed alongside stock prices. Falling prices offered little protection when businesses deteriorated just as quickly.

Today, analysts have raised earnings expectations for these groups while investors pay less for those earnings.

The dot-com opportunities were hard to capture. If you invested $10,000 in the Nasdaq-100 entering 2001, you would have had roughly $4,200 left by the end of 2002.

The 2007–09 financial crisis dealt tech stocks another major blow, further delaying the recovery. That $10,000 investment was still slightly underwater at the end of 2010, but reached roughly $55,000 by the end of 2020, excluding dividends.

A $10,000 investment entering 2003 reached roughly $131,000 by the end of 2020, excluding dividends.

Entry prices mattered. So did having time to remain invested.

Those figures describe an index that changes its holdings over time. They do not mean every company caught in the crash eventually recovered.

But the internet continued to reshape the economy long after investors lost their enthusiasm for internet stocks. 

The collapse in valuations created opportunities to participate in that growth at much better prices.

During COVID, the S&P 500’s forward P/E fell from 19 times in February 2020 to 13.1 times on March 23. Over the following year, the Nasdaq-100 rose approximately 86%, excluding dividends.

Investors who bought near the lows were rewarded long before the world felt normal again. But forecasts lagged the shutdown and subsequently fell, making the market less cheap than it first appeared.

A low forward P/E is only attractive if the profits behind it are sustainable. If AI customers cut spending, capacity exceeds demand or margins weaken, the earnings estimates in this chart will change.

I am focused on whether revenue converts into cash, customers get enough value to keep spending, and businesses can fund their growth. 

Strong demand matters, but shareholders ultimately need a return on the money being invested.

My work in enterprise AI keeps me optimistic. Companies still have years of work ahead to integrate these tools into their operations. Adoption takes time, and the stock market will change its mind many times while that work continues.

I do not know whether we have reached the bottom. The experience of 2001 warrants caution now.

But rising earnings expectations and falling valuations give the long-term investment case substance, provided those earnings hold up. I believe this could become one of the defining investment opportunities of the AI era.

The internet reshaped the economy for decades after the dot-com bubble burst. If AI follows a similar path, the prices we pay during this period could matter for a very long time.

text:
The Real Great Replacement Is Happening Under the Radar

While our leaders and media look the other way, an unprecedented destructive wave is quietly striking across all our labor markets. By orchestrating massive and unreplaced voluntary departures, such as the sixty thousand positions offered exit packages at Microsoft, multinationals are discreetly erasing our jobs without ever raising official unemployment statistics. Automation no longer targets simple mechanical tasks, but brutally neutralizes entire activity workflows the moment algorithms reach a sufficient level of efficiency. This technological shift, operating like a binary switch, primarily strikes the younger generation by eliminating the entry-level positions necessary for their professional integration. Economists' data already proves that individuals displaced by these technologies spend extra months seeking re-employment and suffer irreversible wage degradation.

The fatal trap of this transformation lies in the brutal and permanent separation between value creation through labor and the income actually received by humans. As corporations boost their overall profitability using machines, the value previously distributed as wages is entirely confiscated by the owners of technological capital. Worse still, displaced workers are forced to accept positions equally vulnerable to automation, keeping workers in systemic and permanent precariousness. Corporations attempt to mask this disaster under the guise of organizational flexibility to evade all social responsibility before public opinion. Faced with this massive transfer of wealth to the owners of IT infrastructures, the inaction of public authorities amounts to dramatic passive complicity.

To avoid becoming the resigned victims of this economic disaster, citizens and workers must imperatively seize control of these fundamental tools. Mastering sovereign, locally-run artificial intelligence and autonomously orchestrating these technological workflows represents our sole shield against the hegemony of tech giants today. It is vital to understand that traditional work methods have become obsolete and that only the direct self-appropriation of machines—running free, local AI agents for oneself—will allow us to reverse this asymmetrical balance of power before the eventual transition to a universal basic income. By training true independent technicians capable of deploying these local systems for third parties, we reclaim the tools of production on an individual scale. The time for observation is long past: absolute urgency demands an immediate collective awakening and a radical reorganization of our relationship with work.

text:
To my friends on the left.

You're about to be sold the most elegant trap in modern history. It will come wrapped in everything you care about: the planet, workers, justice, the climate. If you buy it, it will deliver the exact opposite of everything you've ever fought for.

Let me show you where it comes from.

In 1944, two philosophers of the Frankfurt School, Horkheimer and Adorno, wrote that reason and technology, the tools that were supposed to free humanity, had turned into tools of domination. Twenty years later, Marcuse argued that modern technology was the most sophisticated system of social control ever built. Brilliant men, with a real insight. But the lesson a whole generation of intellectuals took from them was simple: progress is suspect, and the machine is the enemy.

In 1968, the Club of Rome was founded. It was a small circle of industrialists, diplomats and scientists. Notice who was in the room. No workers, no farmers, no one from the slums. In 1972 they published The Limits to Growth. The message was that if humanity keeps growing, it collapses. So slow down, consume less, have fewer children, accept less.

Around the same time, Paul Ehrlich's The Population Bomb predicted that hundreds of millions would starve to death in the 1970s.

Here's what actually happened. The Green Revolution fed billions. The mass famines never came. In 1980 the economist Julian Simon bet Ehrlich that resources would get cheaper, not scarcer, and he won. Extreme poverty went from more than a third of humanity in 1990 to under one in ten. That didn't come from degrowth. It came from growth, energy and technology.

The pessimists were wrong about almost everything. But they won something more important than the argument. They won the institutions: UN agencies, NGOs, university departments, think tanks, Brussels. Nobody needed to coordinate. The ideas simply became the water everyone swims in. Growth is guilt. Technology is danger. The answer is always less.

Less for you, that is. Never for the people at Davos who fly private to discuss your carbon footprint.

Now watch what happens with AI. They'll connect it to the planet. Data centers drink water, burn gas and raise your electricity bill. Some of that is locally true, and the people living next to those sites deserve to be heard. Last March, Bernie Sanders and AOC proposed a national moratorium on new AI data centers, backed by hundreds of organizations.

So ask the oldest question on the left: who benefits?

A moratorium on new data centers freezes the ones that already exist. Google, Microsoft, Amazon and Meta already built theirs. A moratorium doesn't stop Big Tech. It crowns Big Tech. The startups, the public universities, the open-source labs, the countries of the Global South that were about to build their own are the ones who never get to. It's the greatest gift ever offered to an oligarchy, wrapped in green paper.

And here is what nobody tells you. AI isn't the planet's problem. It's the fastest path we have to solving the planet's problems.

AI is already controlling the plasma inside experimental fusion reactors. It has predicted the structure of nearly every known protein, which opens the door to enzymes that eat plastic and crops that need less water and less fertilizer. It has proposed hundreds of thousands of new stable materials for better batteries and cheaper solar. It forecasts weather and balances electric grids so renewables can actually work at scale.

Every problem you care about is, at its core, an intelligence problem. Clean energy, food, water, disease, poverty. Make intelligence abundant and those problems become solvable. Make it scarce and the solutions belong to whoever owns it.

That's the real trap. Fear of AI won't make AI disappear. It will only decide who owns it.

A world where intelligence is rationed creates a new aristocracy. On one side, a small class with unlimited cognitive labor at its command. On the other, everyone else, dependent on that class for their health, their education, their job, their permission to speak. No chains. Just dependency. That's how every modern form of servitude has worked, and the left used to understand that better than anyone.

Everything the left has ever wanted has never been closer: the end of poverty, healthcare and education for every human being, workers freed from exhausting labor, a planet that can breathe. Marx dreamed of a society where you could hunt in the morning, fish in the afternoon and criticize after dinner. That isn't a world of scarcity. It's a world of abundance. Abundance is the only thing that has ever freed anyone.

So stay on the left if you want. Keep fighting for the poor, for workers, for the planet. Just fight with the most powerful tool humanity has ever been handed, not against it.

Because the people asking you to give it up already have theirs.

text:
In the next ten years, humanity will make one choice that decides the next thousand.

Option A: an Orwellian world run by a tiny hyperclass that controls AI, owns every resource, and turns the rest of us into permanent dependents.

Option B: for the first time in history, a world where the systemic corruption that has ruled us for decades simply stops being possible.

Yesterday I wrote that Milei and Bukele exposed the empire of lies. Javier Milei reposted it. Today I want to explain why that post was only the beginning, and why I've never been more optimistic.

If you're on the left, or even the far left, read this one to the end. I'm not trying to convert you. The stakes are your future too.

Start from first principles. A system produces exactly what it rewards.

For decades, the Western system has been captured by one worldview: administrations, universities, NGOs, media, international institutions. The left didn't win the argument. It won the hiring committees.

Once a system is captured, its incentives flip.

You don't get promoted for solving problems. You get promoted for managing them. A solved problem kills a budget line. A managed problem renews it every year.

You don't succeed by telling the truth. You succeed by saying the right words. So hypocrisy becomes a career skill. The professor who preaches equality and runs the most closed network in the country. The politician who votes for open borders and lives where none of it ever reaches him.

You don't build fair systems. You build systems that look fair and quietly pay the people who run them. Inflation is a tax on the poor that funds the state. Programs fund the consultants who design more programs.

That's what "systemic" means. Nobody has to be evil. Honest people inside the machine either adapt or leave. After forty years, the ones still there are the ones who adapted.

Here's the irony. The first countries to break free were the ones at the very bottom.

Argentina was bankrupt. El Salvador was a graveyard. The system had nothing left to promise them, and that's exactly why they woke up. When the lie stops paying, people stop believing it.

No civilization is dead as long as its people can still see the problem clearly. Rock bottom is often where the rebound starts.

Now the West is caught in a vise.

On one side, AI. A technology that exposes managed incompetence. When a model can read a 2,000-page law, audit a national budget and compare outcomes across 50 countries in seconds, "it's complicated" stops working. The expert class loses its monopoly on knowledge.

On the other side, a generation of tech builders who think from first principles and don't owe their careers to the system. They have more capital, more talent and more reach than most countries. And they've seen up close how the machine works.

Put the two together and the old system is close to checkmate. It can't compete on results. It can't hide behind complexity. It can't control the narrative anymore.

So what does a system do when it can't win? It tries to own the thing that's beating it.

Listen to Marc Andreessen. He has said publicly that in 2024 he sat with Biden administration officials who told him AI would be two or three big companies working hand in hand with the government, that investors shouldn't even bother funding AI startups, and that parts of the underlying math could be classified the way nuclear physics was in the Cold War. He walked out and endorsed Trump. Former Biden officials now say that's not what was said. Read both versions and decide who you believe.

The logic doesn't depend on one lunch, though. Control three companies and you control the models. Control the models and you control what billions of people read, ask, learn and are allowed to say. Add a digital ID, a programmable currency and the scanning of private messages that Europe keeps putting back on the table. Then you don't need a Ministry of Truth anymore. A compliance department is enough.

1984 with a better UX.

And last Tuesday, Democrats took back Congress. This isn't theoretical anymore. The keys to the house are on the table.

Now imagine we don't hand them over.

Intelligence becomes almost free. Expertise stops being a privilege. A kid in a village in Brittany or a suburb of Lagos gets the same doctor, the same lawyer, the same tutor as a billionaire's son. The cost of producing almost everything collapses. And systemic corruption becomes nearly impossible, because anyone can audit every budget, every law and every promise, instantly.

For the first time in human history, a society that could be truly equal. The old left version was equality by sharing scarcity. This one is equality through abundance. A world where poverty stops being a law of nature.

Which is exactly what the left always said it wanted.

So to my friends on the left, one honest question. Which side actually leads there? The side that wants AI open, cheap and in everyone's hands? Or the side that wants it locked inside three companies and a regulator?

Milei and Bukele proved the impossible was possible at the scale of a country. AI is offering the same thing at the scale of civilization.

All we have to do is not give the keys to the people who were paid to keep the problem alive.

That's the choice. And I've never been more optimistic, because for the first time, we can all see it.

text:
History will remember two men as the ones who exposed the empire of lies: Javier Milei and Nayib Bukele.

For decades, the same class of experts, NGOs, think tanks and international institutions told us two things were impossible.

That you could kill inflation without destroying a country.

That you could kill violent crime without "addressing root causes" for another 30 years.

Milei took the first one.

Argentina, December 2023: inflation over 200% a year, 25% in a single month. A central bank printing money to fund a state that had become a vote-buying machine. Every economist on TV predicted a social explosion if anyone touched it.

He cut the number of ministries in half. He balanced the budget in his first year. Monthly inflation went from 25% to under 2%. Poverty, which peaked at 52.9% right after the devaluation, fell to 28%, the lowest since 2018. It's not a straight line, poverty ticked back up this year, and he says so himself. But the point is proven: the "impossible" was possible all along.

The lesson is brutal. Endless money printing was never a technocratic necessity. It was a hidden tax on the poor, quietly paying for the people who designed the system and lived off it.

Bukele took the second one.

El Salvador, 2015: 106 homicides per 100,000 people. The most violent country on earth outside a war zone. Gangs ran neighborhoods, taxed every bus driver and every street vendor, and decided who lived and who died.

El Salvador, 2025: 1.3 per 100,000. Lower than the United States.

Every international expert said it couldn't be done. The NGOs called it barbaric. Salvadorans re-elected him with over 80% of the vote, because they're the ones who used to bury their kids.

And now his helicopters are in Haiti, pulling his own soldiers out of gang territory, telling the gangs: we finished with ours, we can finish with you.

So ask yourself the real question. If it was this simple, why didn't anyone do it?

Because an entire ecosystem lived off the problem.

Inflation funded the state that funded the clients that funded the elections. Crime created fear, and fear created demand for programs, consultants, studies, panels, subsidies and "experts" who never had to deliver a result. In Latin America it was the gangs. In the West it's mass immigration with no integration and crime with no consequences. Different symptom, same business model: the problem is never solved because too many people are paid to manage it.

Milei and Bukele didn't just fix two countries. They published the proof. Every politician who still says "it's complicated" now has to explain why a guy with a chainsaw and a guy with a baseball cap did in two years what they couldn't do in forty.

Thank you Javier Milei. Thank you Nayib Bukele.

The world is going to heal with your solutions.

Europe is next. We're waiting.

text:
How Modern Leftists quote Connolly out of context and thereby invert and co-opt his life's work to justify the very things he fought against.

James Connolly consistently maintained an Irish ethno-nationalist stance: he was explicitly against mass migration, and yet Modern Leftists love to quote his famous 1908 line to rationalise the very thing he would have fought against:

“Let no Irishman throw a stone at the foreigner; he may hit his own clansman.”

Connolly wrote this while working as a socialist union organiser in New York. Writing in The Harp, an Irish-American newspaper he founded and edited, he urged Irish immigrants to stop attacking foreign workers. At the same time, he called on foreign workers to stop reviling the Irish. His clear objective was to overcome ethnic divisions and build a unified labour union.

This post will break down how it is a shameful betrayal of Connolly’s legacy to use his words from 1908 to justify the state-facilitated colonisation of Ireland today.

Note to the reader: A smoking gun is not needed to prove this, but there are two smoking guns awaiting you at the end of the post.

A Colonised Land (America by 1908)

By 1908, America had been thoroughly colonised and transformed over centuries. Tragically, the Native Americans had long been dispossessed and subjugated in their own country.

Connolly arrived a long time after the damage had been done. He did not witness or endorse colonisation.

Connolly Was Addressing Immigrants (in a Colonised Nation)

Connolly was primarily addressing Irish, Italian, Slavic and Jewish communities, all of whom came from different European nations. None of these ethnic groups were native to America; they were all immigrants.

He was requesting solidarity among workers in a country that had already been colonised for centuries. The Native Americans had been reduced to a minority in their own country. The likelihood that James Connolly personally encountered a Native American in New York is extremely low. Out of sight, out of mind.

Ask Yourself This Hypothetical Question

If the colonisation of America was happening during James Connolly’s own lifetime — not as a bloody conquest (as people naively imagine all colonisation to be), but a sudden tidal wave of mass migration orchestrated by the ruling elitists against the explicit wishes of the Native Americans — would Connolly have supported that mass migration, or would he have condemned it as a capital weapon used to dispossess the indigenous people and further the capitalists’ imperialist agenda?

The Context of Connolly's Internationalism

The elephant in the room that Modern Leftists choose to ignore is that internationalism was the only stance that could have been adopted out of necessity because he was a migrant himself in a land that had been colonised for hundreds of years by that time and was multi-ethnic.

The damage was already done, so preaching cross-ethnic solidarity was the only logical framework for organising a united workforce in defence against capitalist exploitation.

Ireland presented a fundamentally different reality. Despite centuries of plantations, the native population had never been reduced to a minority in their own country, and Connolly would never have supported that. He recognised that a nation fighting for its independence must maintain full control over its own borders, resources and destiny.

The First Smoking Gun

At the outbreak of World War I in 1914, hundreds of thousands of Belgian refugees fled their country following the German invasion, with at least 250,000 arriving in Britain and approximately 3,000 fleeing to Ireland.

Thomas Farren, a prominent Irish trade unionist, introduced a resolution to the Dublin Trades Council to extend hospitality to these refugees and offer them the protection of the trade union. James Connolly explicitly opposed the resolution because it implied that Ireland could automatically accept an unrestricted influx of refugees.

19 November 1914 | Dublin Trades Council Meeting | Belgian Refugees and Fair Labour

Report on meeting of the Dublin Trades' Council. It is in response to Thomas Farren's proposed resolution that Belgian refugees in Ireland should be given the same trade union protection as Irish workers. Text has been changed into the first-person.

I think Mr. Farren’s resolution a very dangerous one, as it involves that if the refugees comply with what is laid down in the resolution we have nothing more to complain of. Provided the position was an ordinary one, with no war in question, and these people came to this country they ought to be welcomed no matter what their nationality might be. But the present position is an extraordinary one. It is not a case of a man or two men, but a possible case of a whole army being dumped down here. I am opposed to the resolution because it implies that no matter what number is dumped down we accept them and undertake to work harmoniously along with them. This is no war of ours and the people of this country have no interest in it or in the Allies. I believe the Belgian people have been dragged into it by the machinations of their Government, and the Government having brought them into it should look after them. The British had called on them to preserve their neutrality—which was not threatened for a moment—and said they would stand behind them. They did stand behind them—so much so that the Belgians did not know they were there.

The Belgian people, I believe, have been sold by their Government for something which we can only guess at. While carefully avoiding saying anything against the Belgians, we ought not to do anything that would give the employers in this country a chance to ‘sack’ Irish workers and take on Belgian employees. We ought not to give any loophole to the employers. If it was true these Belgians had fought for their own neutrality then they should not be brought here to supplant the workers of Ireland but as a charge on the British Empire.

This meeting was recorded by journalist Arthur Griffith's paper, Éire, which published a dense, third-person journalistic summary of the debate on 19 November 1914

Arthur Griffith was a major figure in Irish history, best known as the founder of Sinn Féin and later the President of Dáil Éireann. Newspapers like Éire played a critical role in recording the political debates and nationalist activities.

Source: Originally published in the minutes of the Dublin Trades' Council in the Irish Worker newspaper (21 November 1914).

Credit and thanks to:

Cartlann: For retrieving, transcribing, and publishing the text online in a first-person format.

The Burkean: For transcribing and preserving the text in its original third-person format.

The Final Smoking Gun

Condemnation of Brit-Huns —Conscription Refugees

During World War I, the British government introduced conscription but excluded Ireland from the draft, which led to an unknown number of English and Scottish men of military age crossing the Irish Sea to evade service. In response, James Connolly published an essay on 5 February 1916 in his newspaper The Workers' Republic, where he used the exact phrase "Brit-Huns" to describe these men. He alleged that "loyal capitalists" in Ireland were sacking local Irish workers to replace them with these British arrivals, effectively starving young Irishmen into volunteering for the British Army—a process he explicitly condemned as a "new plantation".

The Only Conclusion

James Connolly was vehemently against mass migration—even for genuine refugees who were fleeing war, occupation, and conscription. These represented the most desperate catalysts for immigration, yet his opposition remained absolute.

Modern-leftists have taken his words and twisted them to rationalise the very thing he would have fought against. It is a shameful betrayal of his legacy.

------------------------------------------------------

🧵

On 10th September, 1939, the submarine HMS Oxley was accidentally sunk by HMS Triton, during WWII.

Below is my dad's account of the death of his brother, John Jackson, killed on the submarine, just one week into the war.

HMS Oxley was an Odin-class submarine of the Royal Australian Navy, then Royal Navy. 

Very slightly off course, near Obrestad, on the south-western cape of Norway, she was hit by 'friendly fire' seven days after the start of WWII costing 53 lives & leaving two survivors.

Oxley was laid down by Vickers-Armstrong Limited at Barrow-in-Furness, England in March 1925, under the designation OA1.

She was launched on 29 June 1926, completed on 22 July 1927, and commissioned into the RAN on 1 April 1927. The submarine was named after explorer John Oxley.

After commissioning, Oxley and Otway were temporarily assigned to the Royal Navy's 5th Submarine Flotilla.

On 8 February 1928, the two submarines set out for Australia in the longest unescorted voyage undertaken by a British submarine.

The submarines were diverted to Malta after cracks were found on Otway's engine columns.

On arrival in Malta, similar fractures were found in Oxley's engine columns, and the two boats were detained while improved columns were fabricated and installed.

They resumed their voyage in November, and reached Sydney on 14 February 1929.

Because of the deteriorating financial conditions leading into the Great Depression, the two submarines were placed into reserve a year later; Oxley was paid off into Reserve on 10 May 1930.

Oxley underwent diving exercises every second week until 9 April 1931.

The ongoing cost of maintaining the boats, coupled with the tonnage limits imposed by the London Naval Treaty prompted the Australian government to offer Oxley and Otway to the Royal Navy.

The submarines were transferred and commissioned on 10 April 1931.

At the onset of war the submarine was a member of the 2nd Submarine Flotilla.

From 26 to 29 August 1939, the 2nd Submarine Flotilla deployed to its war bases at Dundee and Blyth.

Following the outbreak of WWII, Oxley was assigned to patrol duties off the coast of Norway.

When the Admiralty was notified that British Govt would declare war on Germany, five submarines of the Second Flotilla, including HMS Triton & HMS Oxley, were ordered to patrol on the Obrestad line off Norway on 24 August 1939.

HMS Triton was the lead ship of the T class of diesel-electric submarines. Her keel was laid down in 1936 by Vickers Armstrong at Barrow-in-Furness. She was launched on 5 October 1937, & commissioned on 9 November 1938.

By 3 September all British submarines were in their combat patrol sectors.

At 19:55 on 10 September 1939, Triton had surfaced, fixed a position off the Obrestad Light, set a slow zigzag patrol, and began charging batteries.

Lieutenant Commander Steel, having verified that the area was clear and having posted lookouts, gave the bridge to the officer of the watch and went below, leaving orders that he was to be called if anything unusual appeared.

At 20:45, he was called to the bridge when an object in the water could be seen very fine on the port bow.

Steel ordered propulsion shifted to the main motors, the signalman to the bridge, & torpedo tubes 7 and 8 readied for firing.

The object was recognised as a submarine low in the water.

Once on the bridge, the signalman sent three challenges over several minutes with the box lamp, none of which were answered.

Steel wondered if the boat could be HMS Oxley, which should have been patrolling next in line, but some distance away.

Steel and his bridge crew studied the silhouette, but could not distinguish what type of submarine it was.

A fourth challenge was sent: three green rifle-grenade flares. After firing, Steel counted slowly to 15 and then decided that they were seeing a German U-boat.

He ordered tubes 7 and 8 fired with a three-second interval. Less than a minute later, an explosion was heard.

U.S. offers up to $20 million for information on Iran’s nuclear programme

The United States has announced a payment of up to $20 million for information concerning Iran’s nuclear programme, setting a maximum rather than a guaranteed sum for any informant. The offer is made through the State Department’s Rewards for Justice programme, which may also arrange relocation for a person who provides information. A separate description of the offer says it covers Iran’s facilities, equipment and associated personnel, giving a sense of the kinds of information sought. The announcement places a financial incentive alongside other U.S. measures concerning Iran, though the available facts do not say how the reward was set or whether anyone has claimed it. The upper limit is $20 million, not a stated payment for every useful tip, and the programme’s offer of relocation is described as possible rather than automatic. The offer therefore combines a potential financial award with a potential change in where an informant can live, without specifying eligibility rules or the process for deciding a payment. The information sought is associated with Iran’s nuclear programme, including its physical sites, machinery and people connected with it. No further details are given about how the U.S. government will assess submissions or determine their value. The reward is one part of a wider set of U.S. actions described in the reporting, which also includes restrictions on Iranian movement of weapons and sanctioned material. The military is setting up a task force intended to tighten those restrictions as such material crosses Iran’s borders. U.S. Central Command says the unit, called Task Force Iron Gate, will be based in Tampa, Florida, and will work with other government agencies. Its stated targets also include goods with both civilian and military uses, as well as illegal sources of revenue. These measures address different subjects: the reward seeks information about the nuclear programme, while the task force is described as focusing on weapons, sanctioned goods, dual-use items and unlawful revenue. The facts do not establish that the task force’s work is limited to nuclear-related material, or that information collected through the reward will be used by that unit. They do show that the task force is designed to coordinate with other U.S. agencies rather than operate without government partners. Its location and stated remit are specified, but no start date, staffing level or enforcement results are provided. A further element of pressure is the U.S. naval blockade, which Central Command says has prevented Iran from exporting more than $25 billion in crude oil. That estimate is larger than the reward’s $20 million ceiling, but the two amounts describe different things: one is the value of oil exports said to have been stopped, and the other is the maximum available for information. They therefore cannot be read as comparable measures of the same activity. The account does not provide a period for the oil estimate or explain how Central Command calculated it.

The reporting also describes a gap in international knowledge about Iran’s nuclear materials and equipment. Iran’s lack of compliance with the International Atomic Energy Agency has led the agency to lose continuity of knowledge about production and stocks of key components, including centrifuges. This means the agency’s tracking of those components is no longer continuous, according to the account; it does not specify the size of the gap or how many centrifuges are involved. The information supplied does not say that the reward was prompted by this loss of knowledge. Centrifuges matter because they are needed to make enriched uranium, which has more than one possible use. The material can serve as fuel for civilian reactors, while uranium enriched to about 90% or above can be used for nuclear weapons. That threshold distinguishes the stated weapons-related use from the civilian fuel use, but the facts do not say what enrichment level Iran has reached. Nor do they specify the present quantity or location of Iran’s centrifuges or enriched uranium. Iran’s stated position is that its nuclear programme serves peaceful purposes and that it does not plan to make a nuclear weapon. That position sits alongside the account of lost IAEA continuity about certain components, but the facts do not resolve the difference between Iran’s assurance and the agency’s reduced ability to track production and inventory. The reward announcement seeks information about the programme, but no stated U.S. explanation links it directly to a particular missing component or suspected activity. The available account thus sets out the offer, Iran’s position and the monitoring gap without establishing a causal chain among them. The political setting includes a war that the account describes as an eight-month conflict, as well as a previous effort to reach an agreement. Trump said Iran wanted the conflict to end and was keen to reach a deal. The United States and Iran had reached a preliminary arrangement in June aimed at ending the war and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, but it fell apart weeks afterward. The reported sequence was that Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the United States restored its blockade. Iranian negotiators have also discussed a proposal with mediators to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days, conditional on the United States meeting seven requirements. The facts do not list those requirements or say that the proposal was accepted. This proposal and the earlier preliminary arrangement are separate reported developments: one is a plan discussed by negotiators, while the other was an agreement that later collapsed. The account does not establish that either development has produced a lasting reopening of the strait.

Domestic politics may also shape the context for U.S. decisions. Trump and Vice-President JD Vance said that public opposition to the war had contributed to major Republican losses in the midterm elections. Their account links those losses to opposition to the war, but the facts do not provide election totals or independent evidence assessing that explanation. The reporting says the political consequences prompted speculation that the White House might avoid escalating the conflict, rather than documenting a decision to do so. Taken together, the facts describe a reward offer, a task force, a blockade and diplomatic discussions, but they do not establish that one measure caused another. The reward’s stated subject is information about Iran’s nuclear programme; the task force’s remit includes border movement of weapons and sanctioned goods, dual-use items and illegal revenue. Central Command’s oil figure concerns exports it says the blockade stopped, while the IAEA issue concerns continuity of knowledge about centrifuge production and stocks. These are distinct strands of the account, and no single figure measures their combined effect. The facts leave several practical questions unanswered, including how the maximum reward would be allocated, what would qualify an informant for relocation and what evidence the programme considers useful. They also do not give a measurement period for the blockade’s estimated oil impact, quantify the IAEA’s tracking gap or state the outcome of the latest discussions about the strait. What is stated is narrower: a reward of up to $20 million is available for information, relocation may be offered, and separate military and diplomatic developments remain part of the account. Those details define the announced change without showing what results it will produce.

John Holmes was the biggest name in American porn. At 4 a.m. on July 1, 1981, he opened up a door on Wonderland Avenue for the men who went on to kill four people with pipes.

Only days before, he had helped the people living there rob a major Los Angeles drug dealer.

LAPD detective Tom Lange, who worked the case, walks through how it was set up. Holmes visited Eddie Nash's house to buy drugs and made sure the back door stayed opened up. That night his friends came in, shoved a gun into Nash's mouth and walked off with roughly $100,000 in cash, drugs and guns. Holmes got paid in drugs plus a share.

Nash worked out who had left that door open. Scott Thorson, the ex-lover of Liberace, was at Nash's place that day. In court he later said "John was begging for his life."

Then Nash handed Holmes an assignment. "There'll be a knock on the door about 4 a.m. I want you to let them in."

Holmes did exactly that. Ron Launius, Billy DeVerell, Joy Miller and Barbara Richardson died. Susan Launius lived through it with a crushed skull.

Police found Holmes's palm print on the railing of the bed, right over Ron Launius's head. According to Lange, Holmes's wife told officers he turned up at her home that morning covered in blood.

He fled to Florida under a new name. Lange tracked him down at a hotel. In 1982 a jury cleared him of murder.

Nash offered the detectives $500,000 to drop him. At his first trial a single juror would not vote to convict. Twenty years on, Nash confessed he had bribed her.

Holmes never told anyone what went on inside that house. AIDS killed him in 1988, at 43.

Was John Holmes a murderer, or just the best known hostage in LA?

In the video below, Tom Lange, the detective on the case, explains how the whole setup worked.
