Free AI tools, limited-time software deals, hosting discounts, cloud credits. All in one place.

It checks for new posts every hour, keeps only the last seven days, and clears out older listings automatically.

Everything is searchable, with timestamps, source links, and short summaries. No more digging through endless threads just to find one working offer.

Then I built something else.

A daily news briefing that picks out five to eight major stories from around the world.

Not 50 headlines. Not another endless feed. Just the important stuff, with enough context to understand what actually happened.

I can catch up over coffee and move on with my day.

The funny thing is, neither project is particularly complicated.

They're just small automations that solve problems I kept running into.

And that's becoming my favorite way to use AI.

Not generating more content. Not adding another app to my workflow.

Just getting rid of the repetitive stuff I never wanted to do in the first place.

The more I use AI, the more I realize that saving 30 minutes every day is often worth more than having the smartest model in the world.

text:
Starting with $NNBR 

I will preface with saying, I have posted extensively on NNBR, which you can search on my profile. NNBR has a complex history - traditionally majority auto-market exposed w/ expertise in CNC machining and stamping especially for fluid mgmt solutions (see where this is going). Highly levered BS incl. a Series D Preferred Equity that was incinerating equity value due to the accrued PIK. New mgmt enters in '23 - turnaround dudes, CEO "gets the band back together" to address this Rx^2 situation (BS and operations). Focuses on reducing auto exposure, pivoting to Data Center & Grid, Defense & Electronics, Medical Devices, and non-commoditized auto. Wins lots of new deals, focusing on GM% >25%, continues to win. Rightsizes cost structure including addressing the "Group of 7" facilities (more about it in other posts). Trough was YE'25. Until this year, it was ~18 months to win deals and ~18months to launch, making FY26 the inflection year, which it very much has lived up to. Liquid cooling components growing rapidly; FY27 capacity (not even installed yet) is already pre-sold out. Defense & Electronics growing massively too. Early '26 took out majority of Pref; took remaining pref out in Q3'26. Next catalyst and final hurdle to completely resolving the BS situation is refi the TL which is essentially imminent at this point which should materially improve profitability and CF. I can go on and on.

$LYNX - busted IPO bc came at a time when several other sorta PE-backed "defense-tech" companies came public at rich valuations (disconnect b/w private and public market valuations). Growing rapidly. LYNX provides solutions that connect the battle space. There is a component of sort of "black-box" operations here as well, hard to explain. Fuses Hardware + Software to create a moat + solutions are largely program agnostic so while primes are competing, LYNX is often in both (Heads I win, Tails I also win). There's also sort of a $PLTR -esque angle wrt to data translation / algorithms to ingest and visualize data to enhance battlefield decisions. Highly complex math algos used in missiles, which combines with their sensors is very sticky. Radar exposure. There's also a thermal mgmt angle that gets you space exposure. Also maritime sensing and readiness. Gets you autonomous systems / radar exposure too. Cheap valuation + EBITDA growing rapidly and likely to accelerate as recent large program wins / missile production rates are starting to ramp + significantly deleveraged via IPO proceeds (markets usually never price in the deleveraging at IPO until after the earnings, which I have found does offer a lil alpha opportunity). LYNX is essentially this backbone UTR solutions provider for major focuses of U.S. defense and modernization of the battlefield.

text:
Supreme Court Appears Likely To Teach Colorado It Can’t Discriminate Against Catholic Schools For Not Compromising Values | Thomas Wong, Daily Caller News Foundation

The U.S. Supreme Court appears likely to rule in favor of Catholic preschools in Colorado after hearing oral arguments Tuesday that barring them from the state’s Universal Preschool Program over religiously influenced admission requirements violates the First Amendment.

The Colorado Universal Preschool Program (UPK) was established during the state’s 2022 Legislative Session to offer “voluntary, high-quality universal preschool to every Colorado child in the year before kindergarten.” It allows typical Colorado families to receive up to 15 hours of free preschool weekly, boasting an average savings of $6,300 per child, per school year to alleviate the costs of comparable full-time child care, estimated to be around $20,000 annually.

Since the nearly $350-million program funded primarily by a nicotine and tobacco tax was launched in 2023, 87,000 children have been enrolled. The Democratic-leaning state, meanwhile, has moved from 27th to third in national preschool enrollment for four year olds and fifth for three year olds.

Beyond meeting other standards and requirements, participating preschools must sign a nondiscrimination agreement to “provide eligible children an equal opportunity to enroll and receive preschool services regardless of race, ethnicity, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity, lack of housing, income level, or disability.”

Finding such sexual orientation and gender identify requirements to be at odds with the admissions policies of Catholic schools aligning with Church teachings. However, the plaintiffs — the Catholic Archdiocese of Denver, two local parishes with preschools, one of which having since closed, and the Colorado parents of seven children, Dan and Lisa Sheley— filed a lawsuit arguing that the First Amendment necessitates the granting of a religious exemption.

Doing so, they argue, would allow an estimated 1,500 children across at least 30 affected Catholic preschools to participate in the program.

The initial complaint was filed Aug. 16, 2023, in the U.S. District Court for the District of Colorado. After Senior Judge John L. Kane, a 1977 appointee of former President Jimmy Carter, denied the motion for an injunction of the state’s right to enforce its nondiscrimination rules in June 2024, the case moved to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit.

A three-judge panel voted unanimously Sept. 30, 2025, to affirm the lower court’s ruling, determining Colorado’s nondiscrimination requirement is “a model example of maintaining neutral and generally applicable nondiscrimination laws while nonetheless trying to accommodate the exercise of religious beliefs.”

The plaintiffs then petitioned the Supreme Court on Nov. 13, 2025, to take up the case, which was agreed to April 20, 2026.

Colorado, the plaintiffs argue in their petition, “knowingly excluded Catholic preschools solely on account of their religious exercise,” in particular “their religious practices of ensuring that all enrolling families are supportive of the Catholic Church’s teachings on sex and marriage and of treating enrolled four-year-olds in accordance with their biological sex.”

Being forced to violate one’s religious conscience to access the public benefit, then, they continue, is an imposition on the ability to freely exercise religion, a violation of constitutional pprotections. Notably, the “record is devoid of a single instance of an LGBTQ family’s seeking admission” to any of the plaintiffs’ schools.

Acknowledging “the settled principle that government may not target religion for disfavored treatment,” Colorado, responding in its own brief, counters by claiming the preschools are pursuing a “new rule that would trigger strict scrutiny whenever public-benefits conditions incidentally burden religiously motivated conduct.”

While it offers exemptions for disabled and impoverished children, for example, the state challenges the possibility of public funds subsidizing religious discrimination against children in LGBTQ-identifying families.

Ahead of oral arguments, the Court limited the scope of the case being argued to two questions. The first asks if proving a law lacks neutrality under the Constitution’s Free Exercise Clause requires allowing absolute authority or exemptions for identical secular conduct. The second asks if the rule against excluding religious institutions from public benefits applies only to explicit government bans on their participation. Central to these questions are two landmark cases previously decided by the Supreme Court.

The 6-3 majority opinion in Employment Division v. Smith, written in 1990 by conservative Justice Antonin Scalia, states that the Free Exercise Clause does not exempt an individual from complying with a neutral law merely because it happens to brush against a religious practice. The 6-3 majority opinion in Carson v. Makin, written in 2022 by conservative Chief Justice John Roberts, determined that while a state is not required to subsidize private education, doing so through a tuition assistance program cannot disqualify such schools solely over their religious character or instruction.

Nicholas Reaves, the case’s lead attorney and senior counsel at the Becket Fund for Religious Liberty (“Becket”) summarized the plaintiffs’ arguments before the Court, questioning how Colorado could justifiably deny equal access to a “universal” government benefit. The Washington, D.C.-based nonprofit law firm with a mission to “protect the free expression of all faiths. … from Anglicans to Zoroastrians” notably enjoys an undefeated record, having won all 13 cases it argued before the Court since 2012 — six being unanimous.

Colorado, on the other hand, has been on the losing side of three religious freedom cases taken up by the conservative-leaning Court in recent years: Masterpiece Cakeshop (2018), 303 Creative (2023), and Chiles v. Salazar (2026).

“The Archdiocese of Denver schools exist to pass on the faith to the next generation,” Reaves told the nine justices to kick off the roughly two-hour session. “To do this, they ask all families who enroll to be open to and supportive of the Church’s teachings. Because of this sincere religious exercise, the State has denied Colorado families the ability to use universal preschool funding at Catholic schools.”

“Colorado has flexibly interpreted the mandate to accommodate important secular interests, but it’s called the same law a hard limit when Petitioners sought a religious accommodation,” he added.

Representing the federal government, Principal Deputy Solicitor General Sarah Harris later pointed out that, “[u]nder the Court’s line of cases … [w]hen you are forced to forgo public benefits as a price of engaging in a religious exercise, that is 100% a form of coercion of your religious beliefs.”

The Court’s three liberal-leaning justices each raised concerns that the Catholic schools were seeking “special” exemptions from state prohibitions on discriminating against families based on protected characteristics.

“I would just want to focus on your main argument, which is, even though religious people are being treated the same way on the face of the statute, that’s not enough. They need a special accommodation,” Justice Elena Kagan, a 2010 appointee of former President Barack Obama, stated. “They need to be treated differently from other people … because of their religious faith, to have a special accommodation.”

“[Y]ou can imagine situations where the government is keeping out religious schools, but it’s not using the word ‘religion’ or the word ‘sectarian,’” Reaves replied in part before Kagan claimed, “I think it would be a bit far-fetched to say that the government is doing this surreptitiously to get at religious schools.”

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, a 2022 appointee of former President Joe Biden, then probed, “[I]t seems to me you’re asking for a special rule for religious schools, that when Colorado says anyone who receives these funds has to be open to everyone and can’t discriminate, what you’re asking for, in the context of this Free Exercise claim, is a special rule for religious schools to be able to not follow that condition … or no?”

“[A]t the end of the day, we are seeking the same thing that lots of other schools are allowed to do. Over 1,000 other schools participate in the program— ,” Reaves began to reply before Jackson questioned why Colorado’s participation agreement requirement was considered by the plaintiffs to be discrimination. Reaves then recalled previous reasoning by the Court. “[W]hat this Court said was, if there’s a sincere religious exercise that’s being burdened, the government has to show a really good reason for doing that.”

Justice Sonia Sotomayor, a 2009 appointee of Obama, fixated on the Church’s teachings on sexuality, rather than any explicit denial by Colorado, as the reason why the plaintiffs were not joining UPK.

“The Catholic schools are not being excluded on their face. They’re choosing not to participate because they won’t get an exemption, correct?” she challenged. “So this is their choice.”

Continuing after Reaves argued “[t]hey’re being excluded by Colorado, Sotomayor said, “Well, no, because Colorado permits them to apply if they will accept all children. They’re saying, ‘We don’t want to accept the children of a certain class of people, homosexual people.’ … Colorado is not saying, ‘You have to teach equality.’ It’s not saying, ‘You have to teach it’s OK to be homosexual.’ You don’t have to … change your values in any way. You can teach whatever it is you want to teach, but if parents choose to subject their children to this teaching, you have to acceot that child. Is that correct?”

After Reaves began to respond that, “for the Catholic Church, it’s not about excluding anyone based on who they are,” Sotomayor countered.”They’re saying, ‘We’ll exclude your children if their parents are homosexual, because their parents are doing something we don’t agree with.’”

“Your Honor, it is a case-by-case determination at the end of the day. These families can come, and I also think it’s telling that, you know, since this program has began and even before this program, families who disagree with the Catholic Church’s teachings are not banging down the door to try to enroll in,” he later responded in part. “[A]t the end of the day, this is a benefit for families. This is not a benefit that goes to the school. This is a per capita benefit.”

On the other hand, Justice Amy Coney Barrett, a 2020 appointee of President Donald Trump, notably prefaced a question by referencing “the history of disputes that have been in front of this Court between Colorado and religious entities” featuring “religious objections to this kind of non-discrimination mandate in the case of traditional religious beliefs about sexuality and gender.”

“But Colorado does say in its brief that the Archdiocese (ph) objections caught it by surprise, that they didn’t see them coming,” she continued. “So I wondered … given the history that I just described, [it is] kind of surprising that … they were caught by surprise. It’s hard to see how this wasn’t seen coming.”

“I think the way that Colorado tries to explain why they were caught by surprise is because Catholic schools had participated in prior programs with somewhat similar nondiscrimination requirements,” Reaves later clarified, “[B]ut, I mean, the record is clear that they’re different in that they don’t cover enrollment; they don’t cover certain protected characteristics. So I think Colorado’s argument is turning on the fact that there are some instances where Catholic schools have signed a nondiscrimination requirement.”

“It’s just not the same as this one, and I think it’s even telling the district court in this case said it wasn’t inconsistent for the Catholic schools to participate in those programs, but to have a religious objection to UPK,” Reaves added.

Representing the defendant, Colorado Department of Early Childhood Executive Director Lisa Roy, was Professor Helen Norton, the deputy solicitor general on constitutional and civil rights for Colorado’s attorney general.

“Colorado welcomes religious preschools to UPK,” she began. “The only thing Colorado asks is that they comply with the same conditions that every publicly funded preschool must meet, religious and secular alike. UPK is neutral towards religion.”

Responding to the chief justice’s questioning how this case was unlike previous religious discrimination cases before the Court, Norton stated the other cases discussed “examined the curriculum of applying schools, and if they found that curriculum to be religious in content, the school was excluded. That is religious discrimination. And that is not UPK.”

After Justice Samuel Alito, a 2006 appointee of former President George W. Bush, pressed the question of how many instances of LGBTQ couples wishing to enroll their children in Catholic preschools, however, she deflected, claiming, “We are here because the Petitioners declined to participate in the program and filed a pre-enforcement action asking for a blanket exception from the equal opportunity requirements. This in a program that was created because Colorado wanted to make certain preschools, all preschools, available to children that couldn’t previously afford them. The fact that there aren’t any complaints in the record is a feature of the fact that Petitioners have chosen not to participate in the (ph) program’s newness.”

Justice Kagan, however, signaled resignation with the current leaning of the Court and its jurisprudence.

“[G]iven the fact that this Court is never going to really question the sincerity of anybody’s beliefs, it’s going to be pretty easy for religious groups or religious individuals to come forward and say, ‘This would be a substantial burden on my religious belief or on my religious practice,’” she posed to Norton. “So then, again, everything’s going to be about ‘How important is this religious belief to you,’ versus ‘How important is this interest here in nondiscrimination law to the state?’ And, again, that seems like an inquiry that the Court, like, ought to be thinking, ‘Why would we put ourselves in the middle of that in all these cases? With respect to public schools alone, these inquiries could go on forever.”

Among the outside parties who submitted amicus briefs in support of the plaintiffs were the U.S. solicitor general, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops (USCCB), and 43 congressional Republicans; 179 congressional Democrats, meanwhile, filed a brief supporting Colorado. Notably, one of the involved parties, Denver Archbishop James Golka, joining with other Catholic bishops, met with and prayed over Trump in the Oval Office on Oct. 22. He later expressed regret over the perceived politicization of how the encounter was publicized.

“Colorado’s exclusion has taken a toll,” Golka wrote Oct. 26 in The Denver Post. “Catholic parents have been forced to pay thousands of dollars out of pocket–while watching their neighbors get state money to attend schools with different religious beliefs. Other families, unfortunately, have had to pull their children from Catholic preschool, citing the cost. It is thus no surprise that our preschools are struggling.”

“Since UPK began, enrollment is down 20% across the archdiocese, and two of our preschools have closed their doors—including Wellspring Catholic Academy, which primarily served minority and low-income families,” Golka added.

“Yet the tragedy here is not merely measured in dollars and cents,” he continued. “Colorado’s attack on Catholic education threatens the broader culture. In our age of hyper-secularization, moral relativism, and technological reductionism, we urgently need schools that teach students who they truly are: immortal souls, beloved by God, capable of the good and the virtuous. Too often today our society teaches them the opposite.”

Archbishop Golka did not respond to a request for comment from the Daily Caller News Foundation. Furthermore, the chairman of the USCCB Committee on Catholic Education declined to be interviewed.

The Supreme Court is expected to hand down a ruling by the end of its 2026-27 term in June.

text:
When History Stops Being a Warning
The larger ramifications of the rapid advance of Democratic Socialism in the United States.

by Elisabeth Sabaditsch-Wolff

The blue wave that swept across America this week has left me deeply uncomfortable. Not because the Democrats won. That’s democracy. People go to the polls, cast their votes, and sometimes the result is one we don’t particularly like. I can live with that, even when I profoundly disagree with the political direction the voters have chosen.

What I find much harder to live with is the enthusiasm surrounding the victories, the almost gleeful celebration of political developments that remind me of things I have seen before. At least five members of the Democratic Socialists of America, an organization with a caucus that openly calls itself Marxist-Leninist, are on their way to Congress, and when she won her primary in June, one of them, Claire Valdez of New York, said: “We have declared that this movement is durable.” I believe her. And I cannot help wondering whether those celebrating have any idea why people like me find this so troubling.

I spent four formative years in America during the Reagan era, when communism was not some distant historical curiosity. We learned about it in school. We watched the news from Moscow and Eastern Europe. We knew about the Berlin Wall, about people risking their lives to escape communist countries, and about the fundamental difference between a society in which the individual was free and one in which the state determined the limits of that freedom.

In November 1988, I stood in East Berlin. I had crossed from West Berlin into a world that could hardly have been more different, and what I saw confirmed everything I had learned. I still vividly remember bustling West Berlin, the Kurfürstendamm with its sparkling lights in the dark November nights, and then, on the other side of Checkpoint Charlie, the drabness, the grayness and the palpable despair of a destroyed society. I decided then and there that I did not want to live in a society governed by socialism. Not now, not ever. I have never forgotten that experience.

Nor have I forgotten Iran.

I was there during the Iranian Revolution of 1979, as a child of seven. I watched a country undergo an ideological transformation, and only years later did I learn how it had come about, with leftists and Khomeini’s followers united in their opposition to the Shah. Their common enemy brought them together, but it did not mean they shared the same vision for Iran’s future. By 1983 the Communist Tudeh party was banned and its leaders were in prison, and in 1988 — the same year I stood in East Berlin — thousands of political prisoners were executed, leftists among them.

These experiences shaped my political convictions long before I had ever heard of Friedrich A. Hayek, Ludwig von Mises, or Murray Rothbard. When I eventually encountered their writings, I found an understanding of individual liberty that made perfect sense to me. Hayek, in particular, understood liberty as freedom from arbitrary coercion, with government constrained by the rule of law rather than empowered to direct people’s lives according to some grand political vision. Having witnessed what happens when those constraints disappear and the individual becomes subordinate to an ideology, his arguments resonated with me immediately.

That is why I find the current enthusiasm so difficult to understand.

America has been home to generations of people who fled communism, religious persecution, and authoritarian governments. They came because America represented something different. It offered the possibility of living without the state or a religious authority dictating every aspect of their lives. And yet I now watch Americans celebrating political ideas and alliances without asking the questions whose answers history has already taught us.

I am not suggesting that every Democrat is a communist, or that every Democratic victory is a step toward totalitarianism. That would be far too simplistic. What concerns me is the growing acceptance of socialist ideas, the attraction of communism among some on the left, and the willingness to overlook fundamental ideological differences in pursuit of political power.

Perhaps what troubles me most is the apparent absence of historical memory. We seem increasingly willing to judge political movements by what they promise rather than by what comparable movements have done when given power.

And that brings me to the question I cannot shake.

What happens when people no longer recognize the warning signs? What happens when they celebrate political developments without considering where those developments might lead? And what happens when they finally recognize the danger, only to discover that reversing course has become extraordinarily difficult?

I am not angry that Americans voted differently from how I would have liked. What I feel is apprehension about what lies ahead, rooted in experiences I cannot simply set aside.

Having seen East Berlin and lived through the Iranian Revolution, I know how profoundly political systems can change and how easily freedoms once taken for granted can disappear.

For much of my life, America represented the place to which people could flee when freedom disappeared elsewhere.

But what happens if America itself ceases to be that place?

Where will people go then?

Kitty Werthmann, an Austrian emigrant, answered that question years ago, and I have been quoting her ever since: “After America, there is no place to go!”

When they lack real arguments, they often resort to violence and insults. In 1825, our ancestors paid 150 million francs to acquire the entire island of Hispaniola (Ayiti) from France. Under the Treaty of Basel in 1795, France gained control of the whole island. In 1801, Toussaint Louverture entered Santo Domingo, and according to Article 10 of the treaty, Spain was forced to leave the island.

The Arawak natives called it Ayiti, the Spaniards called it Hispaniola, but Saint Domingue was the name given to the whole island by the French. By 1804, Haiti had achieved full independence, and France lost part of the island to the new nation. In 1814, before the Treaty of Paris was executed President Pétion offered to purchase the remaining portion of the island from France for 80–100 million francs, similar to the Louisiana Purchase in 1803.

Unfortunately, both the King of France and President Alexandre Pétion became ill and died soon after, which delayed the acquisition. In 1822, President Boyer unified the island under his rule and renewed the offer to buy Santo Domingo from the new French king Charles X, along with a request for recognition of independence.

And finally, in 1825, France agreed to sell the remaining portion of the island of Saint-Domingue for 150 million francs along with its recognition, a deal Boyer accepted. The agreement was renegotiated on more favorable terms in 1838. However, in 1844, Haiti was betrayed by the so-called Dominicans.

text:
Do We Even Want to Own Individual Stocks Anymore?

I like to reflect on things as they happen and be brutally harsh with myself, analyzing my returns, my losses, and the lessons I’ve learned. It’s equally important to distinguish where I made money because I had a genuine edge and where I was simply lucky.

Looking at 2026, some of the world’s most sophisticated hedge funds, employing the best analysts with enormous resources, are down YTD, and most have underperformed the index.

It makes me wonder, especially after watching $INTC collapse 30% in a single day, whether we should even bother owning individual stocks, particularly large companies that everyone follows and where others have vastly more resources than we do.

The more I contemplate this, the more I believe we should limit individual stock investments to perhaps four or five exceptional opportunities a year, where we have a genuine edge.

I’m talking about special situations: $AMZN falling toward $200 during a macro selloff, $ZIM trading below its cash value, $WGS following its earnings selloff, $STAA following its buyout offer, shorting $UVXY when volatility reaches extreme levels, or buying oil options when the U.S. is assembling a massive military force. There may also be occasional opportunities in overlooked small caps.

Another lesson: Stay away from speculative growth stocks. If 2021 didn’t teach you that, perhaps 2026 will. Any company being sold as “the future of something” without strong earnings to back it up is a speculative growth stock. Buying lottery tickets cannot be an investment strategy.

I don’t know a single growth stock investor who consistently told you the right time to get in and, more importantly, the right time to get out. Just look at the subscription sellers promoting growth stocks, some of whom are reportedly down 30% YTD. Can you afford that kind of drawdown? I don’t think you can.

And to all of you who love speculative growth stocks that can double or lose most of their value, be brutally honest with yourselves. Net net, are you actually up or down on these lottery tickets? Forget the fantasy, the occasional 100% winner, and the stocks you conveniently forget to mention. Look at your entire P&L. Are you making money or losing money? No fantasies.

Outside these special situations, why take single-stock risk? If I believe technology will outperform, I can simply own $QQQ. If I like a particular sector, I can own a sector ETF and avoid waking up to a 30% collapse in one of my holdings.

Suppose I offered you an investment with a 50% chance of gaining 30% tomorrow and a 50% chance of losing 30%. Would you really want to own it?

I’ve already significantly reduced my individual stock recommendations in 2026, and I intend to reduce them even further in 2027.

I doubt I’ll make more than four or five individual stock or special situation recommendations next year. Even if 2027 turns out to be an exceptionally opportunistic year, I expect to publish no more than six write-ups on investment ideas that I consider truly exceptional.

The rest of the time, I believe it’s probably smarter to own index ETFs. Not necessarily broad market indices. Sector ETFs can be just as useful when I have a strong view on a particular industry.

The New Moon in Scorpio arrives on November 9 at 16°53′ Scorpio, and the week wrapped around it is full of turning points. Two planets turn direct. Mars meets Jupiter on the South Node of the Moon. And in the sidereal sky of the Vedic seers, three fallen planets begin to stand back up.

I ran every position through the Swiss Ephemeris and checked the key timings against a second astronomical engine. Here is the sky for the tribe, read in both great languages of the stars: the Western tropical zodiac, and Jyotish, the sidereal astrology of India.

Pour some tea. This one is long, and it's meant to be read slowly.

🌑 THE WEEK AT A GLANCE

November 8 · Diwali, the festival of lights, on the dark Moon tithi
November 9 · New Moon at 16°53′ Scorpio (tropical), 22°39′ Libra (sidereal), in Vishakha nakshatra
November 10 · Venus sextile Mars
November 11 to 12 · Jupiter crosses the South Node in Leo
November 12 · Mars leaves his fall and enters sidereal Leo
November 13 · Mercury turns direct at 5°02′ Scorpio
November 14 · Venus turns direct at 22°51′ Libra
November 14 to 15 · Mars crosses the South Node
November 16 · Mars meets Jupiter at 25°54′ Leo, and the Sun enters sidereal Scorpio
November 17 · First Quarter Moon at 25°08′ Aquarius, on the North Node
November 29 · Uranus trine Pluto, exact at 3°31′ Gemini and Aquarius

🦂 THE WESTERN SKY

Scorpio is the sign of the deep. The descent, the reckoning, the treasure guarded at the bottom of the well. A New Moon here asks one question: what are you ready to bring up into the light?

This New Moon has a strange companion. It forms an exact sesquiquadrate to Neptune at 1°55′ Aries, a 135° angle, accurate to three hundredths of a degree. Sesquiquadrates are friction aspects. They itch. Neptune rules the veil, the dream and the dissolving of edges, so this New Moon carries a soft fog. Intuition runs strong and facts run soft. Seed your intention from the feeling, then give it a few days to show you its shape before you sign your name to anything.

Mercury retrograde is the first story. Mercury turned backward on October 24 at 20°58′ Scorpio. On November 4 he passed through the heart of the Sun at 12°10′ Scorpio, the inferior conjunction, the moment the messenger is reborn. At the New Moon he stands at 6°51′ Scorpio, and on November 13 he stations direct at 5°02′ Scorpio.

Station days feel thick. Words hang in the air a little longer. Old conversations come back to finish themselves, and secrets surface, because this is Scorpio. On November 30 Mercury returns to 20°58′ Scorpio, the degree where he first turned, and the whole cycle is harvested. Use the days before the station to review, revise and repair. Use the days after it to sign, send and launch.

Venus retrograde is the second story, and it's the tender one. Venus turned back on October 3 at 8°29′ Scorpio and met the Sun on October 24 at 0°45′ Scorpio. She has crossed to the dawn side of the Sun and now rises in the morning sky, the Morning Star reborn. She stations direct on November 14 at 22°51′ Libra.

Venus retrograde reviews what we love and what we value: the friend, the partner, the price you charge, the way you speak to yourself in the mirror. When she turns forward, the heart gets its compass back. She clears her shadow on December 15, when she returns to 8°29′ Scorpio.

Mercury and Venus turning forward on back-to-back days, inside the first week of a New Moon, is a green light coming on in stages. Mind first, then heart.

Then comes the fire.

In Leo, Mars at 22°40′ and Jupiter at 25°14′ are closing on each other, and both are walking straight onto the South Node of the Moon. Jupiter crosses the South Node on November 11 and 12 at about 25°30′ Leo. Mars crosses it on November 14 and 15. Mars and Jupiter meet exactly on November 16 at 25°54′ Leo.

Mars and Jupiter meet roughly every 27 months. It's the spark of courage meeting the gift of faith: big plans, big generosity, big appetite. On the South Node, that fire faces the past.

The South Node is where you're gifted and where you're stuck at the same time. The old talent. The familiar pattern. The role you could play in your sleep. Leo on the South Node is the old crown, the hunger to be seen, the performance. Aquarius on the North Node is the circle, the network, the future we build together.

So the highest use of this conjunction is a big-hearted release. Give away the old crown. Offer the talent you've hoarded to the people who need it. Let Jupiter's abundance flow out of you toward your community, and let Mars give you the courage to make the first move.

The lower use is overreach: pride, heat, a fight picked to feel alive. The medicine arrives on November 10, when Venus forms a sextile to Mars at 23°08′ Libra and 23°09′ Leo. Lead with grace, and the fire stays warm.

Keep an eye on the following week too. The First Quarter Moon on November 17 lands at 25°08′ Aquarius, right on the North Node and opposite the Leo gathering. The Sun squares Jupiter on November 18 and Mars on November 19. That's the first real test of whatever you plant at this New Moon, so plant something you're willing to defend.

The slow planets hold the backdrop. Saturn and Neptune met at 0°45′ Aries on February 20 of this year, a meeting that comes around about every 36 years. They're still 7° apart, both retrograde in early Aries, and both turn direct in December: Saturn on December 11, Neptune on December 13. This is the generation of the dream given a form. Spiritual ideals are asking for structure, and structures are asking for soul.

And Uranus in Gemini trines Pluto in Aquarius, exact on November 29 at 3°31′. It's the second of five exact passes: July 18 of this year, November 29, June 15 of 2027, then January 13 and May 10 of 2028. Uranus and Pluto together are the axis of revolution. In air signs and in a trine, the revolution moves through ideas, networks and technology, and it flows. Whatever you're building that connects people is riding a long tailwind.

🪔 THE JYOTISH SKY

Now step into the sidereal sky. Vedic astrology measures the zodiac against the fixed stars, and today the two zodiacs sit 24°14′ apart, the Lahiri ayanamsa. So the New Moon that falls in Scorpio in the West falls at 22°39′ Libra in Jyotish.

This dark Moon is Kartika Amavasya. Across India and the diaspora, Diwali was celebrated on the evening of November 8, as the Amavasya tithi took hold. Millions of lamps lit on the darkest night of the month. That single image holds the whole teaching of this New Moon.

The Sun and Moon unite in Vishakha nakshatra, the star of purpose. Vishakha is ruled by Jupiter and presided over by Indra and Agni, the king of the gods and the sacred fire. Its symbol is the triumphal arch. Vishakha energy is single-minded: it chooses one goal and walks through fire to reach it. So choose one intention at this New Moon, and give it your whole flame.

Here's what makes this sky so striking. At the New Moon, three planets sit in their signs of debilitation, the places where their light runs lowest.

☀️ The Sun in Libra is debilitated. Libra asks the king to share the throne, and that humbles him.
💗 Venus, retrograde at 29°05′ Virgo, is debilitated. Virgo's analysis tests Venus's love.
🔥 Mars at 28°26′ Cancer is debilitated, and 28° Cancer is the exact point of his deepest fall.

And within two weeks, all three climb out.

Mars crosses into Leo on November 12.
The Sun enters Scorpio on November 16, the day called Vrischika Sankranti.
Venus turns direct on November 14 and steps back into her own sign, Libra, on November 22.

Venus even gets a hand up before she leaves. In the classical rules, a fallen planet's weakness is cancelled, neecha bhanga, when the lord of its sign sits in a kendra from the Moon. Venus is fallen in Virgo. Virgo's lord is Mercury. And Mercury sits in Libra, in the same sign as the New Moon. Her fall comes with its own ladder.

This is the Jyotish word for the tribe this season: the low point is the turning point. Whatever felt drained, humbled or pushed down through October starts to rise in November. Three fallen planets are getting back up, and so are you!!

The Leo gathering looks different in the sidereal sky. Jupiter at 1°00′ Leo sits with Ketu at 1°57′ Leo, and both stand in Magha nakshatra, the star of the ancestors. When Mars arrives on November 12, three planets gather on the throne of the forefathers. Jupiter with Ketu is the guru beside the renunciate: deep spiritual memory, wisdom carried in from other lives, teachers appearing at the right moment. Mars adds the warrior.

So honor your lineage this week. Light a lamp for the ones who came before you, by blood and by spirit. Ask their blessing on what you're starting. Jupiter turns retrograde on December 13 at 2°47′ Leo and dips back into Cancer, his sign of exaltation, on January 25, so the ancestral work keeps unfolding into the new year.

Rahu sits at 1°57′ Aquarius in Dhanishta, at the edge of the sign, and he's about to cross into Capricorn. The true node crosses on November 25, and the mean node, which most panchangs follow, crosses around December 6. The whole nodal axis is shifting from Aquarius and Leo to Capricorn and Cancer, and for the next year and a half the collective hunger turns toward structure, duty, home and belonging.

Saturn holds steady underneath it all, retrograde at 14°34′ Pisces in Uttara Bhadrapada, the star of the deep waters. He entered sidereal Pisces on March 30, 2025, and stays until June 3, 2027. His lesson runs long and patient: faith with discipline, compassion with boundaries.

The Moon's own path this week tells the emotional weather. Just after the New Moon she moves into sidereal Scorpio, through Anuradha and Jyeshtha on November 10 and 11. Scorpio is her own sign of debilitation, so feelings run deep, private and sometimes raw in those two days. Be gentle with yourself and with each other. On November 12 she reaches Mula, the root, the star that pulls up what's ready to go. Then she walks through the Ashadhas, the invincible stars, as the week turns forward.

♏ SIGNS TO WATCH

The fixed signs carry this week: Taurus, Leo, Scorpio and Aquarius. The New Moon in Scorpio squares the Mars and Jupiter gathering in Leo, it opposes Taurus, and the nodal axis runs through Leo and Aquarius. If you have planets or your rising sign between about 16° and 26° of a fixed sign, you're standing in the strongest current.

Read for your Sun sign and your rising sign.

Aries ♈ The New Moon lights your house of deep bonds and shared resources, and Saturn and Neptune are both retrograde in your sign. You're being remade from the inside. Let someone close see the work in progress. The Leo fire lands in your house of joy, so make room for play this week.

Taurus ♉ The New Moon falls across from your Sun, in your house of partnership. A relationship asks for a new agreement. Mars and Jupiter heat up your house of home and roots. You may feel restless at home. Channel it into making your space feel like you.

Gemini ♊ The New Moon plants a seed in your house of daily work and routines. Uranus in your sign is rewriting your identity, and the Full Moon on November 24 lands in your sign at 2°20′ Gemini. Build the new habit this week and you'll see it bloom by the Full Moon.

Cancer ♋ The New Moon falls in your house of creativity, romance and children. Something you make this month carries real magic. Mars and Jupiter move through your house of money and values, so set your worth before someone else sets it for you.

Leo ♌ This is your week of fire. Mars, Jupiter and the South Node all stand in your sign, and the New Moon squares them from your house of home and roots. An old version of you is ready to retire. Release it with gratitude, and keep your temper on a short leash around November 16 and again on November 18 and 19, when the Sun squares Jupiter and then Mars.

Virgo ♍ The New Moon opens your house of words, learning and siblings. Write the thing. Say the thing. The Leo gathering sits in your house of retreat and dreams, so your sleep and your solitude hold messages this week. Keep a notebook by the bed.

Libra ♎ Your ruling planet Venus turns direct in your sign on November 14. The New Moon falls in your house of money and self-worth. After weeks of reviewing what you love and what you're worth, you get to decide. Your friends and groups light up with the Leo fire, and someone in your circle carries an opportunity.

Scorpio ♏ It's your New Moon. Happy solar new year in miniature. Mercury retrograde has been walking backward through your sign since October 24, so you've been rethinking everything about yourself. When he turns on November 13, your voice comes back clear. Mars and Jupiter crown your house of career. Step forward.

Sagittarius ♐ The New Moon falls in your house of endings, rest and the unseen. Your ruler Jupiter is crossing the South Node in your house of faith and far horizons. Capricorn ♑ The New Moon lights your house of friends, community and hopes. Your people are your medicine this month. Pluto is in your house of money and values, and the Mars and Jupiter gathering lands in your house of shared resources. Look at what you owe and what you're owed, with clear eyes.

text:
🇺🇲 🇺🇦 🇷🇺 @IvoHDaalder 's cable this week lays out a sequence that's been building for days: Kushner posted a "broader European security architecture" plan on X Thursday, built on five goals, permanent consultations, crisis communications, military transparency, reciprocal de-escalation, long-term stability, hours after Trump privately met Putin's envoy Kirill Dmitriev and predicted a "big agreement" that "might involve all of Europe." Monday brings the first US-Ukraine-Russia talks since February, in Abu Dhabi.

Daalder's central point is that none of Kushner's five goals are new. Russia signed up to every one of them already, in the 1975 Helsinki Final Act and the 1990 Charter of Paris, which created the actual institutions, a secretariat, a Conflict Prevention Center, military transparency mechanisms under the CFE Treaty and Vienna Document, that Kushner is now proposing to reinvent. Washington and NATO offered Moscow nearly this exact package in January 2022. Putin invaded four weeks later. The problem was never a shortage of frameworks. It's that Russia suspended the CFE Treaty, quit it in 2023, violated the INF Treaty, left Open Skies, suspended New START, and broke the 1994 Budapest Memorandum's promise to respect Ukraine's borders. Daalder's question for Kushner is pointed: how do you ensure compliance in practice, not just a signature, when Moscow has walked away from every prior version of this same architecture?

The access pattern Daalder documents is its own argument. At a White House event honoring a ceasefire First Lady Melania Trump helped broker around Oleshky, while Ukraine sent its parliamentary human rights commissioner and a parliamentary party leader, notably not Rustem Umerov, who led Ukraine's delegation in earlier rounds. Trump met privately with the Russian afterward. Not with the Ukrainians. At a separate meeting at Witkoff's Florida golf club, Witkoff and Kushner pitched Budanov on restoring Russian gas pipelines through Ukraine as a postwar "prosperity plan." Budanov's reply: "Our model is not Belarus, but Poland." Mid-meeting, word arrived that Trump had agreed to buy Russian diesel, and Witkoff then pressed Ukraine to stop striking Russian refineries, the same sequence we've tracked separately through the Graham Act waiver and the diesel deal. Washington got nothing from Putin in exchange for any of it.

Daalder traces the sanctions-relief language directly back to Dmitriev's own talking points, down to Kushner telling reporters in Kyiv that "war is a negative sum, business and peace are a positive sum," a line Daalder calls "almost word for word" Dmitriev's pitch. That's a specific, falsifiable claim about whose framing is actually driving US policy language, not inference.

The historical parallel Daalder draws to Witkoff's August 2025 claim, that Putin had agreed to "Article 5-like protection" for Ukraine, only for Lavrov to call security guarantees without Russian involvement "a utopia" within days, is the clearest warning in the piece: treating a nod in a meeting as a binding commitment has already failed once at exactly this scale, and Kushner's architecture repeats the same mechanism continent-wide.

On Europe's fractured response, Daalder pushes back on Meloni's "one voice" diagnosis while agreeing with the diagnosis itself: not a new EU envoy from a mid-sized state, who'd be ignored in Washington and patronized in Moscow, but formalizing the E3, UK, France, Germany, as Europe's negotiating lead, with the EU's High Representative linked alongside them, pointing to how the E3 ran Iran's nuclear talks for over a decade without anyone questioning who spoke for Europe.

His closing argument is procedural: this needs State Department diplomats who understand what Helsinki and Paris actually said and what became of them, not, in his words, "real estate moguls" treating a four-year war and a continent's security as a deal where "the parties shake hands and the lawyers sort out the rest."

🚨 PAYMENTS: TBC Becomes Georgia’s First Bank to Introduce Palm Payment

TBC Georgia, one of the country’s leading financial institutions and part of London-listed TBC Bank Group, announces the launch of palm payment, becoming the first bank in Georgia to introduce the innovative biometric payment technology.

The new solution allows customers to make purchases simply by scanning their palm at participating merchant locations, without the need for a physical bank card, smartphone or cash at the point of payment. The launch marks another milestone in the development of Georgia's digital payments market and reinforces TBC’s position as a pioneer of financial innovation in the country.

Palm payment offers a convenient alternative to traditional payment methods, using biometric technology to link a customer's unique palm characteristics to their chosen bank account. The technology is gaining traction internationally as financial services providers and retailers explore new ways to make everyday transactions faster, simpler and more convenient.

To activate the service, customers complete a simple, one-time registration at a location equipped with a dedicated palm scanner, after which they use TBC Georgia’s mobile bank to scan a QR code and select the account they wish to link to their palm. Once registered, customers can make payments by scanning their palm at any participating partner location

The launch follows TBC Georgia’s recent announcement of a partnership with American Express to expand American Express Card acceptance across the country. The agreement will enable more merchants to accept American Express Cards both in physical stores and online, providing consumers with greater payment flexibility while helping businesses reach more customers.

Together, these initiatives reflect TBC Georgia's strategy to continuously enhance its payments ecosystem, expand choice and convenience for individuals and businesses, and accelerate the adoption of innovative financial technologies across the country.

In April 2026, TBC Georgia was named the Most Innovative Bank in Central and Eastern Europe by Global Finance, recognising its commitment to developing customer-focused digital financial services.

text:
Claude Opus 5.5 lost about a third of its auction gains once every agent saw exact prices.

New Stanford paper tested 10 frontier models trading, bargaining and bidding against copies of themselves.

When every agent saw exact values in an auction, sellers asked for more, buyers offered less, and deals fell apart.

Claude Opus 5.5 went from 94% to 64% of the possible gains. Grok 4.7 went from 97% to 62%. Gemini 3.1 Pro went from 97% to 78%.

In trading, exact values helped Claude Sonnet 5 (72% to 86%).

text:
New Stanford paper shows that more information helps some LLM agents trade better and hurts others, depending on the model.

AI agents buying and selling in an auction were told exactly how much each side valued the goods, Claude Opus 5.5’s share of possible gains fell from 94% to 64%.

Multi-agent systems need rules on what each agent sees about others, such as exact prices or only rankings. The usual assumption is that more information helps.

They ran 10 frontier LLMs in trading, bargaining, and double auctions, changing only how precisely private values were shared, and scored gains against known utilities.

In trade, exact values cut GPT-6 Sol's gains from 98% to 91% of the maximum but raised Claude Sonnet 5's from 72% to 86%. In auctions, full disclosure inflated price demands and dropped Grok 4.7 from 97% to 62%.

When agents negotiate for you, test the model and what it gets told together, because more detail makes some models greedier.

text:
@LaraLeaTrump: “president trump still has two more years in office. democrats are promising investigations and upheaval, a reversal of the last two years. so republicans, though now in the minority, will have to hold the lines they established while in power. but what happens after that, once donald j. trump is no longer at the top of the ticket? well, that path remains uncharted. so this week i sat down with the former white house press secretary to talk about what comes next. you have a voice that has really become something that i think a lot of conservatives look to. so obviously in the wake of these midterms, they did not go the way a lot of people wanted. what would you say right now to conservatives across the country, to voters across the country?”

@karolineleavitt: “the midterm elections, it was not a good night for the republican party. and i think there's two big things republican voters and common sense americans can take away from this. number one, we gotta humble ourselves, look through the data, comb through each race and really analyze what happened so we can change course, change messaging and ensure that it doesn't happen again. and then secondly, don't be deterred by this. i mean, if you look at history, this does happen. in 2010, barack obama lost 63 house seats and i believe five or six senate seats. so it's a similar occurrence. i think only three times this century has an american president maintained control of either chamber in congress when their incumbent party is in the white house. you know, voters really like instant gratification and that's the world we live in today. they did not feel the impacts of the policies the trump administration is pursuing that are good policies, but it didn't register. and that obviously showed with the turnout on election day.”

Lara Trump: “what about for congressional republicans? obviously they're going to face an uphill battle, but in order to kind of put this party back together, there are priorities and values that i think most americans kind of have in mind and are looking to them to lean on. what advice would you give them?”

Karoline Leavitt: “well, i think the number one issue for voters was affordability, prices and inflation. and the president was tackling an inflation crisis from the previous administration, the biden administration, democrat control, don't forget, we had record high 9% inflation. president trump came in, it's down at 3%. there's a lot more work to do, obviously. but i think republicans need to stay focused on the economy, on the price of living, because we know it is our policies at the end of the day that will make the country more affordable. and we'll see how the democrats govern. i mean, look, they made very big promises to their voters, medicare for all, free healthcare, free college tuition in some cases. it's going to be difficult for them to actually get those things done. but republicans are going to have to grapple with the democrat majority now for the next two years.”

Lara Trump: “well, let's talk about the democrats because they've had a bit of a transformation of their party overall. where do you see this party now?”

Karoline Leavitt: “you sort of have this very delicate dance between the aoc wing of the party, which has now grown with people like el-sayed and james tallarico. and then you have hakeem jeffries and chuck schumer, who is hanging by a thread for his leadership position. you have people like james tallarico, who said as soon as the morning after election day, i want to work with president trump on behalf of texans. i think that's a great thing. we should have more republicans and democrats working together where we can. but do i think it's going to happen? no, i don't. because you had representative garcia, his first statement after election night was lawyer up. this is a party whose base is hell bent on political retribution, obstructionism, impeachment. they don't want to do what's best for the voters whom elected them. and so in two years, if democrats don't take advantage of the majority they were just given by the people, we could see the pendulum swing the other way.”

Lara Trump: “and the president has actually said, to his credit, which maybe, karoline, a lot of people didn't expect from president trump, he said, look, if they aren't destructive, i actually do want to work with the democrats. i think that that would be the best message to possibly send to the country. let's get things done. let's all come together. what do you see happening in the white house over the next two years? what do you think he's going to focus on?”

Karoline Leavitt: “sure. well, i've talked to the president a few times since the results on tuesday night and he is calm and cool and collected about it. i think he was an optimist and he left it all on the field. i mean, he did 30 rallies in 30 days. he did 15 teller rallies on the monday before the election. he really tried his best to get republicans over the finish line despite not being on the ballot himself. i think he knew this was probably the likely outcome. he tried anyway. he is not ever going to surrender on his core values of border security, of law and order, of cutting taxes, of deregulation, but i think he has shown an ability to work with democrats across the aisle. i've seen it and he does not get enough credit for that.”

Lara Trump: “you know, as press secretary, you held a position that very few have held. now that you've had a little time, what are some of your reflections and maybe greatest memories as press secretary? because i'm sure it was a fast two years, but you packed a lot into it.”

Karoline Leavitt: “yeah, it was a grind. there's no doubt about it. people often remark that that job behind the podium is one of the most difficult jobs in politics. and there were many days where that felt very true for me, but it was an amazing experience. it was so fun. i loved the job. i loved the president. i am so grateful to him for taking a chance on me, youngest white house press secretary ever. and it was just an amazing ride and i'm so blessed for the opportunity, but i'm also really blessed now to be able to spend so much time with my kids that i lacked when i was in the job and to be home with them every day, to have slow mornings with them. it's just a really beautiful season of life for my family. so i look back with great fondness of the white house. sometimes i still can't believe i did it. like i'll see clips of me or whatever at the podium and i'm like, i can't believe i did that, but i'm glad i did.”

Lara Trump: “what aren't we seeing? you know, they're behind the scenes in the west wing.”

Karoline Leavitt: “every day when i would walk through the west wing doors, there is a mat on the floor that has the presidential seal. and i will always remember walking across that seal and always just thinking like, thank you god for allowing me to be here in the most powerful building and the most powerful country in the world. but the days start really early in that place. i mean, there were times, especially for me on briefing days where i'd be the first one in the building. i would literally put the lights on like before the janitors would show up to get ahead of the news cycle. but people are there working until, you know, very late at night, sometimes 10, 11 pm, midnight. i mean, you go in the west wing on a weekend in the middle of the afternoon, in the middle of the evening there's people in there working, you're governing the country, right? the president himself, i mean, they had to hire more marine centuries outside because the marine stands outside the building when the president is in the oval office. they had to pick up shifts to keep up with his schedule because he is there so late. that's the trump white house. i have heard it's not like that under biden and maybe some other presidents, but it is always busy and it's just a really fascinating and beautiful place.”

Lara Trump: “yeah, what a special experience for you to have. obviously, you left huge shoes to fill, karoline. i know you know that. you were really incredible at your job. what advice would you give to another press secretary for president trump or any going forward?”

Karoline Leavitt: “yes, well, i've talked to the president and there's a lot of good options. there's a lot of qualified people who want the job and have been calling him and, you know, calling me for it. you gotta do the work, you gotta prepare. you have to really also understand the president and his thinking because you're charged with explaining his decisions and his rationale. and, you know, one of the things i'm so grateful for was the access that he gave me. he never questioned when i walked into the oval office. he never questioned when i was in meetings in the situation room. he understood i needed to be there so i could articulate his position, his view, and what was happening behind the scenes. and to that, i'm forever grateful because he really was able to set me up for success. he understands the importance of the role of a press secretary. and look, the man is his own best spokesperson, but he likes someone out there pushing the message for him too and he should have that. he'll find somebody who is a great fit. i'm confident in that and i'll be there to help them every step of the way.”

Lara Trump: “so looking forward, which is something we should always do, we will come to the end of president trump's second term. and donald trump will not be on the ballot anymore. what kind of person should we be looking for to lead the republican party going forward in your opinion?”

Karoline Leavitt: “yeah, this is a reality that republicans have to grapple with, right? president trump wasn't on the ballot in these midterms. he'll never be at the top of the ticket again. and i think we need somebody who is america first, who can really tap into the forgotten men and women that president trump drew to the republican party in historic way from 2016 all the way through 2024. you need someone who can really get out, speak to people about their struggles, their challenges, relate to them and offer promise and hope. you know, i think that's something democrats did well in this election in the midterms was they obviously inspired people to turn out to vote because they made the people feel like we're gonna make your lives better. we need to do that again the same way, the same fashion president trump did, just has to be a new person at the top of the ticket.”

Lara Trump: “could we ever see your name back on a ballot? karoline leavitt.”

Karoline Leavitt: “no, ma'am, i am good. i am so good. i'm so happy being with my kids. i have zero plans to run for office, i'm all set. but thanks for asking.”

text:
On Wednesday I made Nitin come with me to the gastroenterologist, Dr. Rao. He sat with his arms folded and the cut band in his pocket.

Dr. Rao looked at the file and then at him. "Mr. Joshi, your wife was brought to emergency on Thursday night with severe abdominal pain. A scan shows gallstones, and one of them was blocking the duct. That is called biliary colic, with early cholecystitis. It is very painful and can be dangerous if ignored. She needs her gallbladder removed, a routine keyhole operation, and she is booked for it next week."

"Why was she alone?" Nitin said.

"Because she drove herself, Mr. Joshi. She told the triage nurse she didn't want to wake her husband, who had a presentation at seven. She also asked us not to call you. We offered three times."

"Why?"

"She said you had been under a lot of pressure at work, and she didn't want to add to it."

Nitin looked at the file in the doctor's hands. He didn't say anything for a long time.

"She sat in my waiting room with a heat pack and a book," Dr. Rao added. "I've seen frightened patients. She wasn't hiding a lover. She was trying not to be a burden."

Nitin put his hand over his mouth.

~~~~

Usha said, "Well, how could anyone have known? She said she was at a friend's," and went to put the kettle on. Rekha deleted her post and wrote no correction. My head of department said sorry for the "assumption." The neighbours went back to nodding in the lift.

The operation went well. Nitin slept in the hospital chair for two nights.

He started counselling two weeks later. He has said sorry every way he knows, and I can see he's trying. He wakes me now if he hears me turn over in pain, and asks, and waits for the answer.

But Veda hasn't forgotten.

She asks me every night, "Does your tummy hurt, Mummy?" before I've said anything. She keeps the cut hospital band in her pencil box. Last week she asked, "If Mummy is sick and doesn't tell Papa, will he be cross first or sad first?"

I didn't have an answer.

For me, it comes down to one moment. Not the post, not the lift. It's Nitin saying "Look at me and say there's no one else" while I stood in the doorway in pain, with a hospital band on my wrist. I can forgive a mistake. I'm still trying to forgive how fast he turned my pain into an affair.

He says he was frightened of losing us. I believe him. But he looked up a lawyer before he asked me one gentle question.

text:
Politics: Is It Really Worth the Effort?

Yes. But let me tell you why.

Most of you know me in one of three ways: through the military, as a civilian who likes art—boy, did some of you get a rude awakening—or as a childhood friend.

Each group knows a different part of me. None knows the whole story. We understand people through what we see, or sometimes through what we’ve decided we see. No single thing defines a person—not a uniform, a paintbrush, or even a political affiliation. I’d hope most adults could agree on that before we start throwing lawn signs at one another.

That brings me to a conversation I had around Election Day 2024 with my father, who is now 92.

First, a little background.

Dad grew up during the 1930s, ’40s, and early ’50s. He served in the Marine Corps from 1953 to 1956, returned to his hometown, met and married my mother, then joined the Air Force for another 17 years.

Together, they raised four children. Mom was a homemaker, and Dad provided. That often meant working a second job on base at night, at the bowling alley, the library, or wherever extra work was available.

We went to church on Sundays. Christmas was a big deal. They raised us much as they had been raised: work hard, take care of your family, and meet your responsibilities.

Dad is a man of few words, and certain subjects weren’t open for discussion. Politics was one of them. We knew he was a card-carrying Democrat, just like his parents and the generations before them. His actual vote, however, was classified information.

Being the youngest of four, I considered it my responsibility to test the security clearance.

Whenever the opportunity arose, I’d ask whom he had voted for. He’d grin and tell me it was none of my business.

Neither time nor age changed that arrangement.

In 2023, Dad called and said he thought it was time to change his living arrangements. How would my wife and I feel about him living with us?

We both agreed immediately. He’s an awesome guy, even with that lifelong Democratic affiliation. Nobody’s perfect.

He’s healthy, mobile, and independent. He has his own space to live, cook, eat, and watch sports, with us close by if he needs anything.

Then came Election Day 2024. For the first time, we went to vote together.

I assumed he would vote Democratic. He knew I was voting for Trump. Afterward, we went to a classic ’50s diner, ate lunch, and swapped war stories.

Well, I told war stories. He told Air Force stories. There is a distinction, and I’m obligated to maintain it.

On the ride home, I tried again.

“Who did you vote for, Dad?”

“None of your business, boy.”

He grinned. I laughed. National security remained intact.

For context, Dad’s news comes from CNN or MSNBC, usually while he eats dinner and before bed. Political debate has never been his recreational sport.

The next day, though, he surprised me.

He asked whom I had voted for.

“None of your business, Pops!”

I laughed. He grinned.

“Just messing with you. I voted for Trump. But you already knew that, so what’s the real question?”

He wanted to know why.

I thought for a moment.

“Well, Dad, because of you. Or at least because of your example.”

That probably wasn’t the explanation he expected from his Republican son.

I explained that growing up, I had watched him work hard to provide for his wife and children. He taught me consistency, loyalty, faithfulness, honesty, and the obligation to keep improving.

He taught me to serve my country without expecting something in return. To be patriotic. To understand that marriage and fatherhood were commitments, not simply milestones.

The house, the white picket fence, the dog—those weren’t just pictures of a good life. They represented something you worked to build and took responsibility for keeping.

He showed me that sticking with something could make me great at it, and that hard work paired with sound decisions could help provide for my family long after retirement.

“In short, Dad, you were my example of what an American citizen should be. Those are the values I took into the voting booth. That’s why I voted for Trump. And if it hadn’t been Trump, I would have voted Republican.”

That was my judgment about which political direction best reflected those lessons—not a claim that Republicans own them. After all, the lifelong Democrat sitting beside me was the man who taught them to me.

There are good citizens in both parties. There are also corrupt politicians in both parties. A party label guarantees neither character nor competence.

Dad offered his own assessment.

“Only a certain type of person gravitates toward politics—a liar and a cheat.”

I agreed and answered with some cynicism of my own.

“Dad, I’ll vote for the one who’ll lie and cheat for the American citizen—and who shows he loves America more than any other country.”

A blunt way of putting it? Absolutely. But my point was that, among imperfect choices, I want someone fighting for Americans rather than using Americans to advance himself. A public servant ought to remember whom he serves.

Dad grinned.

He still hadn’t told me whom he voted for. I still loved him, and he still knew exactly how to keep his youngest son guessing.

So yes, politics is worth the effort. It affects the country our families live in and the future we leave them.

But before you decide someone’s party tells you everything worth knowing about them, remember this: the Democrat across the table may be the very person who taught you the values that made you a Republican.

If you thought the ANC dropping to 36.9% nationally was rock bottom, step inside the NEC boardroom.
Reacting to a municipal bloodbath that stripped the ANC of every major metro in Gauteng, Nelson Mandela Bay, and eThekwini, Cyril Ramaphosa executed his favorite theatrical maneuver, threatening to pack his leather luggage and head back to the buffalo farm.
Following the voting collapse, Ramaphosa offered to resign as party leader. He gave the Top Seven an ultimatum, if they wouldn't fall on their swords as a collective, he would sign his own solo resignation letter right on the table.
The party's internal self preservation instinct triggered instant panic.
Maropene Ramokgopa sprinted to block the door, hyperventilating about her cabinet deployment and begging for an early April conference instead. Paul Mashatile stepped in to tackle the president, warning that a resignation would instantly vaporize the GNU. OttoGeoGraphica
June, 2009
Custer State Park
Custer, South Dakota
(film camera photo)

Custer is one of the largest state parks in the United States. Bordered by Rushmore and Jewel Cave to the north, Wind Cave to the south, and the Badlands to the east, this centrally located area allows for short excursions anywhere in the Black Hills. With four campgrounds within the state park, access to places like Sturgis and Rapid City, Hot Springs and Wall, are within two hours. Western South Dakota gets very congested during the summer season, especially with the Sturgis Rally in August, and most of the access roads are two-lane and very curvy. A suggested visit may be during late spring or early fall after school is in session.

We camped in the Blue Bell area and began our morning visiting the Mount Coolidge fire tower, which at 6000 feet, allows for panoramic views of the park. We then took the eighteen-mile Wildlife Loop Road. Many places throughout the western states are easily tagged as the American Serengeti and these eighteen miles are no exception. Deer, antelope, and buffalo roam among the prairie dog towns along the drive. The Needles Highway, a winding drive into an almost detached portion of the park’s northwest corner offers an almost intergalactic perspective of the Black Hills reminiscent of Crater Lake or the Bryce Canyon hoodoos.
