text:
Wear your heart on your sleeve. Give people a chance to know you.

Everyone wants to showcase perfect. But we all know how much life asks of us. The friendships get deeper when you’re willing to share the hard parts, too.

I moved to Miami with a bookbag, two suitcases, and my intuition.

I had an amazing life in Atlanta. Leaving something good makes you question yourself. But man, the blessings that have come from taking that leap.

In my first few months here, people have offered me a place to stay, invited me to dinner, sent me business, and checked in just to see how I’m doing.

Genuine, kindhearted people. I’m grateful for every one of them.

X and IG have opened doors I couldn’t have imagined. Connections that were just names on a screen in Atlanta have become friends here in Miami.

Scroll back four years and you can see the whole journey. Self-development. Marathon training. A breakup. Changing offers and industries. Figuring it out in public.

Those introductions mean so much more when you’ve let people see who you are along the way.

All glory to God. But you have to put yourself in motion.

Follow your intuition. Be vulnerable. Look for the good in every day, conversation, and opportunity.

Sometimes you have to leave good to find great.

text:
Musk to Texas Democrats: Our Success Came From Freedom, Not Your Favors

Elon Musk just slapped down a Wall Street Journal story claiming Texas Democrats plan to yank the "white-glove treatment" for SpaceX and Tesla now that they've flipped the state. He made it plain: the companies thrived here because the government stayed out of the way.

"SpaceX and Tesla have prospered in Texas, because we were not constantly operating under an oppressive and extractive state government," Musk wrote.

He explained the practical reasons too. Factories need hands-on leadership. "And I need to be close to the factories, so that I can walk the floor in person. That’s why the first major SpaceX factory was in LA and first major Tesla factory was in SF Bay Area."

Then California turned hostile. "As California became increasingly difficult, due to extreme taxes and overregulation, we moved our major domestic expansions and HQ to Texas."

This is the same pattern that hollowed out California's tech and manufacturing base. High taxes, endless rules, and politicians treating productive companies like piñatas drove the growth elsewhere. Texas offered the opposite: lower burdens, faster permitting, and room to build. Jobs followed. Investment followed. Rockets and cars got built instead of lawsuits.

Now the new Democratic leadership is signaling they want to change the deal. They talk about ending special treatment, scrutinizing land deals, slowing data centers, and reviewing incentives. Translation: they see a successful employer and reach for the regulatory toolbox. The same approach that chased SpaceX and Tesla out of California is being imported to Texas.

Musk is not asking for favors. He is stating the obvious. Companies locate where they can operate without constant extraction and interference. Texas gained by being less California. If Democrats reverse that, the next expansion, the next factory, the next launch complex will simply go somewhere else. Florida has already been mentioned. Other red states are open for business.

The left celebrates the blue wave as a rebuke to Musk's spending. What they are actually celebrating is the chance to punish the companies that create the jobs and tax base they want to spend. History shows how that ends. California wrote the playbook. Texas is now being invited to copy it.

text:
Freedom in Christ isn't a license to neglect the body He gave us. Our Lord made clear that what truly defiles us comes from the heart, and the Church teaches that no food can condemn the soul. But wisdom still asks: is this good for the temple of the Holy Spirit? (1 Cor 6:19-20)

The Old Testament forbade swine as food (Lev 11:7; Deut 14:8). Pork can carry parasites and disease, and a tired, sick body has a harder time praying, serving, and receiving the joy God offers. "All things are lawful, but not all things are beneficial" (1 Cor 10:23).

Consider setting swine aside as an act of discipline and love for the body God made. And whatever is on your plate, bless it before you eat, especially if you choose to pretend swine is actually food. Food is "sanctified by the word of God and prayer" (1 Tim 4:4-5).

text:
Supported Temple @deepigoyal @agingroy I posted about it publicly. Not because I had studied the science. Because an Indian founder was trying to build something original and take it to the world, and I wanted him to win.

Then I read this .. Please do not support us because we are an Indian startup. We don't need/want nationalist support. That one hurt.

Nobody was asking Temple to compete on patriotism. Nobody said, Buy it because it's Indian. What people offered was goodwill. Early cheering. The kind of support every founder in this country has quietly depended on at some point.

@zomato knows this better than anyone. Millions of Indians downloaded the app, defended it, bought the IPO, and cheered when it listed. Much of that was pride in an Indian company making it big. Nobody called it nationalism then.

Wanting to compete globally is great. Every Indian startup should aim for that. But you don't need to push away the people back home to do it. Global ambition and gratitude to your home crowd can sit together. The best founders manage both.

Saying we don't need you to people who were rooting for you isn't confidence. It's arrogance.

The irony is that this support costs nothing and asks for nothing. It's people saying  go win. Rejecting it doesn't make Temple look more global. It just makes it look less likeable.

I still hope Temple succeeds. I just won't be cheering quite as loudly.
You may not want our support. You had it anyway. Not anymore.

text:
Hello everyone. Happy Diwali! 

Thank you for your criticism, your support and your time over the last two days. Gives me much needed clarity on what we need to explain better: 

1.  ⁠Temple is not made for India. It’s made for the world. Please check pricing. We don’t expect any more than 1% of Temples being sold in India. 

2.⁠ ⁠If you are upset that the pricing is too high, I am sorry. There’s a lot of work that went into Temple, and we priced it at what we think it’s worth. If you think its overpriced, you can wait for user reviews to decide if its worth your money.

3.⁠ ⁠Please do not support us because we are an Indian startup. We want to compete globally. We don’t need/want nationalist support. Support us if you want to support early innovation, which could help you live a better life, and will continue to add more proof to its science over the years. 

4.⁠ ⁠There are different audiences which buy products at various levels of proof. Proof goes from whitepaper -> pre-print -> peer reviewed. You are free to sit on the fence until peer reviewed proof arrives. You are free to not believe it even then. Nobody is forcing you to buy. Making announcements is our right; and if we overclaim anywhere, we will inevitably fall into regulatory trouble everywhere in the world. 

5.⁠ ⁠We didn’t make any medical claim. Doctors primarily see things from a medical lens, so they see every claim as a medical claim. I repeat – Temple is strictly a fitness + AI device, and we've made no medical claims. Temple is not proven to diagnose or prevent any disease. It doesn't do anything which replaces the need for you to see a doctor. 

6.⁠ ⁠The main point of Temple is NOT Brain Flow. That’s what we just started Temple for, and studies on Brain Flow are the first ones getting out. 

7.⁠ ⁠The main point of Temple is Entropy (I shared the HomeScreen of Temple three months ago with Entropy as the main thing). Our emails to our waitlisted users only talk about Entropy. We haven’t published anything on Entropy yet. We will. If you want to buy Temple before that, please do. If you don’t want to, don’t.

8.⁠ ⁠Roomdeaf AI is an expansion of the device’s capabilities, and our vision for Temple. It is not a pivot.

9.⁠ ⁠Social media is not the regulator for Temple. Wherever we need regulatory clearances, we will have them before we make any claim needing them. 

10. I will post a detailed note on how we calculate Brain Flow, its uses, and most importantly, its limitations in a bit (tomorrow).

वसुदेवसुतं देवं कंसचाणूरमर्दनम् ।  देवकीपरमानन्दं कृष्णं वन्दे जगद्गुरुम् ॥ (vasudevasutaṃ devaṃ kaṃsacāṇūramardanam | devakīparamānandaṃ kṛṣṇaṃ vande jagadgurum || —I bow to Lord Kṛṣṇa, the son of Vasudevā, the divine one who destroyed Kaṁsa and Cāṇūra, the supreme joy of Devakī, and the Guru of the universe)   Dīpāvalī— āvaḷi refers to an array of dīpā, symbolizing continuous growth. In Kāñcīpuram, renowned as a great temple city, all 184 Śiva temples perform abhiṣekam, adorn the deities with new vastra (garments) and alankara, offer naivedyam such as boondi, and do dīpārādhana on Dīpāvalī Day. For the past 36 years, these special pūjās have continued with Kanchi Mahāperiyavā's āśīrvāda.

Even at ninety-five, He arranged the restoration of numerous temples in Kāñcīpuram. He continued to walk to different temples at the ages of 90, 91, 92, and 93. He ensured that many ancient Vānam Pārtha Śiva Liṅgas (Śiva Liṅgam facing the sky with no roof) throughout Kāñcīpuram were protected by constructing roofs and proper structures over them so that they would not be damaged by rain or harsh sunlight. He was also instrumental in organizing and conducting the Kumbhābhiṣekams of major temples such as Kāmākṣī Amman Temple and Mīnākṣī Amman Temple. He walked to many temples, including Lakṣmīśvara Temple and Karkīśvara Temple, ensured their restoration, and established new temples in Kāñcīpuram. He attached immense importance to temple preservation. 

Through the arrangements and vision of the Kanchi Mahāperiyavā, these special Dīpāvalī pūjās came to be conducted in the temples of Kāñcīpuram, and the tradition continues to this day. On that day, abhiṣeka and archana will be performed in all 184 Śiva temples. It is indeed a most remarkable undertaking. By nurturing bhakti to attain growth and success in many aspects of life, including employment, business, education, and enjoying a radiant life and attaining auspiciousness, as in தீப மங்கள ஜோதி நமோ நம (dīpa maṅgala jyoti namo namaḥ—Salutations to the auspicious divine light of the lamp), we should attain His grace by bowing at His feet, as expressed in the saying, Avan arulale avan thal vanangi (By His grace, we bow at His feet). Hara Hara Śaṅkarā Jaya Jaya Śaṅkarā  #kamakoti  #JagadguruVacanam

text:
Righteous Zeal and Sacred Worship
November 9, 2026
Feast of the Dedication of the Lateran Basilica in Rome

Jesus answered and said to them, “Destroy this temple and in three days I will raise it up.” The Jews said, “This temple has been under construction for forty-six years, and you will raise it up in three days?” But he was speaking about the temple of his Body. John 2:19–21

The Lateran Basilica, officially known as the Archbasilica of the Most Holy Savior and of Saints John the Baptist and John the Evangelist, is the cathedral church of the Diocese of Rome and holds the unique distinction of being the mother and head of all churches throughout the world. It is the oldest of the four major papal basilicas in Rome and was the first Christian basilica built in the city after Emperor Constantine’s Edict of Milan in AD 313 legalized Christianity.

The basilica was dedicated in 324 by Pope Sylvester I to Christ the Savior. Later, it was also dedicated to Saints John the Baptist and John the Evangelist. As the pope’s official cathedral, the Lateran Basilica is the spiritual heart of the universal Church. Its annual dedication feast reminds us of the sacredness of every church building, each one a visible sign of the invisible Church and a privileged place of encounter with the living God.

Today’s Gospel offers a striking portrayal of Jesus, the Son of God, cleansing the temple in Jerusalem with righteous anger. His actions were not impulsive, but deliberate. He made a whip of cords and drove out those who had turned His Father’s house into a marketplace. This dramatic scene challenges us to reflect more deeply on the holiness of places set apart for divine worship and invites us into the mystery of the Church as the Body of Christ.

First, Jesus’ actions reveal the sacred character of our churches. By honoring the Dedication of the Lateran Basilica, we honor every church consecrated for the worship of God. Our churches are not to be marketplaces, theaters, or social halls. At their center is the altar and the tabernacle—places where the divine Presence dwells among us. In these sacred spaces, we listen to the Word of God, offer our lives to Christ, and are spiritually renewed to bring His presence into the world.

Jesus’ cleansing of the Jerusalem Temple also reminds us that our souls are now the true temples of God—the dwelling place of the Holy Spirit and tabernacles of the Most High. Just as our Lord was filled with zeal to cleanse the Temple, so too is He continually moved to purify our souls, calling each of us to repentance and conversion. When considering our own need for cleansing and purification, it’s helpful to ponder Jesus’ zeal in the Temple, seeing Him desiring to cleanse us with the same zeal.

Though this divine purification is personal, it is also ecclesial and communal. The Church, as the Mystical Body of Christ, must always be renewed and transformed. Throughout history, the Church as an institution has strayed from the path of holiness through the sins of her members. When this has happened, God has raised up saints to serve as prophetic voices, calling the members of the Church on earth to holiness, cleansing, and fidelity.

The Church’s cleansing, as well as our own, is not always met with open arms. When the religious leaders confronted Jesus as He cleansed the Jerusalem Temple, He spoke a mysterious prophecy: “Destroy this temple and in three days I will raise it up.” Though misunderstood at the time, He was speaking of His own Body—the true and eternal Temple. Today, He continues to speak those words about His Body, the Church, and about each of us, who are members of that Body through grace. We must die in and with Him so that we will rise renewed as saints and as the holy and spotless Bride of Christ.

Reflect today on the sacredness of your own soul. Ask our Lord to cleanse whatever needs purifying and to raise you up in holiness, so that you may become a more perfect temple of His presence in the world. Pray also for your parish church and the Church universal. With zeal, pray for the purification necessary to make every member of the Church true temples of God.

Most zealous Lord, Your righteous anger is not directed at me or at any member of Your Church, but at the sin and defilement that hinder us from offering You pure and holy worship. Please cleanse me and every member of Your Mystical Body, that we may radiate Your divine presence more fully in this world and draw all people to Yourself. Jesus, I trust in You.

text:
You focus only on the end of the agreement, ignoring the beginning. Why not tell the truth about how this whole situation got started? It was HAITI, not FRANCE, that made the first proposal right after the Paris Treaty in 1814. Why would Haiti suddenly offer France a significant sum of money—80 to 100 million francs— in 1814? Petion had learned of the Paris Treaty, prompting him to quickly propose buying out France before the Paris Treaty was enforced.

By 1822, the entire island of Saint Domingue was under Boyer's leadership. Originally, Haiti offered 100 million francs, while France countered with 150 million francs; by 1825, the deal was finalized, similar to France selling its territory to the Americans in the Louisiana Purchase.

From 1801, when Toussaint entered Santo Domingo, until 1844, when the Spanish-speaking Haitians rebelled and declared their independence, the whole island was governed by Haitians.

If the Treaty of Paris of 1814 was in effect, why did Spain and France allow President Boyer to unify the island in 1822? Why did they also let Haiti rule the entire island for more than twenty years?

The preamble to the ordinance of 17 April 1825 states: "Charles, by the grace of God, King of France and Navarre, to all present and future, Greetings. Having regard to Articles 14 and 73 of the Charter, desiring to provide for what the interests of French trade require, the misfortunes of the former colonists of Saint-Domingue and the precarious state of the present inhabitants of this island". The expression "this island" introduces a general geographical framework.

In 1822, the Haitian government administered the entire island of Hayti (Santo Domingo). King Charles X's ordinance of April 17, 1825, accepted and ratified by Haiti on July 11, 1825, did not create a new administration in the western part of the island and did not expressly require Boyer to renounce the administration of its eastern part. Thus, articles 1, 2 and 3 of the ordinances of April 17, 1825, referred to the entire island of Saint-Domingue.

Leo Frank Scolds the Negro Nightwatchman He Setup to Be Lynched

Leo Frank's Sacrificial Negro, Newton Jasper Lee: Recalled at the Coroner's Inquest in the Atlanta Georgian, May 8, 1913

The Disputed Time Card, Bloodstained Shirt, Murder Notes, and Leo Frank's Private Conversation With Newt Lee

On Thursday, May 8, 1913, Newt Lee, the Black night time security guard who discovered 13-year-old Mary Anne Phagan's body in the basement of Atlanta's National Pencil Company, was recalled to the witness stand at the Fulton County coroner's inquest.

The hearing took place at Atlanta police headquarters presided by Coroner Paul Vernon Donehoo and his six-man jury. The Atlanta Georgian described the crowded proceedings, attended by police officers, detectives, attorneys, reporters, stenographers, and spectators. 

Solicitor General Hugh Manson Dorsey (1871–1948) and defense attorney Luther Zeigler Rosser (1859–1923) were among the participants (AG, 1).

More than a week earlier, Lee had originally testified at the April 30 opening of the inquest at P. J. Bloomfield's undertaking establishment on South Pryor Street. Eight days later, he returned to answer additional questions about his employer, the factory's time clock, a bloodstained shirt found at his residence, and a private conversation with Frank (AG, 2).

By then, three pieces of evidence had raised suspicion against Lee: the disputed time card, the shirt, and two handwritten murder notes apparently accusing a Black factory employee.

Saturday, April 26: Frank Sends Lee Away

Saturday, April 26, 1913, was Confederate Memorial Day, a Georgia state holiday.

Mary Phagan entered the National Pencil Company shortly after noon to collect her wages. She was murdered inside the building, and her body was discovered in the basement early Sunday morning.

Lee ordinarily began work around 6 p.m., but Frank instructed him to arrive at 4 p.m. When Lee arrived, Frank unexpectedly sent him away and told him to return at his regular starting time.

Lee testified that Frank emerged from his office rubbing his hands and apologizing for having asked him to arrive early. Lee considered this unusual behavior.

When Lee returned around 6 p.m., Frank instructed him not to punch the time clock immediately because he wanted to install a new recording tape. Lee held the mechanism while Frank inserted it.

This detail later became significant because Frank's handling of the time clock record became a central issue in the investigation (AG, 2).

Sunday, April 27: Frank Declares Lee's Time Card Correct

Early Sunday morning, Lee discovered Mary Phagan's body and notified the police.

Investigators brought Frank back to the factory, where he opened the time clock and removed the paper record of Lee's nighttime rounds.

Former county policeman W. W. "Boots" Rogers later testified that he examined the slip and remembered seeing a punch at every numbered position. He recalled the first two morning punches at approximately 6:01 and 6:32.

Frank initially indicated that the punches were correct.

Lee separately remembered Frank declaring the record satisfactory. Detective John R. Black also confirmed that Frank had described the time slip as regularly punched.

Factory foreman N. V. Darley acknowledged that there were no blank numbered positions, although he later explained that closer examination revealed irregular intervals between some punches.

This last point requires attention. A card could contain a punch at every numbered position while still recording intervals longer than 30 minutes.

Nevertheless, the testimony established that Frank initially described the record as satisfactory before subsequently identifying irregularities (AG, 3; AJ, 4).

Monday, April 28: Frank's Story Changes

By Monday, April 28, Frank was telling investigators that Lee's time record contained several missing half-hour punches.

On Wednesday, April 30, the Atlanta Georgian published an article titled "Clock 'Misses' Add Mystery to Phagan Case."

The newspaper reported that Frank had previously described the punches as regular and the record as satisfactory. Yet the slip subsequently examined at police headquarters appeared to show three omissions.

This raised an obvious question: Why did Frank initially declare the record correct, then use alleged irregularities to question Lee's movements?

How did the time slip that remained in Leo's custody go from being punched all right to being punched wrong? 

The first disputed interval occurred after 9:32 p.m. on Saturday night, several hours after investigators believed Mary Phagan had been murdered.

Even if Lee missed several nighttime rounds, those omissions did not place him in the factory during the afternoon when the killing was believed to have occurred.

Frank's defense maintained that he had initially overlooked the irregularities during a quick examination. That explanation was possible, but it depended on accepting Frank's account of how he handled the evidence.

The record had been in Frank's possession and had not remained under continuous independent police control.

The allegation that the time card was altered or substituted therefore deserves scrutiny, although the available testimony does not conclusively establish that Frank personally falsified it (AG, 5).

The Bloodstained Shirt Discovered at Lee's Residence

A second suspicious discovery appeared to strengthen the case against Lee.

Detectives John Black and Fred Bullard searched his residence behind 40 Henry Street and discovered a shirt with suspected bloodstains at the bottom of a barrel containing discarded clothing.

The police theory suggested that Lee had left the factory, returned home, changed his clothes, concealed the bloody garment, and resumed his rounds.

But the evidence did not establish that Lee had worn the shirt on the night of the murder.

Lee said the garment resembled an old shirt he had owned but that he had not seen it for nearly two years.

His landlady, Lorena Townes, denied that he had returned home during the night. The arrangement of the house made an unnoticed visit difficult because Lee ordinarily had to pass through her room to reach his quarters.

Corinne Holsey, another resident, also believed she would have heard unusual movement.

The Atlanta Georgian reported these circumstances under the headline "Confirms Lee's Story of Shirt" (AG, 6).

Detective Black's May 8 testimony described the shirt as washed but not ironed.

The prosecution later argued that the garment had been planted to incriminate Lee.

Frank's attorneys denied that their client had anything to do with the shirt, maintaining that he lacked knowledge of Lee's clothing and residence.

Neither explanation conclusively established how the shirt acquired its stains or who placed it in the barrel (AG, 7).

The Two Murder Notes That Pointed Toward a Black Night Watchman

The third suspicious item consisted of two handwritten notes discovered near Mary Phagan's body.

The Atlanta Georgian reproduced both on Monday, April 28, under the headline "Incoherent Notes Add to Mystery in Strangling Case."

The notes contained unusual spelling, confused sentences, and references to a tall Black man.

One included the expression "night witch," apparently referring to a night watchman.

Although neither note identified Newt Lee by name, their wording naturally directed suspicion toward the factory's Black night watchman.

Investigators initially compared the handwriting with samples obtained from Lee.

Those comparisons increased suspicion against him.

But in late May, Jim Conley, a Black sweeper employed at the factory, admitted writing the notes.

Conley alleged that Frank instructed him to prepare them, supplying their substance while Conley used his own spelling and manner of expression.

Frank denied Conley's accusation and maintained that Conley was responsible for the murder.

The defense questioned Conley's credibility, pointing to changes in his statements.

Those criticisms warranted examination. Nevertheless, Conley's admission that he wrote the notes seriously weakened the earlier attempt to associate them with Lee's handwriting (AG, 8; AJ, 9).

April 30: Lee Publicly Accuses Frank

By Wednesday, April 30, Lee believed that his employer's statements were directing suspicion toward him.

The Atlanta Georgian published his accusation under the headline "Looks Like Frank Is Trying to Put Crime on Me, Says Lee."

Lee maintained that he had punched the clock regularly and knew nothing about Mary Phagan's murder before discovering her body.

He challenged the contradiction between Frank's original statement that the clock punches were correct and the later claim that several punches were missing.

Lee also explained that his duties did not require searching every corner of the basement on every round. According to him, Frank had instructed him to check for fire rather than inspect the entire basement.

That explanation helped account for why Lee had not discovered the body immediately after starting his shift.

The April 30 article preserved Lee's early suspicion that the evidence was being used to make him appear responsible for a crime he denied committing (AG, 10).

May 8: Newt Lee Recalled Before Coroner Donehoo

At approximately 4:10 p.m. on Thursday, May 8, Lee returned to the witness stand.

The Atlanta Georgian printed his examination under the heading "Lee Repeats His Private Conversation With Frank."

Lee described sitting in a room at police headquarters, handcuffed, when Frank entered.

He complained about being detained despite knowing nothing about Mary Phagan's murder beyond finding her body.

According to Lee, Frank initially told him that he believed Lee was innocent.

But Lee then attributed a warning to his employer, including the expression "we will both go to hell."

Lee also testified that he told Frank he would have known if Mary Phagan had been murdered in the basement during his nighttime watch.

According to Lee, Frank discouraged discussion of that subject, saying, "Don't let's talk about that."

If accurately remembered, this was troubling behavior. Lee was explaining why a murder committed during his shift would have been difficult for him to overlook, yet Frank allegedly tried to end that discussion.

Frank offered a different account.

He claimed that police detectives had instructed him to question Lee privately in hopes of obtaining additional information.

Detective John Black confirmed that officers had asked Frank to speak with Lee. However, Black testified that police had not provided particular words for Frank to use. They had instructed him generally to encourage Lee to tell the truth.

That testimony confirmed that the meeting was arranged by investigators. It did not independently verify that detectives instructed Frank to make the warning Lee described or discourage discussion of the basement.

Frank's defense therefore had an explanation for why the meeting occurred, but Lee's account left an unresolved question about precisely what Frank said (AG, 2; AG, 7).

Lee's Additional May 8 Testimony

Coroner Donehoo continued questioning Lee about events inside the factory.

Lee testified that the furnace had been fired on Saturday night.

He repeated that Frank had behaved unusually when he arrived early for work, emerging from his office, rubbing his hands, and apologizing for calling him in before his regular starting time.

Lee said Frank had not ordinarily greeted him in that manner.

He was also questioned about the basement trap door and the machinery room floor. Lee said the trap door was generally open and that he had noticed nothing unusual on the floor.

The examination then returned to the time clock.

Lee explained that Frank had instructed him to hold the mechanism while he installed the new recording tape.

Lee denied missing his rounds.

When questioned about the shirt found at his residence, he said it resembled one he had owned and explained that Mrs. John Bowen had made a shirt for him.

His testimony remained consistent with his earlier position: he had followed his regular work routine, had not concealed a bloodstained shirt, and knew nothing about Mary Phagan's murder before finding her body (AG, 2).

The Problem Facing Frank and His Defense

Frank and his attorneys offered explanations for each disputed circumstance.

The defense maintained that Frank had initially misread Lee's time card, that detectives had arranged his private conversation with Lee, and that Conley had written the murder notes without Frank's direction.

Frank's attorneys also denied that he had arranged for the shirt to be planted.

But those explanations did not independently establish what happened to the clock record, how the shirt became stained, or whether Conley's allegations were true.

The time card presented a particular problem because Frank had access to the mechanism, initially declared the record satisfactory, and subsequently reported irregularities.

The shirt raised questions because investigators had not established that Lee returned home during his shift or that the garment's stains were connected to the murder.

The murder notes raised additional questions because Conley admitted writing them and accused Frank of directing him.

The May 8 conversation introduced another dispute. Detective Black confirmed that police arranged the meeting but did not corroborate the specific statements Lee attributed to Frank.

At trial, defense attorneys Luther Z. Rosser and Reuben R. Arnold challenged the prosecution's interpretation of these circumstances.

Rosser's August 22 closing argument included discussion of Lee and the murder notes, even though Conley had already admitted writing them.

The defense's position deserves examination because suspicion could continue to surround Lee after evidence initially associated with him had been traced to another employee (AG, 11).

Coroner Paul V. Donehoo

Paul V. Donehoo was approximately 35 years old when he presided over the Mary Phagan inquest.

He reportedly lost his eyesight at approximately six years of age following meningitis.

Despite his blindness, Donehoo pursued an education, studied law, and became Fulton County's elected coroner.

He attended Georgia's school for the blind and Mercer University and later pursued legal training in Atlanta.

Donehoo developed an extensive memory for spoken testimony and legal information. During the inquest, he questioned witnesses about the factory's operations, their movements, and contradictions between their statements.

The May 8 Georgian described him seated at the head of a long table, surrounded by jurors, witnesses, stenographers, reporters, and attorneys.

His blindness did not prevent him from supervising the proceedings or conducting detailed examinations.

His exact birth and death dates remain unverified in the sources used for this article. His approximate birth year was 1877 or 1878 (AG, 1; Oney, 12).

The Coroner's Verdict and Lee's Release

On May 8, the coroner's jury found that Mary Phagan had died by strangulation and recommended that both Frank and Lee be held for further investigation.

This was a preliminary finding, not a criminal conviction.

Lee remained imprisoned while the investigation continued.

His attorneys subsequently sought his release, arguing that grand juries had failed to indict him.

He was ultimately released from the Fulton County jail in August 1913.

Frank was indicted, tried, and convicted of Mary Phagan's murder.

Lee's release ended the effort to prosecute him for the crime, although it did not resolve every question about the time card, shirt, or notes.

Conclusion

Newt Lee entered the investigation as the employee who discovered Mary Phagan's body and notified the police.

Within days, the time card, bloodstained shirt, and murder notes appeared to implicate him.

The clock record initially described as satisfactory became evidence of supposedly missing rounds.

A suspicious shirt was discovered at his residence despite testimony questioning whether he had returned home during the night.

Two murder notes appeared to accuse a Black night watchman, but another factory employee later admitted writing them.

Lee publicly accused Frank of trying to place the crime on him on April 30.

When recalled before Coroner Donehoo on May 8, Lee testified that Frank had discouraged him from explaining why he would have known if a murder occurred in the basement during his watch.

Frank maintained that detectives had directed the conversation. Detective Black confirmed that police arranged the meeting but did not corroborate the precise warning Lee attributed to Frank.

The surviving evidence raises serious questions about whether suspicion was deliberately directed toward Lee. It does not conclusively establish that Frank personally altered the time card, planted the shirt, or dictated the notes.

The April 30 and May 8 editions of the Atlanta Georgian nevertheless preserve Lee's early concern that his employer's statements were implicating him and his sworn testimony concerning their private conversation.

Further Reading

For an expanded examination of the Mary Phagan murder, the investigation, the evidence against Leo Frank, and the subsequent trial and appeals, see Mary Phagan Kean's revised and expanded 2025 edition of The Murder of Little Mary Phagan. The book incorporates historical commentary and primary-source material from the case. Readers should compare its interpretations with the original newspaper and court records (Kean, 13).

The book and information about the revised edition are available through https://t.co/E5koX0QMAi and https://t.co/roCdPGO7eJ

Mary Phagan Case Files | You Are There

Leo Frank's "Negro Patsy":

Newton Jasper Lee, National Pencil Company Graveyard Shift Security Guard at the Coroner's Inquest in the Atlanta Stationhouse Being Questioned Under Oath

The Atlanta Georgian, April 30, 1913

How Prosecutors Built-up a Case that Accused Atlanta Georgia Bnai Brith President and Factory Superintendent Leo Max Frank of Framing His African-American Night Watchman With a Forged Time Slip, a Blood-Soaked Shirt, and the Mary Phagan Murder Notes

Principal newspaper: The Atlanta Georgian, Wednesday, April 30, 1913.

Headline: “Newt Lee on Stand at Inquest Tells His Side of Phagan Case.”

On Wednesday, April 30, 1913, Old Newt Lee, the Negro night watchman who discovered 13-year-old Mary Anne Phagan's body at Atlanta's National Pencil Company, testified in Atlanta Police Headquarters before legally-blind Fulton County Coroner Paul Vernon Donehoo.

Lee had discovered her body early Sunday morning, April 27, and reported it to police by using the phone in Leo Frank's second floor business office. Three days later, he was under suspicion himself.

The Atlanta Georgian published several articles about Lee that Wednesday, covering his testimony, missing time-clock punches, a bloody shirt found at his home, and handwriting evidence that appeared to connect him with the murder notes found beside Mary's body.

Lee suspected his employer, factory boss Leo M. Frank, was trying to frame him. The Georgian published his accusation under the headline:

 “Looks Like Frank Is Trying to Put Crime on Me, Says Lee.”

Lee declared:

“It looks like Mr. Frank was trying to put the crime on me” (AG, 1).

The prosecution later argued that Frank had attempted to place the murder on his own night watchman. The evidence centered on three things: the murder notes, Lee's time-clock record, and the bloody shirt.

Newt Lee Before the Murder

Newt Lee is believed to have been born around 1860, making him approximately 53 years old in 1913. He lived in a studio apartment at the rear of 40 Henry Street in Atlanta.

He had worked as a night watchman at another National Pencil Company plant before transferring to its downtown factory at 37–41 South Forsyth Street about three weeks before the murder.

His duties included guarding the building, checking doors and windows, watching for fire, and punching a mechanical time clock every thirty minutes. His regular hours began at 6:00 p.m. on weekdays and 5:00 p.m. on Saturdays. He worked until about dawn, when he was scheduled to hand over his shift to the day watchman at 6:30 a.m.

Frank had personally shown Lee around the factory and explained his duties. As the man who hired and trained Newt Lee, Frank would have known where Lee would patrol during his overnight shift. Frank would also as his employer know where he lived. 

Saturday, April 26: Frank Sends Lee Away

On Friday, April 25, Frank instructed Lee to report an hour early the following afternoon, at 4:00 p.m. Saturday was Confederate Memorial Day, a Georgia holiday.

Lee arrived shortly before four and found the inner stairway doors locked, which he considered unusual. After unlocking them, he went upstairs and announced his arrival.

According to Lee at the trial, Frank emerged from his office rubbing his hands, something Lee had never seen him do before.

Frank apologized for bringing him in early but insisted that he leave until six. Lee wanted to sleep in the shipping room, where he sometimes rested before his night shift, but Frank refused.

Lee went toward Decatur Street and watched an outdoor medicine show by a Negro mountebank. He returned shortly before six.

Frank then prepared Lee's time-clock slip. Lee later testified that Frank seemed nervous and took longer than usual inserting the paper (AG, 2).

Gantt's Visit and Frank's Telephone Call

Shortly after Lee returned, James Milton Gantt, a recently discharged employee, appeared at the factory to retrieve shoes he had left inside.

Lee initially refused him entry without Frank's permission. When Frank learned Gantt was there, Lee said the superintendent appeared frightened. The brief of evidence records this observation. 

Frank acquiesced and allowed Gantt inside, instructing Lee to accompany him. Gantt retrieved his shoes and departed.

Lee later saw Frank leave the factory but could not establish whether he returned, since Frank had a key.

That evening, Frank telephoned Lee to ask whether everything was all right. Lee considered the call unusual because Frank had never previously called during his night watch (AG, 2).

Sunday, April 27: Lee Discovers Mary's Body

Shortly after 3:00 a.m., Lee went into the basement to use the toilet. While checking the rear of the building for fire and inspecting the back entrance, he noticed something lying near a partition.

At first, he thought someone had placed an object there to frighten him. Moving closer, he discovered a human body.

Lee hurried upstairs and telephoned police headquarters. Responding officers followed him into the basement and found Mary Phagan's body, along with two handwritten notes.

Lee was arrested during the early investigation once the notes were found at 3:40 a.m on Sunday morning, April 27, 1913.

Sunday Morning 8:15 a.m. Leo Frank Says the Clock Record Is Correct

After police brought Frank back to the factory, he opened the time clock and removed Lee's slip.

Newt Lee, W. W. “Boots” Rogers, and factory foreman N. V. Darley witnessed the examination.

Lee testified:

“Mr. Frank opened the clock and said the punches were all right, that I hadn't missed any punches” (BOE, 3).

Rogers personally examined the slip and testified that it contained a punch for every numbered position. Darley looked over Frank's shoulder and agreed that it appeared correct.

Frank then carried the paper toward his office.

The April 30 Georgian also reported that Frank had told one of its reporters Sunday afternoon that Lee's clock record was correct.

But on Monday, the story changed.

Monday, April 28: Frank Reports Missing Punches

Detective John R. Black later testified that Frank began telling police on Monday and Tuesday that Lee's clock had been mispunched three times.

According to Black, Frank also suggested the gaps could have given Lee enough time to leave the factory, go home, and return.

The April 30 Georgian questioned this change in its article “Clock 'Misses' Add Mystery to Phagan Case.”

A regularly punched record supported Lee's account of making his rounds. Missing punches suggested he might have been away from his duties.

Frank maintained that he had first checked the numbered positions without examining the actual times. He said a closer examination revealed longer intervals.

The prosecution questioned that explanation because Frank, Rogers, and Darley had initially considered the slip correct (AG, 1; BOE, 7).

Monday Morning: Herbert Haas Demands a Search of Frank's Home

At approximately 11:30 a.m. Monday, Frank's attorney, Herbert Haas, insisted that police search Frank's residence at 68 East Georgia Avenue.

Detective Black testified that Haas told Chief of Detectives Newport A. Lanford he was acting as Frank's lawyer and wanted nothing left undone.

Officers accompanied them to the house and examined Frank's clothing, including his dirty laundry. Nothing incriminating was found.

Solicitor General Hugh M. Dorsey later argued that the request was part of an attempt to direct police toward Lee.

His theory was that searching Frank's clothing would lead investigators to search the night watchman's clothing as well.

That same Monday, according to Black, Frank was discussing missing clock punches that could have allowed Lee to go home and return (AJ, 4).

Tuesday, April 29: A Blood-Soaked Shirt Appears at Lee's Home

The next morning, Detective Black searched Lee's room on Henry Street and found a heavily bloodstained shirt near the bottom of a barrel containing old clothing and rags.

The garment became State's Exhibit F. Blood appeared on both sides and high inside the shirt near the armpits.

If Lee had left the factory during one of the longer clock intervals, the shirt could suggest that he had gone home, changed clothes, and hidden evidence.

But Lee had been arrested Sunday morning and had not returned home before the shirt was discovered Tuesday.

The Georgian investigated the claim and published “Confirms Lee's Story of Shirt” on Wednesday, April 30.

Lorena Townes said Lee had not returned Saturday night. She explained that his usual entrance passed through her room. Another entrance led through a yard, but its gate was locked at night.

Corinne Holsey also said she would have heard unusual movement.

Lee told the Georgian the shirt resembled one he owned but that he had not worn it for nearly two years. He kept old clothing in the barrel for rags (AG, 5).

The prosecution later argued that the shirt had been planted to implicate him.

Wednesday, April 30: Lee Before Coroner Paul Donehoo

At approximately 11:45 a.m., Lee testified before Donehoo's coroner's jury at Atlanta police headquarters.

He described Frank sending him away Saturday afternoon, Gantt's visit, the telephone call, his nightly rounds, and the discovery of Mary's body.

The police challenged his description of the body. Lee said Mary had been lying on her back, but the responding officers said they found her face down.

Lee denied moving her.

Officers also questioned whether his dirty lantern provided enough light for him to identify the victim. Lee maintained that he had approached close enough to recognize her hair and exposed skin.

The Georgian reported that his account remained substantially consistent despite repeated questioning.

Meanwhile, police were examining three pieces of evidence that could be used against him: the bloody shirt, the disputed time slip, and the handwritten notes (AG, 2).

The Murder Notes and Handwriting Evidence

Two handwritten notes found beside Mary's body appeared to direct suspicion toward a Black man.

One referred to a tall Black man. Another contained the words “night witch,” which investigators connected with the night watchman.

Sergeant Levi S. Dobbs testified that Lee recognized the apparent reference to himself when the notes were read.

The Georgian published Dobbs's account on April 30, page 4, column 3, under the headline “Tells of Watchman Lee Explaining the Notes” (AG, 10).

That same day, the Georgian reported that F. M. Berry, assistant cashier of the Fourth National Bank, had compared the notes with handwriting samples attributed to Lee.

Berry believed the writing was similar. Detective J. N. Starnes identified samples Lee had written during police questioning.

The newspaper published “Handwriting of Notes Is Identified as Newt Lee's” (AG, 6).

But on May 24, factory sweeper Jim Conley admitted writing the notes himself. He claimed Frank had instructed him to write them. Frank denied that accusation.

The defense challenged Conley's changing accounts and argued that he had written the notes to protect himself and Lee.

Conley's admission settled who physically wrote the notes, although the question of who directed their wording remained disputed.

The Time Slip: Four Missing Half-Hour Punches

Defendant's Exhibit 1, reproduced on page 253 of the 1913 Brief of Evidence, shows four unusually long intervals.

Saturday, 9:32 to 10:29 p.m.: 57 minutes.

Saturday, 11:04 p.m. to midnight: 56 minutes.

Sunday, midnight to 1:07 a.m.: 67 minutes.

Sunday, 2:03 to 3:01 a.m.: 58 minutes.

The four intervals total 238 minutes, or 3 hours and 58 minutes.

Lee was supposed to punch every thirty minutes. Each interval appears to contain one missing expected half-hour punch, making four altogether.

The gaps covered nearly four hours of clock time, including approximately two additional hours beyond the normal schedule. They do not establish that Lee was absent for four hours.

The Georgian initially reported three missing punches, and Frank, Black, and Darley also referred to three irregular periods. The surviving exhibit contains four longer intervals.

The prosecution argued that Frank had used the record to create suspicion against Lee.

But how easily could a time record be manufactured?

Four Witnesses Explain How Quickly the Clock Could Be Punched

During Frank's trial, witnesses demonstrated that someone familiar with the machine could create a full night's series of punches in minutes.

Detective J. N. Starnes testified that a watchman demonstrated the clock in less than five minutes.

Former factory timekeeper James Milton Gantt estimated about five minutes for twelve hours of punches.

Foreman N. V. Darley said someone familiar with the clock could punch an entire night's record in five or ten minutes.

Former watchman L. T. Kendrick testified that he could do it in two or three minutes. His test slip became State's Exhibit P (BOE, 7).

The machine recorded mechanical punches without identifying the person operating it.

A replacement slip could therefore contain genuine clock-made punches representing hours that had not actually passed.

That established the mechanical possibility of manufacturing a record. It did not prove Frank had done so.

Frank's Defense

Darley testified that he and Frank had looked at the numbered positions without calculating the time between punches.

A slip could have a mark beside every numbered position yet still show gaps of nearly an hour.

That explanation also fit Rogers's testimony that he saw a punch for every number.

The prosecution questioned whether everyone had made the same mistake, particularly because Frank took the paper toward his office and its subsequent custody was disputed.

Rosser argued that no witness had seen Frank alter or replace the slip.

The jury had to consider both explanations (AG, 8).

Dorsey Connects Haas, the Clock, and the Bloody Shirt

During Detective Black's testimony on July 30, Solicitor Dorsey explained the prosecution's theory.

The Atlanta Journal reported his argument on Thursday, July 31.

Dorsey pointed to Haas's request to search Frank's home, Frank's later statements about Lee's missing punches, and the bloody shirt found at Lee's residence.

Black testified that the search of Lee's room followed Frank's discussion of the clock irregularities. He also recalled Frank suggesting the gaps gave Lee time to go home.

Dorsey argued that the bloody shirt was part of a scheme to place suspicion on the night watchman.

The defense denied that Frank or Haas had planted the shirt. Rosser argued there was no proof Frank even knew where Lee lived (AJ, 4; AG, 8).

Hooper: “He Would Sacrifice Newt Lee”

On Thursday, August 21, prosecutor Frank A. Hooper connected the time slip and bloody shirt during his closing argument.

The Atlanta Constitution reported his remarks on Friday, August 22, page 2.

Hooper reminded jurors that Frank had first pronounced Lee's clock record correct. He then displayed the shirt found at Lee's home.

Hooper declared:

“It had to be planted. Gentlemen, it was planted!”

He then accused Frank of being willing to sacrifice his watchman to save himself:

“He would sacrifice Newt Lee that he might live!” (AC, 9).

The prosecution argued that the murder notes, clock record, and shirt were parts of the same attempt to frame Lee.

Frank denied wrongdoing, and the defense challenged both the alleged planting and the claim that the time slip had been changed.

Newt Lee's Release

The coroner's jury completed its investigation on Thursday, May 8, recommending that Frank and Lee be held for further investigation.

The Fulton County grand jury indicted Frank in May. Lee was never indicted but remained imprisoned as a material witness.

He testified at Frank's trial on July 28 and 29.

After Frank's conviction on Monday, August 25, Dorsey asked Judge Leonard Strickland Roan to release Lee because investigators had not found evidence connecting him with the murder.

At 11:10 a.m. on Tuesday, August 26, Lee left the Fulton County Tower after approximately 121 days in custody.

He carried two baskets of belongings and told reporters he needed employment and was uncertain about his home and marriage.

On September 16, the grand jury formally returned a no-bill against Lee.

The Atlanta Constitution reported the decision on September 17, page 3, column 3, under the headline “No Bill Is Found Against Newt Lee” (AC, 11).

Newt Lee's Later Life

The 1920 census contains a possible record of Lee.

On January 8, 1920, an Atlanta enumerator listed a Black man named Newt Lee, age 60, born in Georgia, working as a laundry laborer.

Elizabeth Lee, age twelve, appeared on the next line. Both were recorded as boarders.

If this is the same Newt Lee, he was born around 1859 or 1860 and survived until at least January 1920.

Elizabeth may have been his daughter, although the census does not establish their relationship. There is an unconfirmed lead that she lived into the 1980s.

Lee's death date remains unknown (Census, 12).

Coroner Paul V. Donehoo: Blind Since Childhood

Paul V. Donehoo lost his eyesight following an illness when he was approximately six years old.

He attended the Georgia school for the blind, studied at Mercer University, and worked as a professional musician before entering law.

Around 1911, he completed his legal education at Atlanta Law School. By 1913, he practiced with Arnaud and Donehoo in the Fourth National Bank Building.

Donehoo had already been elected and reelected Fulton County coroner.

He presided over Mary Phagan's inquest with a six-member jury headed by Homer C. Ashford.

On April 28, the jury viewed Mary's body and inspected the factory. Witness testimony began April 30 and continued until May 8, when the jury found that Mary had died by strangulation and recommended further investigation of Frank and Lee.

Donehoo married Alverta Benson in September 1913. The ceremony took place in Decatur, Georgia, with Rev. S. R. Belk officiating. The couple lived at 62 Oak Street in Atlanta's West End.

The Atlanta Journal reported his marriage and career on September 29, 1913 (AJ, 13).

The Atlanta Georgian: Founded in 1906

The Atlanta Georgian began publication in 1906, founded by Fred Loring Seely, with John Temple Graves as its first editor.

It competed with The Atlanta Constitution and The Atlanta Journal, using large headlines, illustrations, low prices, and frequent afternoon editions.

In 1907, Seely acquired the competing Atlanta News.

William Randolph Hearst purchased the Georgian in 1912, making it part of his national newspaper organization. Keats Speed, formerly of Hearst's New York Evening Journal, became editor.

Hearst also introduced the Atlanta Sunday American in April 1913.

Charles H. Henry: In Charge During the Phagan Investigation

On February 15, 1913, Editor & Publisher reported that Charles H. Henry had succeeded Keats Speed, who had returned to New York.

Henry previously served as the Georgian's business manager and was placed in charge of the afternoon newspaper.

He was directing the paper when Mary Phagan was murdered on April 26, 1913.

The Georgian published at least eight editions on April 28 as the police investigation developed.

Its April 30 coverage included Lee's statements, the coroner's testimony, missing time-clock punches, the bloody shirt, and handwriting examinations.

James B. Nevin, a political writer at the Georgian, later became editor in 1914. Foster Coates, another newspaper executive associated with the Hearst organization, died in Atlanta in November 1914 (EP, 14; NGE, 15).

The Murder of Little Mary Phagan, Second Revised Edition, 2025

Mary Phagan-Kean, great-niece and namesake of Mary Anne Phagan, published an expanded second revised edition of The Murder of Little Mary Phagan in 2025.

The original edition appeared in 1987.

The revised 500-page edition contains historical documents, photographs, court records, newspaper reports, and references. It presents the Phagan family's account of Mary's murder, Frank's trial, the appeals, and the continuing controversy.

Publisher: American Mercury Books.

ISBN: 9781737966012 (MP, 16).

Was Newt Lee Being Set Up?

When I read the April 30 Atlanta Georgian beside the later trial testimony, I keep returning to the same question.

Was Newt Lee being prepared to take the blame for Mary Phagan's murder?

The prosecution believed he was.

Frank pronounced Lee's clock record correct on Sunday. Rogers examined it, and Darley agreed.

By Monday, Frank was pointing out missing punches that supposedly gave Lee enough time to leave the factory and return.

That same Monday, Herbert Haas insisted that police search Frank's home. Nothing incriminating was found.

On Tuesday, a bloody shirt was discovered at Lee's residence.

Two handwritten notes found beside Mary's body also appeared to point toward the night watchman. Conley later admitted writing them and claimed Frank had directed him to do so.

The prosecution argued that these events were connected.

Witnesses demonstrated that an entire night's time-clock record could be made in minutes. Frank's defense maintained that the original slip had simply been misread.

No eyewitness testified to seeing Frank manufacture another slip or plant the shirt.

But Dorsey and Hooper asked jurors to consider the evidence together: Frank's handling of the clock record, his later statements about Lee's movements, Haas's request to search Frank's home, the bloodstained shirt, and the murder notes.

Lee himself had raised the accusation in the Georgian on April 30, only three days after discovering Mary's body.

He called the police to report a murder. Within days, three pieces of evidence threatened to make him the chief suspect.

The prosecution argued that Frank had tried to turn his own night watchman into a patsy.

Frank denied the accusation. The identity of whoever placed the bloody shirt or altered any time-clock record was never separately established.

Lee was released after Frank's conviction and formally cleared in September 1913.

He remained in the historical record as the night watchman who discovered Mary Phagan's body, reported the murder, and spent nearly four months in jail while investigators tried to determine who was responsible.

🚨DeKalb County Couple Offers $10,000 Reward After Arsonist Destroys Vehicles in Driveway
​
📍DEKALB COUNTY, Georgia. 

Authorities are searching for an arsonist who deliberately torched two vehicles parked outside a DeKalb County home early Sunday, November 1, 2026, destroying a family's primary transportation and a crucial work truck.

​A $10,000 reward is now being offered for information leading to an arrest and conviction.

​The incident unfolded shortly after 1 a.m. at the residence of Billye and Keith Green, who have lived on the property for more than two decades.

 Home surveillance footage captured an individual walking up the driveway carrying a container resembling a gasoline can. 

The suspect poured a suspected flammable liquid over the couple’s SUV and pickup truck before igniting the blaze and fleeing the scene.

​Billye Green woke up to find both vehicles engulfed in flames and immediately alerted her husband. Keith rushed outside with a fire extinguisher, but the flames which he estimated reached 15 feet into the air quickly overwhelmed the equipment.

​Fortunately, neither resident was injured, and the fire did not spread to the house, a disaster the couple noted could have been much worse. 

However, the destruction of Keith’s work truck, upon which their small business relies, has created a severe financial burden.

​Victims of a crime they cannot explain, the Greens said they have no enemies and questioned whether the arsonist may have targeted the wrong home.

​Investigators are actively reviewing home surveillance and neighborhood security footage, including video from a neighbor showing a vehicle speeding away immediately after the fire. 

Authorities are also analyzing data from Flock Safety automated license plate recognition cameras in the area to track down the suspect.

​During a recent interview, Billye indicated that investigators may be eyeing a person of interest, though no official arrests or identifications have been publicly released.

​Georgia Arson Control is offering a reward of up to $10,000 for tips. Anyone with information is urged to contact the confidential tip line at 1-800-282-5804. The investigation remains active.

ChatGPT is making your kid bad in school.

Why? in 1970, Stanford offered 4-year-olds a deal: 1 treat now, or 2 if they waited 15 minutes. years later, the kids who waited had higher SAT scores.

It doesn't mean that you should teach your kid to restraint themselves from eating candies, but the idea behind holds. the kids who do well can sit with something hard a little longer.

Academic success works the same way as ignoring treats. when you're stuck, the answer looks like a marshmallow. and the problem is that AI-powered homework-solvers or general LLMs like ChatGPT or Claude are racing to give them to your child, because they optimise for engagement.

Research proves it. In a study of nearly 1,000 high schoolers, the ones who practiced with ChatGPT solved more problems, but then scored 17% lower on the exam.

On the contrary, productive struggle is one of our product principles at Sophie (among writing first or one-to-one tutoring).

Kids do not need fast AI models answer to learn ; they need a tutor who can patiently wait for them.

My take on Sunderland 1-0 Chelsea.

1️⃣ Sunderland deserve serious credit. Frustrating Chelsea under pressure is a statement. They competed for every ball and defended well today.

2️⃣ Brobby had a good game. Forget the missed goal; he troubled Chelsea all day and baited Colwill into fouling him in the box.

3️⃣ The Levi Colwill penalty will be debated. Chelsea can complain, but defenders must be careful in their box. Don't give the referee a decision; Colwill made it easy.

4️⃣ Sunderland show you don't need possession to compete with better teams. Intensity, organisation and fighting for second balls proved crucial.

5️⃣ Chelsea's Caicedo, Henderson and Lavia midfield should offer control and ball-winning. Three midfielders don't guarantee dominance. Where is the creativity and penetration?

6️⃣ Chelsea need to wake up. They have the quality to turn it around, but the longer Sunderland lead, the more pressure builds.

7️⃣ Sunderland's defensive discipline was impressive. They stayed compact, protected central areas and forced Chelsea wide.

8️⃣ Cole Palmer must take more responsibility. Chelsea need their creators to produce against deep defences. Too much possession, not enough end product.

9️⃣ Xabi Alonso, why are you not starting Welback again? He’s the perfect replacement for Pedro but still not seeing him as a direct threat to turn midfield numbers into clear chances.

🔟 Sadiki was important in midfield. His energy, work rate and second-ball wins disrupted Chelsea's rhythm.

Sunderland showed tremendous fight while Chelsea lacked ideas in possession. This is huge for the Black Cats looking for signing to ignite their season. #SUNCHE

text:
Opening Day Shock for Punters

By Sharan Kumar

The Bangalore Winter Season got off the blocks on Sunday, as expected, though the authorities had to wait until rather late to secure the licence to conduct the races. The last-minute clearance provided enough nervous moments for the administrators and racegoers alike. By the end of the opening day's proceedings, the authorities could heave a collective sigh of relief. The punters, however, had rather less reason to celebrate. If the authorities were waiting for a licence, the racegoers were desperately waiting for a winner!

The opening card turned out to be a minefield for those who fancied themselves as experts in picking winners. Long shots dominated the proceedings, and even when the fancied horses obliged, the betting ring often presented a three-horse puzzle, making it difficult to identify the right one. Where conviction was strong, favourites obligingly disappointed; where there was hesitation, the fancied runners came through. Racing, after all, is a game of snakes and ladders, except that the snakes seem to have a permanent reservation and the ladders are always in short supply!

The day's feature event, the 1400 metres Rajyotsava Cup, a terms race for three-year-olds and over, saw Efficacy being backed down from a generous quote to emerge as a firm favourite by race time. Ice of Fire was initially preferred, before money began flowing towards Once You Go Black. In the end, it was Efficacy who had the last word. Winless for nearly 100 days, the horse chose an appropriate occasion to rediscover winning ways, leading from the start and winning with a fair measure of comfort.

Ricardo, who chased the winner from the outset, held on gamely until the closing stages before being overwhelmed by the late-finishing Galahad and Emphatic, who fought out the battle for the runner-up berth. Ricardo weakened to finish fourth. The soft underfoot conditions perhaps did not suit Once You Go Black, who was never in the hunt, while Ice of Fire, who was content to bring up the rear, failed to make any meaningful progress. The two horses who attracted considerable attention in the betting ring ended up providing little entertainment on the track.

Darius Byramji-trained Fine Silver, who had gone down as a short-priced favourite at Mysore, made amends in the 1400 metres Bangalore City Police Cup, a race for maiden three-year-olds. Like several progeny of Phoenix Tower, Fine Silver appeared to relish the cut in the ground. She chased the front-running favourite Tyche well into the straight before asserting herself in the closing stages.

Tyche had opened up a substantial lead and looked to have the race in safe keeping, but began to run out of steam in the final furlong. Fine Silver gradually reeled her in and went on to win with something in hand under Aashad Asbar, who was enjoying a particularly rewarding afternoon with a treble. Shining Path stayed on to take the third spot.

The 1400 metres Jog Falls Plate, for horses rated 20 to 45, saw Valor Queen being backed to the exclusion of the rest. The favourite appeared to be travelling comfortably towards victory, but Irfan Ghatala-trained Fortissima had other ideas. Languishing towards the rear until entering the straight, Fortissima began to make rapid progress along the rails. Jockey Alex Roazio then angled her out towards the wide outside, and despite the rather adventurous route, the filly found her stride and came home with giant strides to collar the favourite with something to spare. Kaori finished third, narrowly ahead of Joyful Spirit.

Michael Eshwer-trained Hazel provided another shock in the 1200 metres T B Hanumantharaj Memorial Trophy, for horses rated 40 to 65. Deep Respect, who was withdrawn, bolted while being led to the starting gates and was subsequently taken out of the race. With Doncaster Belle and Auspicious King among the prominent contenders in the betting, the race offered little clarity as to where the winner would come from.

Doncaster Belle, ridden by Trevor Pate, looked the likely winner down the final furlong. But the opening day's proceedings had already established that looking the winner was a rather dangerous occupation. Hazel, who had moved from Prasanna Kumar's stable to Michael Eshwer's care, came from well off the pace, made progress along the rails and was then angled out in the final 100 metres. Despite running into the back of Doncaster Belle momentarily, Hazel gathered momentum and surged past the fancied runner to score an upset win under Shamaz Shareef. Joondalup produced a strong late flourish to finish third.

Prasanna Kumar-trained Knotty Imperador delivered a knockout blow to the punters in the 1400 metres Udupi Plate, for horses rated 40 to 65. Sulaiman Attaollahi-trained Circle of Dreams, who has developed an unenviable reputation for raising expectations before dashing them, once again failed to deliver as a strongly supported favourite.

Knotty Imperador was entrusted with a start-to-finish mission by jockey Arul, and the front-runner had enough ammunition to skip clear in the final furlong and register an effortless victory. Glorious Strides, the second favourite, ran on to finish behind the winner with Mister Brown occupying the next position. Circle of Dreams once again lived up to his unflattering reputation. Punters would perhaps do well to admire this horse from a safe distance, particularly when he appears superior on paper. Some dreams, it seems, are best left unbacked!

Hilton Sequeira has brought Quattro from Hyderabad to Bangalore with an eye on the classics, and the Deccan Derby fourth made a successful start to his campaign in the 1600 metres event. Quattro was the only firm favourite to oblige during the eight-race card, providing some much-needed relief to those who had been looking for a familiar face in the winner's enclosure.

Aashad Asbar had Quattro settled towards the rear before taking him on the wide outside inside the final 300 metres. The horse devoured ground and stormed home to win by a distance. Irish Coffee just managed to hold off Lux Aeterna to save place money. For once, the punters who stood by a favourite had something to smile about.

Aashad Asbar completed his treble with another well-backed winner, Jade Mountain, from trainer Lokanath's yard, in the 1200 metres Malaprabha Plate, for horses rated 20 to 45. There was substantial support for Big B, who led the field in earnest from the start. El Rey measured the front-runner in the final 100 metres, but Jade Mountain, who had been travelling in a handy position, produced a powerful burst in the final furlong to sweep past the leaders and score a confident victory. Big B weakened to finish third.

The day's opener, the 1200 metres November Plate, for horses in the basement class, saw Pradeep Annaiah-trained debutant Victoria Moon installed as a firm favourite ahead of Hold Your Breath. However, Dominic-trained Anzac Parade, who was running well below his past winning form, had other plans. Ridden by apprentice Darshan N, Anzac Parade went straight to the front and made every post a winning one, scoring without much difficulty over the favourite. Hold Your Breath finished third.

text:
⚔️ Free groceries, tinted windows and the FBI: Kalshi vs Polymarket

Kalshi and Polymarket let customers trade on the future. Their own rivalry has produced free groceries, disputed sponsorship announcements, suspicions of office espionage and meetings with federal prosecutors.

Some of this is documented. Some remains accusation.

The grocery offensive

On 3 February 2026, Kalshi offered shoppers up to $50 of groceries at a Manhattan supermarket.

Nine days later, Polymarket opened a temporary free shop, where customers could fill a branded bag. It also donated $1 million to Food Bank For NYC.

Polymarket suspected Kalshi had copied its campaign. Kalshi denied receiving inside information or stealing the idea.

One promotion had a spending limit. The other had a bag limit. Neither lacked publicity.

The exclusivity that wasn’t

Polymarket became MLB’s official prediction market exchange on 19 March. Its league-level rights still allowed clubs to sign separate partners.

On 25 August, Kalshi announced five club partnerships, initially describing all five as exclusive.

The Braves and Giants deals were not. Kalshi corrected the announcement after Front Office Sports reported the discrepancy.

Two clubs had not abandoned exclusivity overnight. They had never granted it.

Kalshi also secured a Madison Square Garden partnership in May. According to the New York Times, Polymarket had explored a similar agreement but would not match its rival’s offer.

The windows across the street

In June, the New York Post reported that Polymarket had compiled a dossier of suspected copying.

Its office faced premises rented by Paradigm, a Kalshi investor. Staff reportedly worried about visible computer screens, tinted some windows and considered possible internal leaks.

Kalshi and Paradigm rejected the spying allegations. Worried staff and tinted glass do not establish corporate espionage.

Trading the competitor’s court trouble

In January, a Massachusetts judge approved a preliminary injunction concerning Kalshi’s sports contracts and state licensing requirements.

Polymarket offered a market on whether Kalshi would stop offering those contracts in Massachusetts by 31 January. It resolved No.

The injunction was subsequently stayed pending appeal. The original decision was preliminary, not a final judgment ending Kalshi’s business there.

One death, different payouts

After Ali Khamenei was killed on 28 February, similar-looking departure markets produced different results.

Polymarket’s international platform paid out on relevant contracts. Kalshi applied a death exception and used a pre-death price rather than simply resolving Yes.

That exception already appeared in a May 2025 CFTC filing. It was not invented after his death.

Two traders nevertheless filed a proposed class action challenging disclosure and settlement. Kalshi said it reimbursed fees and net trading losses.

The roughly $54 million cited in the complaint was trading volume, not established customer losses. A complaint is not a verdict.

Prosecutors enter the story

The most serious episode began earlier: the FBI searched Polymarket founder Shayne Coplan’s apartment in November 2024.

The New York Times later reported that Kalshi’s lawyers had met federal prosecutors beforehand about Americans accessing Polymarket. That does not establish that Kalshi caused the raid.

The paper also described a Kalshi employee directing an influencer campaign against Coplan. CEO Tarek Mansour later expressed regret about staff conduct.

Those investigations were reported closed without charges in July 2025. That was an outcome of particular inquiries, not permanent regulatory clearance.

An adviser on both sides

Donald Trump Jr. has interests on both sides:

• Kalshi: strategic adviser since January 2025.
• Polymarket: advisory board appointment announced in August 2025.
• 1789 Capital: a partner at the fund, which invested in Polymarket.

Overlapping interests, yes. Guaranteed winnings, no.

Polymarket’s separate regulated US operation should also not be confused with its international platform.

The rivalry makes headlines. For anyone putting money on the platform, the more useful question is whether Polymarket is safe.

Before trusting the probability, read the contract.

For nearly 300 years, the Barbary states of North Africa preyed upon European shipping and coastal communities. Their corsairs plundered ships, captured men, women, and children, and sold human beings into slavery. 

Even Europe's great maritime powers paid tribute to protect their commerce. For centuries, extortion became an accepted cost of doing business. 

Then came a young, upstart nation called the United States of America. Following independence, America was nearly bankrupt and lacked a navy capable of protecting its merchant ships. 

Washington inherited an impossible bargain: pay tribute to protect American commerce and ransom captive sailors, knowing that payment offered no lasting guarantee against further demands.

But Washington understood that diplomacy without the power to defend American interests left the young republic vulnerable. So America began building a navy.

In 1801, Jefferson sent American warships to the Mediterranean. In 1815, under Madison, the United States forced Algiers to abandon its demands for American tribute.

America had decided that paying indefinitely was no solution. There's a lesson here that reaches beyond the Barbary Wars.

Today, Americans are once again debating how much taxpayer money should be spent accommodating a problem rather than resolving it - particularly when it comes to illegal aliens and publicly funded assistance, whether administered directly by government or through NGOs.

The circumstances are different. The underlying question of governmental responsibility remains: At what point does paying to manage a problem become an excuse for never solving it?

History doesn't repeat itself perfectly. But it does give us questions worth asking.

As Republicans reel from devastating midterm losses, one Southern governor who survived the blue wave — Sarah Huckabee Sanders of Arkansas — might represent the party’s path forward from the wilderness

Sanders, the daughter of U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee and a press secretary during Donald Trump’s first term, can’t fully escape the shadow of a president who voters currently find deeply unpalatable, in no small part because of a war in Iran that has driven up prices.

But her experience behind the podium for Trump taught her to channel his populist appeal while sanding down the sharper edges.

Furthermore, Sanders’ time outside of Washington offers not distance and space to develop her own governing model away from the national spotlight — just in case 2028 calls.

text:
8/10
It is still unclear whether this offer was even real or just another attention-seeking stunt. CNN reported that a source said White had declined the position. But then White himself said he would fly to Washington to meet with Trump at the White House on Monday. There has also been speculation online that there is another person named Dana White who works in the White House press office, and that Trump may have heard that name being discussed as a possible replacement for press secretary and confused that person with his friend from the UFC. We don’t know if that is true, but I think it is worth mentioning because, at this point, neither possibility is surprising. The one takeaway from all of this is that qualifications, experience, and the ability to actually do the job continue to be the least of Donald Trump’s concerns. He only cares that someone is blindly loyal to him and that they make him feel powerful.
