text:
THE WHITE HOUSE: THE GODFATHER, HIS ADVISOR, AND THE MAGA FAMILY
By @BPartisans 

That took some nerve. After the Republicans’ crushing defeat in the midterms, Donald Trump had two options: understand the voters’ message or declare war on those who had sent it. True to his genius for self-destruction, he chose the latter. And to organize the counteroffensive, he appointed Stephen Miller as chief of staff.

Axios describes him as his “wartime consigliere.” That says it all!

In the Sicilian and American mafia world, the consigliere is the Godfather’s trusted advisor, his confidant, his strategist, the one who looks out for the Family’s interests. A term immortalized by Mario Puzo in The Godfather in 1969.

Mind you, the comparison is literary, not legal. But politically, it’s delightful.

Welcome to the White House, Corleone-style. Donald in the Godfather’s chair, Miller in the role of the wartime consigliere, and Republican elected officials urged never to forget to which Family they owe their careers.

Except that Don Donald has a little problem: the Family just got trounced at the polls.

So what! In this administration, a defeat never proves that the strategy was flawed. It simply shows that they didn’t hit hard enough. An admirable logic, generally shared by generals who’ve just lost their army.

Stephen Miller embodies this philosophy perfectly. For him, the executive branch must push its limits; judges become suspect when they thwart the president; and the political opposition resembles an enemy within more than a legitimate component of democracy.

The separation of powers? An administrative formality. Checks and balances? Obstacles to unchecked rule. Compromise? A weakness reserved for losers.

And since Americans have punished an administration mired in controversies, the war against Iran, and broken promises, what could be smarter than promoting one of the regime’s most uncompromising ideologues?

Such is the splendor of Trumpist reasoning: when the ship is taking on water, you don’t repair the hull. You appoint an arsonist to be in charge of fire safety.

Miller promises confrontation with a Democratic Congress. Investigations, institutional standoffs, legal battles: the next two years could resemble a never-ending trench war between constitutional branches of government.

But the real danger for Trump may not be the Democratic opposition. It’s his inability to understand that voters did not give him a mandate to turn every disagreement into a political civil war.

In The Godfather, the consigliere advises the boss on how to preserve the Family.

In Washington, the consigliere might well advise the Godfather until the entire dynasty is politically buried.

For Don Donald’s problem isn’t a lack of enemies. It’s his stubborn insistence on creating the conditions for his own defeat.

And this time, no consigliere will be able to make voters an offer they can’t refuse.

text:
States routinely compete with large packages of tax abatements, grants, infrastructure funding, job-creation credits, and (less often) tailored regulatory adjustments to attract major investments.

Concrete examples from other states

•  Nevada – Tesla Gigafactory: The original 2014 package was roughly $1.3 billion in sales, property, and payroll tax abatements plus transferable tax credits (tied to investment and jobs). A 2023 expansion for additional battery production and the Semi added about $330 million more in abatements. 

•  Ohio – Intel fabs: Ohio and local partners offered roughly $2.1 billion (cash grants, infrastructure including water/roads, 30-year job-creation tax credits, and property-tax abatements) for Intel’s New Albany project, initially announced at ~$20 billion and later scaled higher. This was on top of federal CHIPS Act funding. 

•  Arizona – TSMC (and Intel): Arizona has attracted tens of billions in semiconductor investment (TSMC’s multi-fab Phoenix campus alone is in the $65 billion+ range, with later expansions reported far higher). 

State support has included property-tax reductions, infrastructure, and workforce programs, layered on federal CHIPS Act awards (e.g., up to $6.6 billion direct funding for TSMC). 

•  Amazon HQ2: New York offered a package in the $1.7–3 billion range (tax credits and grants); Amazon ultimately withdrew amid local opposition. 

Virginia’s deal centered on performance-based workforce grants (around $22,000 per qualifying high-wage job), with potential totals in the hundreds of millions tied to job creation. 

•  Other patterns: Oregon has provided Intel with well over $1 billion in property-tax abatements over many years via its Strategic Investment Program. Dozens of states (around 38) offer dedicated sales- and property-tax exemptions for data centers. 

Wisconsin’s original Foxconn package was initially framed around nearly $3 billion in credits (later renegotiated sharply downward after job and investment shortfalls).

In short, the tax, grant, and abatement side of the Texas packages is standard interstate competition for large private investment.

text:
When Paul Merson joined Walsall in the summer of 2003, he had just helped Portsmouth win promotion to the Premier League and was hoping to finish his career closer to his family in the Midlands.

His debut could hardly have gone any better, scoring twice in a 4-1 win over West Brom that sent Walsall to the top of the First Division. The following morning one newspaper had a headline waiting for him: “The Messiah Is Back!”

But away from football Merson’s life was falling apart. His wife Louise had left him after years of problems with gambling, and in an attempt to cope with it he had put £60,000 on a bet. It lost. “I checked my bank account the next day and I could see I was rapidly throwing away every last penny I’d earned with Villa and Pompey. It was me that needed the saviour, not Walsall.”

By February 2004 his second marriage was over, his children had moved out and he was living alone in a small flat near Walsall’s Bescot Stadium. And there was another problem. Merson had turned 35. “At 35 professional footballers can draw on their pension. Sure, they can leave it in there and watch the money go up and up and up until they’re 65, but some people want to take it all out in one lump.”

Merson had spent nearly twenty years earning that money through football, and his pension was worth £800,000. “I drew out all £800,000 of it in one hit and blew it in a couple of months. I went betting crazy.” He was putting £60,000 and £80,000 on individual bets, gambling on just about anything he could find.

Walsall didn’t even have their own training ground at the time, so the players would get changed at Bescot before travelling to a nearby school to use the pitches. Sometimes they had to wait for the schoolchildren to finish their hockey lessons. And while the rest of the team were waiting to train, Merson was on the phone to his bookmaker. “While I was sitting there, I’d ring up a bookie and bet £10,000 on something like who would be the first batsman out at Lord’s that day. I was that off my head.”

Eventually somebody got hold of his betting records. Merson went to the newsagent one Sunday morning, picked up the News of the World and found his face plastered across the back page. The newspaper had published a list of his bets, including the amounts he had been gambling. He immediately rang his bookmaker. “My God, what’s happened? I bet with you because of the confidentiality. I could get booted out of Walsall tomorrow because of this.”

The man on the other end apologised and explained that somebody had managed to get access to his account details. The company had already held a meeting about it and decided to offer Merson some compensation. “We’re going to give back what you lost last month.” Merson wanted to know how much that was. “Oh, it’s £90,000.” He accepted it straight away. “I was just happy to claw back some of my money I’d lost.”

But rather than using the money to get himself out of trouble, he carried on betting. “It meant I could gamble and gamble some more until every last penny had gone.” By that point the £800,000 pension he had spent his entire football career building up had disappeared. “I’d wasted my pension away to nothing. I’d lost my wife, kids, house and all my money.”

Merson eventually went to Walsall chairman Jeff Bonser and admitted he needed help. “We need to get you help, son.” The club arranged for him to meet the Professional Footballers’ Association, who found a treatment centre in Arizona that cost £20,000 a month. Merson didn’t even have £20 left, so Walsall agreed to lend him the money and recover it from his wages.

For a player who had won league titles with Arsenal, represented England at a World Cup and earned millions throughout his career, it was a desperate situation. Merson later put the scale of his gambling into perspective. “At that time in my life I’d blown around seven million quid with the bookies.”

text:
People will observe Remembrance Day today, share photographs, remember those they have lost, and offer prayers. But for me, this day carries a pain I cannot put into words.

Last year, on this very day, I lost someone who meant so much to me. My favourite aunty, Liliana, the woman who had loved me, supported me, and treated me like her own child, died in a ghastly road accident.

She had called me the previous evening to tell me she was planning to visit us. We spoke for almost twenty minutes, laughing about family matters and discussing what she wanted to cook when she arrived. Before ending the call, she promised to bring me something she knew I loved. I had no idea that would be our last conversation.

text:
Here’s a realistic early-November 2026 prediction for where each of MLB’s top free agents by position lands:

C – Ryan Jeffers → Yankees
Top offensive catcher available. Twins gave him the QO and he’s open to returning, but New York showed interest at the deadline and needs a bat behind the plate. Three-year deal in the $45-55M range.

1B – Jake Bauers → Brewers
NLCS MVP on the champs. Milwaukee tendered the QO; he either accepts it or takes a short multi-year deal to stay. Arizona is the main alternative if he hits the open market.

2B – Brandon Lowe → Giants
Power + improved defense (35 HR, Gold Glove finalist). Pirates want him back but the longer/more expensive deal he can get elsewhere makes San Francisco (need at second) the cleaner fit.

SS – Mauricio Dubón → Braves
Versatile Gold Glove utility who just had a strong year in Atlanta. Low-cost, high-value reunion makes the most sense.

3B – Teruaki Sato → Yankees
Japanese Triple Crown winner being posted. Young power bat with 3B/OF flexibility. New York has been linked and has the resources and need.

LF – Randy Arozarena → Phillies
Career-year 25-25 season in Seattle. Phillies need another impact bat in the outfield/lineup; he fits the profile of what they’ve chased before.

CF – Daulton Varsho → Pirates
Down year overall (.636 OPS) but still a strong defensive center fielder. Short-term, low-risk deal for a team that can use the glove and buy the bounce-back.

RF – Seiya Suzuki → Blue Jays
Consistent 25+ HR hitter with solid defense. Toronto needs power and a right-field solution; multiple reports have flagged them as a clean match.

DH – Joc Pederson → Rangers (or similar)

📣 PINELLAS COUNTY INVESTIGATION (3/3): THE DSA BOYCOTT AND POLITICAL NETWORK

The Pinellas County chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America announced a new campaign called Apartheid Free Pinellas in its November newsletter.

The campaign is organized by the chapter's International Solidarity Working Group, with its first meeting scheduled for November 11 at 6:30 p.m.

Organizers plan to approach local businesses and encourage them to stop stocking products included on Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) lists. Participating merchants would be encouraged to offer alternatives and display campaign materials identifying their involvement.

The chapter describes the campaign as a way for shoppers to avoid supporting what it calls Israel's genocide against Palestinians.

The campaign follows the national DSA's No Appetite for Apartheid initiative, launched in 2022, and the broader BDS movement's Apartheid Free Zones organizing model.

The BDS guide encourages recruiting businesses, obtaining public commitments, displaying campaign materials, and expanding participation into other institutions, including labor organizations, cultural organizations, and local government.

Pinellas DSA hasn't publicly identified participating merchants or released a list of local businesses it intends to approach. Political product boycotts and discrimination against people based on religion or national origin are legally different matters; the campaign's actual practices will determine whether additional civil rights questions arise.

THE DSA NETWORK IN LOCAL GOVERNMENT

Pinellas DSA's November newsletter celebrates the election of Lindsey Grove to St. Petersburg City Council District 6.

With Grove joining Richie Floyd, the chapter says two of the city's eight council seats are held by DSA members.

The same newsletter identifies Ashley Herrmann as a Tampa DSA member elected to Florida House District 69 and discusses Angie Nixon's U.S. Senate campaign.

The chapter also operates a Socialists in Office Working Group, which connects its organizing activities with members holding elected office.

Its October newsletter described Floyd bringing a discussion about Flock surveillance cameras before the St. Petersburg City Council, an issue DSA had been campaigning on.

The chapter's published activities identify these organizations, committees, and campaigns:

Tampa DSA
Pasco-Hernando DSA
St. Pete Tenants Union
Housing Working Group
International Solidarity Working Group
Electoral Committee
Ecosocialist Working Group
Socialists in Office Working Group
Steering Committee
Proposed Growth & Development Committee
Dump Duke
Public Power St. Pete

Its newsletter also describes organizing at Osprey Pointe Apartments, Reserve at Lake Pointe, and Enclave at Sabal Pointe, alongside campaigns involving property taxes, tenant organizing, surveillance cameras, and a publicly owned electric utility.

The chapter's published records show electoral, neighborhood, and regional organizing. They don't identify either the mosque application or Ordinance 26-1773A as DSA-sponsored initiatives.

UPCOMING DATES

November 11, 6:30 p.m. — First Apartheid Free Pinellas organizing meeting.
November 17, 6 p.m. — First county hearing on Ordinance 26-1773A.
November 25 — DSA's scheduled Socialists in Office Working Group meeting.
December 5 — Pinellas DSA chapter convention.
December 15, 6 p.m. — Second scheduled county hearing on Ordinance 26-1773A.

The November 17 county hearing is scheduled at 333 Chestnut Street, Palm Room, Clearwater, with Ordinance 26-1773A listed as agenda item 46.

Residents can ask commissioners which land-use applications would lose countywide hearings, how public notices would change, who could request additional review, and what options would remain for challenging decisions. They can also ask why several major planning changes were combined into one ordinance.

County planners estimate that 60% or more of countywide land-use hearings could disappear. Residents deserve to understand exactly what that means before the commissioners vote.

text:
AWACS emerged as an anchor for multi-domain operations during Marka e Haq and even back then.

When the US Air Force invaded Iraq, the outcome of the air war was largely determined before Iraqi forces could mount any meaningful resistance. Iraq lacked an effective AWACS capability, airborne surveillance aircraft and a properly integrated air defence network. USAF achieved air superiority so rapidly that the Iraqi Air Force had very little opportunity to demonstrate its capabilities or effectively challenge American air operations.

We witnessed a similar dynamic during the 2019 India-Pakistan aerial confrontation. Pakistan reportedly shot down 2 Indian Air Force aircraft (MiG-21 Bison and Su-30MK), while 9 Indian aircraft were reportedly tracked or locked by Pakistani F-16 and JF-17 fighters. An important factor was the Pakistan Air Force's Saab 2000 Erieye AWACS, which provided airborne surveillance, situational awareness and data-sharing capabilities, allowing Pakistani fighters to receive information beyond the detection range of their own onboard systems and missile seekers.

A similar, but much larger, role was attributed to airborne early-warning and control aircraft during the 2025 Indo-Pak military skirmishes. Pakistan claimed 8 aerial kills, and the reported outcome was not attributed solely to the PL-15 BVR missiles or the J-10C fighters. The Saab 2000 Erieye AWACS reportedly played an important supporting role by providing a broader operational picture.

China is also advancing its airborne early-warning capabilities, with its emerging KJ-3000 programme, based on the Y-20 transport aircraft, representing an important development. It is expected to provide China with significantly enhanced long-range airborne surveillance, command-and-control and battlespace management capabilities. If its anticipated capabilities are realised, it could become one of the most advanced AWACS platforms in the world.

China's next-generation airborne early warning and control aircraft, the KJ-3000, is based on the upgraded Y-20B strategic transport platform. Powered by four indigenous WS-20 high-bypass turbofan engines, it offers improved efficiency, longer range and higher payload.

KJ-3000 introduces the first digital radar architecture with advanced data links, passive target identification, and sophisticated anti-jamming features. Its rotating AESA dome on the Y-20B airframe delivers true 360° coverage and high-energy detection of stealth targets beyond 360 km.

text:
Washington State 

SEPARATIST STATE

‘The blue wave isn’t applicable to trans people’: advocates in Washington State prepare to fight ban

Legal challenge against ballot initiative that bans transgender girls’ participation in girls’ school sports is poised to set off a battle over rights

By Adam Willems in Seattle
Nov. 8, 2026

A coalition of advocacy groups are preparing to mount a legal challenge against a Washington State ballot initiative that bans transgender girls’ participation in girls’ school sports, which voters approved in last week’s midterm election and will go into effect next month.

The challenge is poised to set off a protracted legal battle over the rights of trans youth in Washington, which has functioned as a safe haven for thousands of trans people fleeing states that have enacted anti-trans laws in recent years.

If enforced, the ballot measure, Initiative 638, would be “the most extreme” trans sports ban of its kind, according to its opponents. The initiative’s official text says it would require all girls participating in school sports to “verify biological sex”, which could include confirming their “reproductive anatomy”. Opponents say that language potentially subjects tens of thousands of girls to invasive genital exams in order to participate in girls’ school sports.

“There are parents that are going to be asking, ‘Is my kid going to have to have a choice of dropping their pants in front of a complete stranger or missing the track season?’ We don’t know the answer right now,” said Lexi Koren, a spokesperson for No Hate in Washington State, the campaign against I-638.

Advocates say the state’s courts represent the likeliest path forward for any litigation, given relevant legal precedent, as well as strong state-level privacy and anti-discrimination statutes.

The initiative was put forth by Let’s Go Washington, a conservative political group that has backed 20 ballot proposals since its founding in 2022. Washingtonians voted against the group’s two other initiatives on the ballot this year, including an effort to repeal the state’s new income tax on high earners, and Initiative 001, which would have forced schools to share sensitive student records with parents. Initiative 638 holds a double-digit lead in its favor – approximating the Democrats’ projected national popular vote margin during the midterms.

“I don’t think, unfortunately, that the blue wave is really applicable to trans people,” said Danni Askini, executive director of Gender Justice League, a trans advocacy group based in Washington State.

According to a source familiar with the impending legal challenge, the coalition spearheading the lawsuit includes local and national groups, including the ACLU of Washington, Planned Parenthood, and No Hate in Washington State. The lawsuit would be filed before 3 December, when the initiative’s enforcement will go into effect. The source added that, while I-638’s forcing girls, and not boys, to verify their sex might violate federal legal precedent, the US supreme court is a less likely venue for the advocates’ lawsuit, in part given some of the court’s past rulings on trans rights.

Washington State case law suggests courts may strike down measures tying participation in school sports to potentially privacy-violating policies. In 2008, the Washington State supreme court ruled against a school district’s random drug tests of student athletes, affirming that the state’s constitution offers privacy protections beyond those guaranteed by the federal constitution.

Story continues in comments.

text:
Natalee Holloway's killer asked her mother for $250,000 to reveal where the body was.

Beth paid $25,000 up front. He pointed at a house that wasn't there when her daughter vanished.

Netflix's new docuseries on the case just aired the FBI tape of that handoff.

Joran van der Sloot was the last person seen with the Alabama teen in Aruba in 2005. Police arrested him more than once and released him for lack of evidence.

In March 2010 he emailed the offer to the family's lawyer, John Q. Kelly, who brought in the FBI.

On May 10, 2010, the two met in an Aruba hotel room while agents secretly recorded. The lawyer later explained the setup:

"I had to pretend like I thought this was a binding agreement. I knew she wasn't going to pay him another $225,000."

Kelly counted out $10,000 in cash. Then $15,000 more went by wire to a Dutch bank account. Joran led the lawyer to a lot and claimed the body was in the foundation of a house there. Within a week, an email from him in Peru admitted the whole thing was a lie.

Joran later told a Dutch newspaper the scam was payback, because the family had made his life hard. When the offer of money came, he thought why not.

The cash had come from Beth. NBC reported it probably paid for the trip to Peru, where he went to play in a poker tournament. In Lima he killed Stephany Flores, a 21-year-old student, on the fifth anniversary of Natalee's disappearance.

He got 28 years there for that murder, while in the US the only charge in the Holloway case was still the $25,000. In 2023 he was extradited to Alabama and pleaded guilty to extortion and wire fraud.

Under the plea deal, he had to tell everything. Joran confessed to killing Natalee on a beach and pushing the body into the sea. Still, the 20-year sentence was for the extortion, served alongside the Peru term rather than after it.

After the hearing, Beth called the case solved. She had waited since 2005 for that confession.

The killing happened in Aruba, out of reach of a US court. He has never been charged with Natalee's murder, and her body is still missing.

The only crime he was ever sentenced for in this case is taking a grieving mother's $25,000.

Did Beth Holloway get justice, or did the killer get off with an extortion charge?

text:
🚨 NEARLY 32,000 MARYLAND SENIORS FACE MEDICARE PLAN DISRUPTIONS — AETNA PULLS OUT AS INSURERS CUT COVERAGE OPTIONS

Thousands of Maryland seniors are being forced to reconsider their healthcare coverage as major insurers eliminate Medicare Advantage plans for 2027.

An analysis of federal Medicare data estimates that 31,835 Maryland enrollees — approximately 15% of the state’s Medicare Advantage population — are in plans that won’t be offered in their counties next year.

That’s higher than the national rate of 10.6%.

▪️ AETNA: Exiting Maryland’s Medicare Advantage market entirely.

▪️ HUMANA: More than 20,700 Maryland enrollees affected by discontinued plans or geographic restrictions.

▪️ FREDERICK COUNTY: Approximately 31% of Medicare Advantage enrollees face plan changes.

▪️ CARROLL COUNTY: Nearly 59% face disruption, among the highest rates in Maryland.

▪️ OUT-OF-POCKET COSTS: Maryland insurance regulators warn that many continuing plans are increasing patient cost-sharing.

These cancellations don’t mean seniors are losing Medicare eligibility. But they may have to change insurers, doctors, prescriptions or coverage arrangements.

And the clock is ticking.

Medicare open enrollment ends December 7, with changes taking effect January 1.

text:
Dominion contractor who worked the long overnight shift in Detroit and described vans of ballots, boxes coming in through the back, and large stacks appearing right before the shift change. She put those details under oath, including the instruction to go to the TCF Center instead of the regular elections building and the timing of the deliveries. When that kind of firsthand account is on the record and the response is still that nothing irregular ever happens, it leaves the gap between the testimony and the public dismissal feeling wider than it should.

That same gap shows up when people look at the numbers coming out of places like Texas, California, Michigan, Minnesota, and New York this cycle. Turnout and registration figures in some of those states have produced swings that don’t line up cleanly with prior patterns or with the rest of the country, and the explanations offered so far stay general. I keep coming back to how often the same process—late additions, contested instructions, or large batches arriving late—gets described in different cities and then treated as routine once the totals are certified. Whether any of it rises to the level of the 2020 claims is still an open question, but the pattern of dismissing the accounts before the records are fully compared makes it harder to close the discussion on the numbers alone.

text:
Not my post, but I'm behind it 100%

I appreciate Indians and other immigrants who come to the United States, build honest livelihoods, and become productive members of society. Immigration has always been part of America's story. However, what concerns me is the growing concentration of one immigrant community across political institutions, corporate leadership, technology, and real estate markets in Western countries, particularly the United States and Canada.  Look at Canada, where the Foreign Minister is of Indian origin. In the United States, Indian-origin individuals have become mayors in cities such as Los Angeles, San Jose, Edison, and Charlotte. There are also Indian-origin city council members, legislators, and members of Congress. This raises legitimate questions about the scale and long-term implications of immigration.  Consider the immigration pipeline. Almost every major American corporation has engineering or corporate operations in India. Companies recruit substantial workforces there and transfer employees to the United States through L-1 visas, with many eventually transitioning to H-1B visas and permanent residency. Add their spouses, children, and subsequent family-sponsored immigration, and the numbers accumulate over generations. Even if family sponsorship takes 10–15 years, the pipeline remains continuous.  Then consider Canada, which has historically offered relatively accessible immigration and citizenship pathways. Many Indian-origin Canadian citizens subsequently move to the United States through TN visas, adding another dimension to this migration pipeline.  There is also a growing concern about professional networks and hiring practices. In some companies, Indian-origin individuals occupy multiple levels of the hiring process, from recruiters and HR personnel to hiring managers and senior leadership. When professional networks become concentrated within one community, legitimate questions arise about whether opportunities remain equally accessible to people outside those networks.  Beyond employment, there are concerns about competition for housing, rising real estate prices, and the growing influence of concentrated economic and political networks. Immigration should create opportunities, not contribute to a system where existing residents feel increasingly displaced.  What is particularly frustrating is that neither Republicans nor Democrats seem willing to have an honest discussion about these issues. Are political leaders overlooking the consequences? Are corporations exercising disproportionate influence over immigration policy because they benefit from global labor pipelines? Whatever the explanation, these questions deserve serious scrutiny.  I appreciate Indian immigrants who contribute positively to society. But appreciating immigrants and questioning immigration policy are not mutually exclusive. Governments have a responsibility to protect fair access to employment, housing, and economic opportunities for everyone.  If these trends continue unchecked over the next 10–20 years, we could see even greater concentration of corporate leadership, political representation, economic influence, and expensive real estate ownership within particular immigrant communities. The question is not whether immigrants should succeed. They absolutely should. The question is whether immigration policy is being managed fairly and in the long-term interests of the entire population.

text:
Life of Willibrord, by Alucin, c.796
.
1. There was in the island of Britain, in the province of Northumbria, a certain householder of Saxon descent, whose name was Wilgils, living a devout Christian life together with his wife and family. This fact was later borne out by miraculous events, for after he had given up his worldly career he devoted himself to the monastic life. Not long afterwards, as his zeal for the spiritual life increased, he entered with even more intense fervour on the austere life of a solitary, dwelling in the headlands that are bounded by the North Sea and the river Humber. In a little chapel there, dedicated to Saint Andrew, the Apostle of Christ, he served God for many years in fasting, prayer and watching, with the result that he became celebrated for his miracles, and his name was in everyone’s mouth. People flocked to him in great numbers, and when they did so he never failed to instruct them with sound advice and the Word of God.
.
He was held in such high esteem by the king and the nobles of that nation that they made over to him, in perpetual gift, a number of small landed properties that lie near those headlands for the purpose of building there a church to God. In this church the reverend father gathered together a rather small but devout company of those who wished to see God, and there also, after the many trials of his spiritual labours, going to his reward, his body lies at rest. His successors, who still follow the example of his holiness, are in possession of this church to the present day. It is I, the least of these in merit and the last in time, who am now in charge of this little chapel, which has come to me by lawful succession, and I am writing this account of Willibrord, the holiest of fathers and the wisest of teachers, at the request of you, Bishop Beornrade,[l. Beornrade, abbot of Willibrord’s monastery at Echternach and later Archbishop of Sens.] who, by the grace of God, have succeeded him in the episcopate, in the line of family tradition and in the care of those sanctuaries, which, as we know, he built for the glory of God.
.
2. Now, in order to relate more fully the facts concerning Willibrord’s birth, and recall the signs which show that even whilst he was in his mother’s womb he was chosen by God, I shall return to the point where I began. Just as the most holy fore-runner of our Lord Jesus Christ, blessed John the Baptist, was sanctified in his mother’s womb and preceded Christ, as the morning star precedes the sun and, as the Gospel tells us, was born of devout parents in order to bring salvation to many, so likewise Willibrord, begotten for the salvation of many, was born of devout parents. Wilgils, the venerable man of whom we have already spoken, entered upon the state of matrimony for the sole purpose of bringing into the world a child who should benefit many peoples. Thus it was that his wife, mother of holy Willibrord, beheld, at dead of night whilst she slept, a heavenly vision. It seemed to her as if she saw in the sky the new moon, which, as she watched, slowly increased until it reached the size of the full moon. Whilst she was gazing intently upon it, it fell swiftly into her mouth, and when she had swallowed it her bosom was suffused with light. Filled with fear, she awoke at once and went to recount the dream to a holy priest, who asked her whether during the night on which the vision came to her she had known her husband in the customary way. When she assented, he replied as follows: ” The moon which you saw changing from small to great is the son whom you conceived on that night. He will disperse the murky darkness of error with the light of truth, and wherever he goes he will carry with him a heavenly splendour and display the full moon of his perfection. By the brightness of his fame and the beauty of his life he will attract to himself the eyes of multitudes.” This interpretation of the dream was borne out by the actual course of events.
.
3. When her time was come the woman bore a son, and at his baptism his father gave him the name of Willibrord. As soon as [5] the child had reached the age of reason his father gave him to the church at Ripon to be instructed by the brethren there in religious pursuits and sacred learning, so that living in a place where he could see nothing but what was virtuous and hear nothing but what was holy his tender age should be strengthened by sound training and discipline. From his earliest years divine grace enabled him to grow in intelligence and in strength of character, at least as far as was possible at such an age, so that it seemed as if in our day there had been born another Samuel, of whom it was said: ” The boy grew up and advanced in favour both with God and with men.”
.
4. When this youth, as highly endowed with sacred learning as he was with self­-control and integrity, reached the twentieth year of his age he felt an urge to pursue a more rigorous mode of life and was stirred with a desire to travel abroad. And because he had heard that schools and learning flourished in Ireland, he was encouraged further by what he was told of the manner of life adopted there by certain holy men, particularly by the blessed bishop Ecgbert, to whom was given the title of Saint, and by Wichtberct, the venerable servant and priest of God, both of whom, for love of Christ, forsook home, fatherland and family and retired to Ireland, where, cut off from the world though close to God, they lived as solitaries enjoying the blessings of heavenly contemplation. The blessed youth wished to imitate the godly life of these men and, after obtaining the consent of his abbot and brethren, hastened quickly across the sea to join the intimate circle of the said fathers, so that by contact with them he might attain the same degree of holiness and possess the same virtues, much as a bee sucks honey from the flowers and stores it up in its honeycomb. There among these masters, eminent both for sanctity and sacred learning, he who was one day to preach to many peoples was trained for twelve years, until he reached the mature age of manhood and the full age of Christ.
.
5. Accordingly, in the thirty-­third year of his age the fervour of his faith had reached such an intensity that he considered it of little value to labour at his own sanctification unless he could preach the Gospel to others and bring some benefit to them. He had heard that in the northern regions of the world the harvest was great but the labourers few. Thus it was that, in fulfillment of the dream which his mother stated she had seen, Willibrord, fully aware of his own purpose but ignorant as yet of divine pre-ordination, decided to sail for those parts and, if God so willed, to bring the light of the Gospel message to those people who through unbelief had not been stirred by its warmth. So he embarked on a ship, taking with him eleven others who shared his enthusiasm for the faith. Some of these afterwards gained the martyr’s crown through their constancy in preaching the Gospel, others were later to become bishops and, after their labours in the holy work of preaching, have since gone to their rest in peace.
.
So the man of God, accompanied by his brethren, as we have already said, set sail, and after a successful crossing they moored their ships at the mouth of the Rhine. Then, after they had taken some refreshment, they set out for the Castle of Utrecht, which lies on the bank of the river, where some years afterwards, when by divine favour the faith had increased, Willibrord placed the seat of his bishopric.6 But as the Frisian people, among whom the fort was situated, and Radbod, their king, still defiled themselves by pagan practices, the man of God thought it wiser to set out for Francia and visit Pippin, the king of that country, a man of immense energy, successful in war and of high moral character. The duke received him with every mark of respect; and as he was unwilling that he and his people should lose the services of so eminent a scholar, he made over to him certain localities within the boundaries of his own realm, where he could uproot idolatrous practices, teach the newly converted people and so fulfill the command of the prophet: “Drive a new furrow and sow no longer among the briars.” [Jeremiah 4:3]
.
6. After the man of God had systematically visited several localities and carried out the task of evangelization, and when the seed of life watered by the dews of heavenly grace had, through his preaching, borne abundant fruit in many hearts, the aforesaid King of the Franks, highly pleased at Willibrord’s burning zeal and the extraordinary growth of the Christian faith, and having in view the still greater propagation of religion, thought it wise to send him to Rome in order that he might be consecrated bishop by Pope Sergius, one of the holiest men of that time. Thus, after receiving the apostolic blessing and mandate and being filled with greater confidence as the Pope’s emissary, he would return to Preach the Gospel with even greater vigour, according to the words of the Apostle: ” How shall they preach unless they sent?” [Romans 10:15]
But when the king tried to persuade the man of God to do this he was met by a refusal. Willibrord said that he was not worthy to wield such great authority, and, after enumerating the qualities which Saint Paul mentioned to Timothy, his spiritual son, as being essential for a bishop, asserted that he fell far short of such virtues On his side, the king solemnly urged what the man of God had already humbly declined. At length, moved by the unanimous agreement of his companions, and, what is of more importance, constrained by the divine will, Willibrord acquiesced, anxious to submit to the counsel of many rather than obstinately to follow his own will. Accordingly he set out for Rome with a distinguished company, bearing gifts appropriate to the dignity of the Pope.
.
7. Four days before Willibrord arrived in Rome the Apostolic Father had a dream in which he was advised by an angel to receive him with the highest honours, because he had been chosen by God to bring the light of the Gospel to many souls: his purpose in coming to Rome was to receive the dignity of the episcopate, and nothing that he asked for was to be refused. The Apostolic Father, forewarned by this admonition, received him with great joy and showed him every courtesy. And as he discerned in him ardent faith, religious devotion and profound wisdom, he appointed a day suitable for his consecration, when all the people would be assembled together. Then he invited venerable priests to take part in the ceremony, and, in accordance with apostolic tradition and with great solemnity, he publicly consecrated him archbishop in the church of blessed Peter, Prince of the Apostles. At the same time, he called him Clement and invested him with episcopal robes, conferring upon him the sacred pallium as a sign of his office, like Aaron with the ephod. Moreover, whatever he desired or asked for in the way of relics of saints or liturgical vessels the Pope gave him without hesitation, and so, fortified with the apostolic blessing and loaded with gifts, he was sent back, duly instructed, to his work of preaching the Gospel.
.
8. Having received the blessing of the Holy See, the devoted preacher of God’s Word returned with increased confidence to the King of the Franks. The king welcomed him with every mark of esteem and then despatched him, armed with his authority to preach the Gospel, more especially in the northern parts of his dominions, where, owing to the scarcity of teachers and the obduracy of the inhabitants, the light of faith shone less brightly. The more clearly the man of God saw the need of overcoming the ignorance and arresting the spiritual famine in these districts, the more vigorously he preached the Word of God. How great was the success which, through the help of divine grace, attended his labours is attested even in these days by the people whom in the cities, villages, and fortified towns he brought to a knowledge of the truth and the worship of almighty God by his holy admonitions. Other evidence is to be found in the churches which he built in each place and in the communities of monks and nuns whom he gathered together in various localities.
.
9. The man of God tried also to propagate the Gospel teaching outside the boundaries of the Frankish kingdom. He had the boldness to present himself at the court of Radbod, at that time King of the Frisians and like his subjects, a pagan. Wherever he travelled he proclaimed the Word of God without fear; but though the Frisian king received the man of God in a kind and humble spirit, his heart was hardened against the Word of Life. So when the man of God saw that his efforts were of no avail he turned his missionary course towards the fierce tribes of the Danes. At that time, so we are told, the Danish ruler was Ongendus,[Ongendus has been identified with Ongentheow of Beowulf.] a man more savage than any wild beast and harder than stone, who nevertheless, through divine intervention, received tbe herald of truth with every mark of honour. But when the latter found that the people were steeped in evil practices, abandoned to idolatry and indifferent to any hope of a better life, he chose thirty boys from among them and hastily returned with them to the chosen people of the Franks. On the journey he instructed the youths in the faith and baptized them, so that if they perished from the long sea voyage or through the ambushes of the savage dwellers of those parts he should suffer no loss in their regard. In this way he desired to anticipate the aaft of the devil and to strengthen these redeemed souls by the sacraments of the Lord.
.
10. Now whilst this energetic preacher of the Word was pursuing his journey he came to a certain island on the boundary between the Frisians and the Danes, which the people of those parts call Fositeland,[Fositeland or Heligoland.] after a god named Fosite, whom they worship and whose temples stood there. This place was held by the pagans in such great awe that none of the natives would venture to meddle with any of the cattle that fed there nor with anything else, nor dare they draw water from the spring that bubbled up there except in complete silence. On this island the man of God was driven ashore by a storm and waited for some days until the gale died down and fair weather made it possible to set sail again. He set little store by the superstitious sacredness ascribed to the spot, or by the savage cruelty of the king, who was accustomed to condemn violators of the sacred objects to the most cruel death. Willibrord baptized three persons in the fountain in the name of the Blessed Trinity and gave orders that some of the cattle should be slaughtered as food for his company. When the pagans saw this they expected that the strangers would become mad or be struck with sudden death. Noticing, however, that they suffered no harm, the pagans, terror­-stricken and astounded, reported to the king what they had witnessed.
.
11. The king was roused to intense fury and had a mind to avenge on the priest of the living God the insults which had been offered to his deities. For three whole days he cast lots three times every day to find out who should die; but as the true God protected his own servants, the lots of death never fell upon Willibrord nor upon any of his company, except in the case of one of the party, who thus won the martyr’s crown. The holy man was then summoned before the king and severely upbraided for having violated the king’s sanctuary and offered insult to his god. With unruffled calmness the preacher of the Gospel replied: “The object of your worship, O King, is not a god but a devil, and he holds you ensnared in rank falsehood in order that he may deliver your soul to eternal fire. For there is no God but one, who created heaven and earth, the seas and all that is in them; and those who worship Him in true faith will possess eternal life. As His servant I call upon you this day to renounce the empty and inveterate errors to which your forebears have given their assent and to believe in the one almighty God, our Lord Jesus Christ. Be baptized in the fountain of life and wash away all your sins, so that, forsaking all wickedness and unrighteousness, you may henceforth live as a new man in temperance, justice and holiness. If you do this you will enjoy everlasting glory with God and His saints; but if you spurn me, who set before you the way of life, be assured that with the devil whom you obey you will suffer unending punishment and the flames of hell.” At this the king was astonished and replied: “It is clear to me that my threats leave you unmoved and that your words are as uncompromising as your deeds.” But although he would not believe the preaching of the truth, he sent back Willibrord with all honour to Pippin, King of the Franks.
.
12. The latter was delighted at his return and begged him to persevere in his divinely appointed task of preaching the Word of God and to root out idolatrous practices and sow the good seed in one place after another. This the devoted preacher strove to carry out with characteristic energy. He traversed every part of the country, exhorting the people in cities, villages and forts where he had previously preached the Gospel to remain loyal to the faith and to their good resolutions. And as the number of the faithful increased day by day and a considerable multitude of believers came to the knowledge of God’s Word, many began in their zeal for the faith to make over to the man of God their hereditary properties. These he accepted. Shortly afterwards he ordered churches to be built there, and he appointed priests and deacons to serve them, so that the new converts should have places where they could assemble on feast days and listen to wholesome instruction and where they could learn the principles of the Christian religion from those servants of God who had baptized them. Thus the man of God, favoured by divine grace, made increasing progress from day to day.
.
13. It came about, however, that Pippin, King ofthe Franks, died,[Pippin died 14 December 714. At this juncture Radbod revolted, and during the disturbances that followed Willibrord retired to his monastery at Echternach.] and his son Charles became head of the realm. Charles brought many nations under the power of the Franks, and among these were the Frisians, whose lands were added to his dominions after the defeat of Radbod. At that time Saint Willibrord was officially appointed to preach to the Frisian people, and his episcopal see was fixed at the fortress of Utrecht. Being given greater scope for the preaching of the Gospel, he now attempted to bring into the Church by baptism the people that had recently been won by the sword. He allowed no error or past ignorance to pass unnoticed and lost no time in shedding upon them the light of the Gospel, so that soon among that people the statement of the prophet was fulfilled: “In that place where it was said unto them, Ye are not my people, it shall be said unto them, Ye are the sons of the living God.” [Hos 1:10]
.
14. Many miracles were also wrought by dinne power through His servant. Whilst the ministry of preaching the Gospel is to be preferred to the working of mirades and the showing of signs, yet, because such miracles are recorded as having been performed, I think mention of them ought not to be suppressed; and so that glory may be given to God who vouchsafed them, I will insert them into this narrative, and in this way what we know to have been achieved in former times may not be lost to future ages. Thus, when the venerable man, according to his custom, was on one of his missionary journeys he came to a village called Walichrum, where an idol of the ancient superstition remained. When the man of God, moved by zeal, smashed it to pieces before the eyes of the custodian, the latter, seething with anger, in a sudden fit of passion struck the priest of Christ on the head with a sword, as if to avenge the insult paid to his god. But, as God was protecting His servant, the murderous blow did him no harm. On seeing this, Willibrord’s companions rushed forward to kill the wicked man for his audacity. The man of God good-naturedly delivered the culprit from their hands and allowed him to go free. The same day, however, he was seized and possessed by the devil and three days later he ended his wretched life in misery. And thus, because the man of God followed the Lord’s command and was unwilling to avenge the wrongs done to him, he was vindicated all the more by the Lord Himself, just as He had said regarding the wrongs which the wicked inflicted upon His saints: “Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.”
.
15. On another occasion, when the blessed man was on his way to a cell belonging to him called Susteren, from the name of the stream that flows past it, he took a narrow path running through the cornfields of a certain wealthy landowner. When the keeper of the fields saw this he was furious and began to revile the man of God. Those who accompanied him [Willibrord] wanted to punish the man for insulting him, but the servant of God mildly restrained them, not wishing that anyone should perish on his account, since his whole happiness lay in bringing salvation to all. When he found it impossible to calm the fury of the foolish man, Willibrord did not persist but returned by the way he had come. Next day, however, the wretch who had not feared to heap insults upon the servant of God was struck down on that very spot with sudden death before a crowd of onlookers.
.
16. Whilst the divinely inspired man in his urgent desire to preach the Gospel was travelling through the coastal regions where the people were suffering from the lack of fresh water he noticed that his companions could hardly bear the pangs of thirst. So he called one of them and bade him dig a small trench inside his tent. There, upon his knees, he secretly prayed to God that He, who had brought forth water from the rock for his people whilst they were in the desert, would with like compassion bring forth water for his servants from the sandy soil. At once his prayer was heard and a spring of sweet water straightway filled the trench. His followers on seeing this gave thanks to God, who in this manner had glorified His saint and condescended to hear his prayer. And when they had drunk their fill they took with them as much water as they thought would satisfy their needs on the journey that lay before them.
.
17. Again, when the holy priest of God was pursuing his way in a certain place, he saw twelve poor beggars asking alms from the passers­-by. Being extremely kind­-hearted, he gazed on them with compassion and bade one of his companions take his own flask and give a drink to Christ’s poor. All the twelve drank from it as much as they would, and the remarkable fact was that as the company went on their way they found that the flask from which so many had drunk was just as full as it was before of the most excellent wine. When they discovered this they all blessed the Lord, saying: ” Indeed, the saying of Christ in the Gospels “Give and it shall be given unto you” [Luke 6:38] has been fulfilled.”
.
18. Once, the saintly man came to his monastery [at Echternach][The property for this foundation had been given to Willibrord in 714 by Plectrude, wife of Pippin II.] to make a visitation, and after praying to God, greeting the brethren and speaking peaceably with them, the holy father went round the cells of each one of the brothers to see if anything in them might be improved. On going into the store-­house, he found there only a small supply of wine in one cask, into which, as a sign of his blessing, he thrust his staff, praying the while, and then went out. The same night, the wine in the cask began to rise to the brim and then to over-fiow. When the steward noticed it he was astounded at the unexpected increase, and, knowing it to have been wrought by God’s mercy through the blessing of His servant, he did not dare to keep it secret. Next morning, he ran after the holy father and, falling at his feet, reported what he had seen. Willibrord, as usual, gave thanks to God, but, bearing in mind our Lord’s command to His disciples not to make public the glory of the Transfiguration before the day of the Resurrection he forbade the steward to speak to anyone of the miracle he had witnessed until the day of his [Willibrord’s] death...

text:
This week’s team of the weekend happens to not be a Chicagoland team! 

Congratulations to the Morris Warriors

In the most anticipated Class 4A matchup of the year the undefeated Morris Warriors walked out of it as clear winners.

Montini came in as b2b state champions looking for a three-peat, led by 5-star Miami commit Israel Abrams. Morris, sitting at a perfect record, had other plans. The Warriors controlled the game and pulled away for a 41-7 victory.

Junior quarterback Marion Persich (LaSalle-Peru transfer, Miami of Ohio offer) put on a Herculean effort. He accounted for over 300 all purpose yards and kept Morris moving all night. The win wasn’t just about one guy, though. 

Sophomore Mayson Munson returned a punt for a score, and late in the game Caden Medler picked off a pass and took it the distance to seal it for the Warriors.

Abrams was injured in the third quarter and taken off the field. Montini wideout Damacio Ortegon still finished with over 100 receiving yards (Saginaw Valley State commit), but the Broncos never got going after the early going.

What Now: 

Coach Alan Thorson has taken Morris to two state runner-up finishes before. This group looks like the one that could finally get over the hump. The Warriors are now averaging 47.5 PPG while allowing just 9.3 outscoring opponents by 38.3 points a night.

Next up: Morris hosts Sterling on Saturday (time TBD).

text:
IF I WERE YOU, holding an index fund, a pension or a few shares of the companies building artificial intelligence, I would look at one line in their cash flow statements before I looked at anything else: the line that used to say "repurchases of stock" and now says "proceeds from issuance". The direction of the money has reversed, and nobody sent you a letter.

Big Tech stopped buying its own shares. It started selling them to you. Here is the record, from the companies' own filings, and then the argument. The interpretation is mine and is labelled as such.

THE REVERSAL

For five years the most profitable company in America had one dependable habit. Every quarter, without exception, Alphabet bought back its own shares: about $14 billion a quarter on average, close to $300 billion between 2021 and 2025, more than any other company in the AI race. Thirty-three consecutive quarters, from the end of 2017 to the end of 2025.

First quarter of 2026: zero. Second quarter: zero. Third quarter: zero. The $70 billion authorisation the board approved in April 2025 is still there, $69.5 billion of it unused. Nothing stopped Alphabet from buying. It chose to sell.

On 1 June the company announced an $80 billion equity raise, upsized two days later to $84.75 billion: $20.5 billion of common stock sold to the public at around $355 a share, $10 billion placed privately with Berkshire Hathaway, $19 billion of mandatory convertible preferred paying 6.25%, and a $40 billion at-the-market programme to sell shares over time. The largest equity offering in history, in any industry, beating the $70 billion Petrobras raised in 2010. In the third quarter Alphabet sold a further $12.4 billion through the at-the-market programme and $28.7 billion of bonds. It spent $51.4 billion on property and equipment against $42.3 billion of operating cash flow. Free cash flow: minus $9.1 billion, for the second quarter in a row.

The thesis in one line. The buyback era financed shareholders with cash. The AI era finances capex with shareholders.

EVERYONE EXCEPT MICROSOFT

Alphabet is the cleanest case, not the only one.

Meta spent $44.5 billion on buybacks in 2021, $30.1 billion in 2024 and $26.2 billion in the first nine months of 2025. In the first nine months of 2026: nothing. Third-quarter capex, including finance-lease principal, was $34.9 billion against $32.8 billion of operating cash flow, a negative free cash flow quarter, which, to my knowledge, the company had not reported since its 2012 listing. The 2026 capex guide rose at every release: $115-135 billion in January, $125-145 billion in April, $130-145 billion in July, $135-145 billion in October, which implies $49 to $59 billion in the fourth quarter alone. On 26 October Meta sold $25 billion of common stock through forward sale agreements at $625 a share, five times oversubscribed, plus $12.5 billion of convertible preferred and $1.9 billion more when the underwriters exercised their option; a week later it was back in the bond market. From 19 January 2027 it will distribute a new class of non-voting shares, one for each existing share: a currency it can issue indefinitely without diluting its founder's control, and, according to the offering filing as summarised by TIKR, one it intends to sell to the tune of up to $60 billion from the first quarter of 2027, taking the programme to about $95 billion. Meta's own release lists its funding mix as operating cash flow, investment-grade debt, strategic partnerships and equity capital. Read the list in order.

Oracle bought back $36.6 billion of stock in fiscal 2019 and about $20 billion a year through 2021. In fiscal 2026: $206 million. Capex that year was $55.7 billion against $32 billion of operating cash flow. In February it announced a plan to raise $45 to $50 billion in 2026, half debt and half equity: a $25 billion bond, a $5 billion mandatory convertible at a 6.5% dividend, and a $20 billion at-the-market programme. The stated purpose of the equity: to keep an investment-grade rating while spending.

Amazon, which bought back $6 billion of stock in 2022 and nothing since, and pays no dividend, had little to stop. It borrowed: about $54 billion of bonds in March, after $15 billion in November 2025, and $115 billion of long-term debt over nine months. Third-quarter capex was $77.3 billion, nearly $20 billion above estimates, against $42.4 billion of operating cash flow. Trailing twelve-month free cash flow: minus $42.4 billion, from plus $14.8 billion a year earlier. The 2026 plan is $220 billion, raised from $200 billion in July, and the chief executive says 2027 will be meaningfully more.

Microsoft is the exception, and it is instructive. It still bought back $4.4 billion of stock in the September quarter and paid $6.8 billion in dividends while spending $39.4 billion on plant against $58 billion of operating cash flow. Free cash flow: $18.6 billion. Its CFO says the company stays free-cash-flow positive through fiscal 2027 with capex approaching $170 billion. It is also the only one of the five that has not yet termed out its capex in the long-dated bond market. Microsoft kept the old model because, so far, its cash still covers it. Even so, its buybacks fell from $32.7 billion in fiscal 2022 to $22.3 billion in fiscal 2026.

For a control group, look at Apple, which is not building data centres. Fiscal 2026 buybacks: $86.4 billion. Capex: $9 billion. Operating cash flow: $145 billion. Apple puts 6% of its operating cash into plant and 60% into its own shares. The AI builders have inverted the proportions.

FROM CASH TO DEBT TO EQUITY

The sequence matters, because it tells you where the constraint moved.

Until 2024 the build-out was financed from operating cash flow. The five hyperscalers issued an average of $28 billion of bonds a year between 2020 and 2024, according to Bank of America. In 2025: $121 billion. Oracle's $18 billion in September, Meta's $30 billion in October, the largest non-acquisition high-grade deal ever, Alphabet's $17.5 billion and Amazon's $15 billion in November. In 2026 the dollar issuance of Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, Oracle and SpaceX passed $180 billion by late October, by TwentyFour Asset Management's count, with Street estimates of $250 billion by year-end and about $400 billion once the wider technology and AI complex is included. Barclays expects total US investment-grade issuance of $2.46 trillion this year and names hyperscaler capex as the main upside risk to that number.

The debt is not only bigger; it is longer. Across 2025 and 2026, 41% of hyperscaler issuance carried maturities beyond 15 years, against 16% for the investment-grade index. Amazon sold dollar bonds due 2076. Alphabet sold a sterling bond due 2126, a century bond, alongside the largest corporate deal ever in Swiss francs and the largest Canadian corporate bond on record. These companies now make up about 4.5% of the US corporate bond index. The 30-year Treasury, at 5.25%, yields about 40 basis points more than at the start of the year, and the supply of 30-year corporate paper competing for the same pension and insurance money is one reason.

Then the constraint moved again. Bloomberg's credit desk reported that the bond market might not absorb all the hyperscalers' needs. Meta's bonds, rated AA-, trade in line with BBB issuers. Oracle's five-year credit default swaps tripled after its September 2025 deal, and in January a group of its bondholders sued, alleging the company had not disclosed how much more it would need to borrow. Keeping an investment-grade rating became the binding constraint, and the answer to that constraint is equity.

So the equity came. Oracle in February: $5 billion of mandatory convertible, $20 billion of at-the-market authority. Alphabet in June: $84.75 billion. SpaceX in June: a $75 billion initial public offering, $85.7 billion with the greenshoe, the largest in history, at $135 a share, followed eleven days later by a $25 billion bond that drew $89 billion of orders and priced about 0.4 percentage points wider than comparable BBB paper. Nvidia, awash in free cash flow, sold $25 billion of bonds the same month, its first in five years. Meta in October: $39.4 billion. OpenAI and Anthropic are preparing listings. The supply of AI equity coming to the public in 2027 will be measured in the hundreds of billions.

THE DEBT MATH

Alphabet's total debt passed $100 billion this year, several times what it carried five years ago; it raised more than $85 billion in twelve months across six currencies. At the 5.5% to 7% coupons now prevailing on long-dated hyperscaler paper, each $100 billion of debt costs $5.5 to $7 billion a year in interest, before the preferred dividends. That is affordable for companies earning $25 to $30 billion a quarter. It is also permanent in a way buybacks never were: a buyback can be paused in a bad quarter, as 2026 has proved; a coupon cannot. The order books are still deep, 3.6 to 4.6 times covered at the 30-year point for Oracle, Meta and Alphabet, better than the 3 times average for the investment-grade market. But a market that absorbs $250 billion this year is being asked, on the Street's own estimates, for more than that next year, when group capex passes $1 trillion. The equity raises of 2026 are what happens when a treasurer looks at that number and decides not to find out where the bond market's limit is.

THE TELL IN THE FOOTNOTES

Two details in the filings say more than the headlines.

First, Alphabet's third-quarter report states that the at-the-market programme is primarily intended to meet the tax obligations associated with employee equity grants. For years Alphabet paid those withholding taxes in cash and bought back enough stock to absorb the dilution from stock-based compensation, which ran at $8.6 billion in the third quarter alone. Now it sells new shares to pay the tax, and buys nothing back. The share count, which fell year after year for most of the past decade, is rising. The trend has not paused; it has inverted. Employees are still paid in stock. The cost of that stock has moved from the company's cash to the shareholder's ownership.

Second, the structure of the preferred. Alphabet's mandatory convertible pays 6.25%. Oracle's pays 6.5%. SpaceX's longest bonds yield 6.65%. Those are the coupons of high-yield debt, attached to instruments that convert into the common equity of companies rated AA. When the most creditworthy issuers on earth pay junk coupons for capital that turns into their own shares, the market is telling you how much capital they need and how fast.

WHO IS BUYING, AND AT WHAT PRICE

Alphabet sold common stock to the public at $355.20 on 3 June. The shares closed at $324.89 on 28 October, the day of its third-quarter results, and traded below $293 that evening after the capex figure and the negative free cash flow were digested. SpaceX priced at $135 and fell about 23% from its post-listing high within two weeks. Meta's forward sale was struck at $625; after its results on 21 October the stock had traded around $720. On 5 November, the day after the midterms, the chip and data-centre complex lost roughly $3 trillion of market value on fears that new Democratic governors in Texas, Ohio and Georgia would slow the construction of the very facilities this capital is meant to fund.

Who bought? Berkshire Hathaway took $10 billion of Alphabet, the anchor that made the rest of the book possible. Reports around Meta's sale said Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom, the companies to which Meta's capex is paid, were weighing up to $5 billion of the offering; if confirmed, that is suppliers funding their customer's purchases of their own products, the money loop I described in September, now running through the equity market. The rest was taken by the institutions that always take it: index funds, pension funds, sovereign funds, and through them every household with a retirement account.

That is the transfer this piece is about. In a buyback, the company uses its cash to buy from shareholders who want to leave; the remaining holders own a larger share of a smaller cash pile. In an issuance at the top of a capex cycle, the company sells to new shareholders who want to join; the existing holders own a smaller share of a larger capital base whose return is not yet known. Good or bad depends on one number: whether the return on the new capital exceeds the cost of the equity sold to raise it. A company selling stock at 25 times earnings to build assets that return 17% creates value. A company selling stock at 25 times earnings to build assets that return 6% transfers value from old holders to the build-out, and from the build-out to whoever sold it the chips.

Nobody knows that number yet, and the people selling the shares know that nobody knows it. That is not fraud. It is the definition of selling at the top: the moment when the price reflects the promise and the cash flow has not yet arrived to test it.

A WORKED EXAMPLE, FOR THE HOLDER

Take a company with 100 shares, $100 of earnings and a share price of $25, a multiple of 25 times. It sells 10 new shares at $25 and raises $250. If the $250 earns 17%, the company adds $42.50 of earnings; earnings per share rise from $1.00 to $1.30 and the old holder is better off, even though he owns 9% less of the company. If the $250 earns 6%, the company adds $15 of earnings; earnings per share fall from $1.00 to $1.05 before depreciation and below $1.00 after it, and the old holder has paid for someone else's data centre. The difference between the two cases is the return on the new capital, which nobody will know until the assets have been running for two or three years.

Now add the detail from Alphabet's filing. Suppose the company also pays its staff 2 shares a year and used to buy those 2 shares back with cash. If it stops buying and instead sells 1 more share to pay the tax on the grants, the old holder's dilution is 3 shares a year, not zero, on top of the 10 sold for capex. Over three years that is roughly a fifth of the company transferred to new holders and employees, in exchange for assets whose return is still a forecast.

WHAT THE RETURN LOOKS LIKE SO FAR

Precision, because this is not an argument that the demand is imaginary.

Alphabet's revenue grew 25% in the third quarter to $127.6 billion; Google Cloud's operating income tripled to $11.1 billion; its backlog stood at $467.6 billion at the end of the first quarter, nearly double the year-end figure. AWS grew 39%, the fastest in five years, with a $578 billion backlog. Azure grew 48%, with $678 billion of contracted cloud revenue, though 45% of that backlog in January was tied to one customer, OpenAI, which is still losing money. Oracle's remaining performance obligations reached $523 billion. TwentyFour's analysts note that with a 20-year average return on invested capital of 17.75%, funding at 5.5% to 7% clears the hurdle. The revenue is real. The contracts are real.

Three other things are real. First, capex guidance moved in one direction all year: Alphabet from $175-185 billion to $195-205 billion, Amazon from $200 to $220 billion, Meta from $125 to $140 billion at the midpoint, with 2027 expected to exceed $1 trillion for the group. The only cut, Microsoft's $190 to $175 billion, was an accounting change: it extended the assumed life of its data centres from 15 to 25 years, which lowers reported capex and spreads depreciation thinner. Second, committed spending that appears on no balance sheet yet is enormous: about $800 billion of leases signed but not commenced across the group by mid-year, $329 billion at Microsoft alone, with the lease payments typically servicing debt raised by the developers who build the sites. Third, the depreciation has barely started. Assets bought in 2026 hit the income statement in 2027 and 2028, and a 25-year life on a building does not change the four-to-six-year life of the servers inside it.

The honest summary: the revenue is proven, the return on the incremental dollar is not, and the capital to fund the gap is now raised from the public at prices set before the proof arrives.

THE ACCOUNTING OF A 25-YEAR LIFE

Microsoft's July decision to extend the assumed useful life of its data centres and office buildings from 15 to 25 years, effective at the start of fiscal 2027, cut its calendar-2026 reported capex guide from about $190 billion to about $175 billion without changing a single construction plan. The mechanism is lease accounting: longer lives, lower annual charges. The same change lowers depreciation in every future year. There is nothing improper in it; buildings do last. But the servers inside the buildings do not last 25 years, and the companies that have been quietly extending server lives since 2020 know it. When the reported cost of a build-out falls because of an assumption rather than a decision, the right response is not to adjust the model but to note that the model's inputs are now, in part, chosen by the people being modelled.

THE REVERSE OF PRIVATISATION

Six weeks ago I wrote about the privatisation of growth: companies financed and scaled in private markets, listing only after the growth has been captured by a closed circle of early investors. The AI build-out is the inverse. Growth is made public precisely when it costs cash, and the public is offered the bill rather than the harvest. SpaceX listed to fund an AI expansion that had produced no revenue; it raised $86 billion from the public and borrowed $25 billion eleven days later. Alphabet, Meta and Oracle, public for decades, reopened the primary market they had spent twenty years closing. The IPO pipeline of 2027 is not a list of companies that have finished growing. It is a list of companies that need to keep spending.

FIVE OBJECTIONS, ANSWERED

"Issuing equity at a high multiple is cheap capital; this is good capital allocation." It is cheap for the company and expensive for the holder if the return on the project falls short of the cost. The claim is only true after the fact, and the fact is three years away.

"Berkshire bought; that is the signal." Berkshire bought $10 billion at $351.81, a negotiated private placement, with an anchor's influence on terms. The public bought at $355.20 without it.

"These companies have $100 billion of cash each; they do not need the money." Alphabet had $126.8 billion at the end of the first quarter, Amazon $114.2 billion, Meta $82.5 billion. They raised anyway, because the cash covers one or two quarters of capex, not a multi-year plan, and because the rating agencies count gross debt.

"The depreciation life extension is standard." It may be. It is also a change that lowers this year's reported capex by $15 billion and next year's depreciation charge, made in the same quarter the market began to ask about returns.

"Capex is demand-driven; the backlogs prove it." They prove contracted revenue. They do not prove margin, and the largest single backlog, Microsoft's, was 45% one customer that loses money. A backlog is a promise from a buyer; capex is cash from the seller. The asymmetry is the whole question.

THE POLITICS ARRIVED THIS WEEK

One more variable entered the equation on 5 November. A day after Democrats won both chambers of Congress and governorships in Texas, Ohio and Georgia, the AI complex lost about $3 trillion of value in a session. Forty-one local ballot measures to slow data-centre construction were decided on 3 November and most passed. The new governor of Texas, where about 27% of planned data-centre capacity sits, campaigned on an immediate moratorium. Ohio's governor-elect has proposed a conditional moratorium unless data centres pay 100% of their grid costs. The capital raised in June and October was raised on the assumption that the facilities could be built on schedule and that the grid would be paid for by someone else. Both assumptions now have a constituency against them. The equity holders of 2026 bought a promise; the voters of 2026 just added a condition to it.

WHO CAPTURES, WHO PAYS

The sellers of the shares capture certainty: capital raised now, at today's multiple, with no covenant and no maturity. Suppliers capture the capex, in cash, this year. Founders with dual-class structures, and from January a third class, capture control without funding it. Bondholders holding 2076 and 2126 paper capture a coupon and a very long wait.

The public, which includes every index fund and every pension, pays the price of the promise and holds the residual claim on whether it is kept. Existing shareholders pay in ownership: at Alphabet, the dilution from stock-based pay that buybacks used to cancel is now theirs to keep. Employees, paid in the same shares, discover that their compensation is funded by shareholder dilution rather than company cash. The bond market pays in duration, carrying 50- and 100-year claims on assets with five-year lives.

WHAT I WOULD MONITOR

Alphabet's fourth-quarter report in late January: whether buybacks resume, and how much of the remaining $27.6 billion of at-the-market capacity is used. Buybacks alongside continued issuance would be the strangest signal of all.

Meta's Class C distribution on 19 January and what follows. A non-voting share class is built to be sold. The first sale will show the price at which control-free Meta equity clears.

The pace of Oracle's $20 billion at-the-market programme and the next rating action. Oracle has the least margin for error and the most explicit dependence on equity to keep its rating.

Free cash flow at Alphabet, Amazon and Meta in the fourth and first quarters, against the 2027 capex guides due in late January and February. If the three stay negative while guiding higher, the equity raises of 2026 will not be the last.

The spread between Meta's and Oracle's bonds and the BBB index, and the 30-year Treasury. Widening means the bond market is closing; narrowing gives the companies room to stop selling shares.

The pricing of the AI listings of 2027, OpenAI and Anthropic among them, against what SpaceX did after its debut. If the next IPOs price below their last private rounds, the public market has started to set the price of the promise itself.

Whether the data-centre moratoria proposed in Texas and Ohio become law before the 2027 capex guides are given. If they do, a financing question becomes a permitting question, and the equity raised in 2026 funds capacity that cannot be built on time.

The criterion of success is measurable: free cash flow positive at the three largest builders while they hold their capex guidance, and buybacks resumed without new issuance. On that day the reversal of 2026 was a bridge. Until then it is the new model, and the model is this: the company that once paid you to leave is now charging you to stay.

If I were you, I would not sell on that. I would stop pretending I had not been told.

This has also exposed the incompetence of international organizations and NGOs, including the United Nations, which have repeatedly failed to offer effective solutions.

I believe Rubio still has an opportunity to accomplish much more. He could help secure the international funding needed to rebuild Haiti and establish an international commission, with Bukele playing a leading role, to help Haitians develop a new political class free from criminal influence. He could also help accelerate the transition of power in Venezuela and finally bring an end to communism's influence in our hemisphere.

So, unlike Vance, I believe Rubio has a substantial record of accomplishments to show for his time in government, and, more importantly, the potential to achieve even greater things. That is the kind of leadership and political experience I would like to see in a Republican presidential candidate.
